* Shaykh: They became the opposite, yes. They became ﴿apes, despised﴾, and verses came censuring them. So the verses do not contradict one another, but there are things that cause the rulings of some verses to change, because the cause is absent.
* Another benefit of the verse: when Muslims conquer the lands of the disbelievers, they come to own them. From where do we take this?
* Student: ﴿and We will make them the inheritors﴾.
* Shaykh: From His words: ﴿and We will make them the inheritors﴾. And an inheritor owns what he inherits, right? The inheritor owns what he inherits. So God makes them fully inheritors. For this reason the scholars said: the lands become owned property.
* Another benefit of the verse: lands are not purely spoils of war. Here He said ﴿We will make them the inheritors﴾, although the Messenger ﷺ said: "Booty has been made lawful for me, and it was not made lawful for anyone before me" [Agreed upon; Al-Bukhari (335) and Muslim (521/3), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah]. Look now at this claim I am making. See whether it is correct or not.
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: I think it is not correct, because God made the Children of Israel inherit their land and their wealth, the land and wealth of the people of Pharaoh. God said in Surah Ash-Shu'ara: ...
* Student: ﴿Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 59].
* Shaykh: No, before it: ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs (57), and treasures and a noble station (58). Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 57-59]. There is no doubt that the treasures are spoils, and He says: ﴿We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾. So how do we answer the hadith?
The answer is that we say: these people did not inherit them through fighting. Spoils, as is well known, are what is taken through fighting the enemies. These people did not inherit them by fighting, but by the power of God, mighty and majestic, which they had no way to reach. On this basis, the statement of the Messenger ﷺ, "Booty has been made lawful for me, and it was not made lawful for anyone before me," is not contradicted.
* Student: The houses and lands that (...)?
* Shaykh: Houses and lands are treasures too.
* Student: So they fall under (...)?
* Shaykh: No, I said: the claim. Did I claim whether it is correct or not?
* Student: On (...).
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: Yes, lands have value, yes. Lands have value, yes.
* Student: Do they enter into the spoils?
* Shaykh: We said that spoils are movable things. Then we refuted this and said that the Children of Israel were given the lands and were given the treasures, and treasures are movable things, right?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: And we raised this objection against the statement of the Messenger ﷺ: "Booty has been made lawful for me, and it was not made lawful for anyone before me."
Suppose you say: lands are not among the spoils, but treasures are among the spoils. We answer this: the Children of Israel's possession of the land and treasures of the family of Pharaoh was without fighting, and the spoils that are owned are those obtained through fighting. This is what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "it was not made lawful for anyone before me."
* Student: Were there spoils, Shaykh, in earlier times?
* Shaykh: In what came before?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: There were spoils, but they were not lawful for the fighters.
* Student: And what was their status?
* Shaykh: Their status was that they were gathered, then fire would descend upon them from heaven and burn them. Furthermore, if there was some misappropriation (ghulul) in them, the fire did not descend. Glory be to God the Mighty! It would not descend, so that nothing would be lost. If something was lost, the fire would descend and burn them.
* Student: What is the wisdom in burning the spoils (...)?
* Shaykh: The wisdom is to cut off attachment to them completely, because if they remained, people would trade them, buy and sell them, benefit from them, and they would come to own them.
* Student: And this nation is the last of the nations.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: So if, for example, it were forbidden from the spoils, that would be better, because its faith is stronger.
* Shaykh: No, this is not correct, that is not the reason. But God, glorified and exalted, has supported this nation with things so that it may be assisted by them. There is no objection to a person who is more excellent being supported with things to reach virtue. Did not the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, have his past and future sins forgiven by God? Yet he still asks God's forgiveness. And we too are commanded to send blessings upon him, although God says: ﴿Indeed, God and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [Al-Ahzab 56]. Yes indeed. Reaching perfection does not require that a person abandon striving by means.
* Student: The Prophet gave a reason, Shaykh: he saw our weakness and inability, so he made them lawful for us.
* Shaykh: Yes, that is it. Even the Messenger said: "My provision has been placed under the shade of my spear" [Ahmad (5114), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar], in order to help us in this.
* Student: (...) the story of the one who found the misappropriation?
* Shaykh: But the problem is that Ibrahim says: how can they be made lawful for us while we are the best of nations? Why is the matter not left to our merits and virtues?
We say: this is from the blessing of God. It is from the completion of God's blessing that we reach the level of perfection, and these spoils are made lawful so that we may be assisted by them in (...).
* From the benefits of the noble verse: empowerment in the land, a person's establishment in the land, is one of God's blessings upon us, because of His words: ﴿and We will establish them in the land﴾ [Al-Qasas 6]. Right? Because this is among what God bestowed upon the Children of Israel, that He empowered them in the land. So a person being empowered in the land, whether this empowerment is through authority, the authority of a ruler, or through the authority of the Qur'an.
Note, O people, that empowerment in the land does not mean that a person rules over people so as to be a sultan over them. No, among empowerment in the land is that God empowers him so that his word becomes authoritative over the believers.
For example, Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah: was he empowered in the land or not? He was empowered in the land more greatly than the rulers of his time. The empowerment of the rulers of his time ended with their deaths, but God's empowerment of this man, so that his word remained respected among people up to now, is what is lasting. So although empowerment in the land may first come to mind as the empowerment of a ruler, we should say: empowerment of what? Of the Qur'an. In other words, whoever stands up for the truth, his word will have authority and strength. This is also supported by the hadith: "When God loves a servant, He places acceptance for him on earth" [Agreed upon; Al-Bukhari (3209) and Muslim (2637/157), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. That means he will have acceptance and his word will have effect. This is among the empowerment of God in the land.
* Another benefit of the verse: its circumstances are what we mentioned. But His words: ﴿and We will show Pharaoh﴾ [Al-Qasas 6] are among the examples of the power of God, mighty and majestic.
* From its benefits: Pharaoh and his people were wary of the Children of Israel, so God showed them what they were wary of. Here there is a difficulty: how did God show them what they were wary of, when they perished?
* Student: When drowning overtook him, he said: ﴿I believe that there is no god except the one in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am among the Muslims﴾ [Yunus 90].
* Shaykh: Did you mean ﴿and We will show Pharaoh﴾?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: ﴿and Haman and their soldiers, what they were wary of﴾ [Al-Qasas 6].
* Student: Their soldiers were with them. Those who drowned, all of them (...)
* Shaykh: Yes, but I say: whoever drowned did not know (...)
* Student: He knew. When they drowned, all of them (...), each person and each individual knew that the Children of Israel had (...)
* Shaykh: You mean at the moment his soul departed, for example?
* Student: At the last moment.
* Shaykh: Alright, at the last moment he knew.
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: Yes, is that so? This is the basic meaning. Some said that ﴿and We will show Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers what they were wary of﴾ does not mean destruction. What is meant by ﴿what they were wary of﴾ is the contest of the family of Pharaoh. When Moses was sent, the Children of Israel became strong, and the story of the magicians is clear in this. When they gathered and the people gathered on their day of festival, at mid-morning, in the brightest part of the day, the defeat fell upon whom? Upon the family of Pharaoh. They were defeated physically and morally, right? They were defeated physically when the staff of Moses, peace be upon him, began to swallow what they were faking. And they were defeated morally when the magicians themselves believed and declared before the assembly that Pharaoh had compelled them to do magic, and they made clear that the true Lord is the Lord of Moses and Aaron, glory be to Him and exalted. This is a moral defeat, in addition to the physical defeat. Did this not enrage the family of Pharaoh?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: It enraged Pharaoh, Haman, and their soldiers with a great rage.
So we can answer this with two answers:
The first is what you mentioned: that each person, in the last moment of his life, becomes clear to him that he is a loser and that the Children of Israel are the victors.
The second is that we say: God, exalted is He, showed them the contest of the Children of Israel against them and the Children of Israel's triumph over them in that great gathering: ﴿Your appointment is the day of adornment﴾ [Ta-Ha 59]. ﴿The day of adornment﴾ is the day of festival on which people adorn themselves. ﴿and that the people be gathered﴾, they assemble. ﴿in the morning﴾ [Ta-Ha 59], at mid-morning, in the brightest part of the day.
This appointment was from Moses, and it was he who proposed it, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, was certain that God would give him victory. This gathering took place on this day, and it became in reality a day of festival for the Children of Israel and a day of evil and misfortune for Pharaoh, similar to what Abu Jahl said: we will not return until we reach Badr, slaughter camels, drink wine, have singing girls play for us, and the Arabs hear of us, so they will always fear us. (...) True, the Arabs and the non-Arabs also heard of this battle, but were the singing girls singing for them, or against them? For them or against them?
* Student: Against them.
* Shaykh: Against them in reality. They heard what revealed their disgrace and, God forbid, their arrogance, until God, exalted is He, honored Islam and the Muslims in (...)
* Student: (...) ﴿And indeed we are a cautious multitude﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 56].
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: There was fear in what they were wary of.
* Shaykh: Yes, this supports the second answer.
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Do you see that there is no objection to us (...) going on a little. The point is the benefit, yes.
* Student: The benefit (...) that He made every battle (...) to make them leaders?
* Shaykh: Yes. The word "jaʿl" (making) has multiple meanings in reality. All its meanings return to "taṣyīr" (causing to become) in reality. All its meanings, with respect to God, mighty and majestic, return to causing to become. But causing to become means turning what is non-existent into something existent.

.. Those stories are recited to them so that they may believe.
If they are for those who believe?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Firmness in faith, and an increase in it. Good.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and He spares their women﴾ [Al-Qasas 4]. What is its meaning?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is, He keeps their lives spared.
* Student: He keeps their lives spared.
* Shaykh: Or does He renew life in them?
* Student: The first meaning. Originally they are alive.
* Shaykh: Yes, originally they are alive. And also, no one can renew life except who?
* Student: Except Allah.
* Shaykh: Except Allah, glorified and exalted is He.
So ﴿yastahyi﴾ means He keeps their lives spared, not that He renews them.

Good. The phrase ﴿yudhabbihu﴾ ﴿wa-yastahyi﴾: what do you say about the clause? What is its place in i'rab (grammatical analysis)?
* Student: A circumstantial clause (ḥāl).
* Shaykh: A circumstantial clause of what?
* Student: ﴿He slaughters their sons and spares their women﴾, (...).
* Shaykh: Read the verse. That is, we do not agree with (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is, is it from the subject (the doer) or from ﴿ʿalā﴾ (upon)?
* Student: (...) from the subject.
* Shaykh: From the subject, correct. Because the verb cannot be a circumstantial clause from ...?
* Student: From ﴿ʿalā﴾ and ﴿jaʿala﴾.
* Shaykh: (...).

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We wish to bestow favour upon those who were deemed weak in the land﴾ [Al-Qasas 5]. Is the will here cosmic (kawniyyah) or legislative (shar'iyyah)?
* Student: Cosmic will.
* Shaykh: The will is cosmic? What is the evidence? How do you judge by what you do not know from the Book of Allah?
* Student: We say: the will is legislative, and what is meant by it is love.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And here..
* Shaykh: The will is synonymous with..
* Student: With the (divine) will/decree (mashī'ah).
* Shaykh: With the mashī'ah, good. And also, what is the object (mutaʿallaq) of the cosmic will?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The legislative ruling or the decreed (qadarī) ruling?
* Student: The decreed ruling.
* Shaykh: This is connected to the decreed ruling. ﴿We wish to bestow favour upon those who﴾: is it understood, everyone?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Good. So the difference is in two respects: the first is in meaning, and the second is in the object. The cosmic will is synonymous with mashī'ah, in the sense of "He willed." The legislative will is synonymous with what?
* Student: With love.
* Shaykh: With love.
And the second, with respect to the object: the cosmic will relates to cosmic matters, and the legislative will relates to legislative matters. Does Allah will for us to pray in congregation legislatively or cosmically?
* Student: Legislatively.
* Shaykh: Legislatively. Clear?

His words: ﴿and We make them imams﴾ [Al-Qasas 5]?
* Student: ﴿Imams﴾ may be (...). An imam can be in good or evil. The Exalted said: ﴿And We made them imams guiding by Our command﴾ [Al-Anbiya 73].
* Shaykh: And here the intended meaning is imams?
* Student: Here, imams in goodness.
* Shaykh: Imams in goodness, because the imam is everyone who is followed.

His words: ﴿and We make them the inheritors﴾ [Al-Qasas 5]. Inheritors of whom?
* Student: Of Fir'awn and his soldiers.
* Shaykh: Of Fir'awn and his soldiers. The Exalted said: ﴿And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit it﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 59].
Good, let us now return to the benefits.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: From the Children of Israel?
* Student: From the Children of Israel.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: At that time we do not know of anyone (...).
* Student: (...) everyone whom Fir'awn oppressed, He bestows favour upon them.
* Student: Everyone whom Fir'awn oppressed, He bestows favour upon them.
* Shaykh: That is, what is (yamunnu, "bestows favour")?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: We bestow favour upon them with guidance. For this reason the present tense verb ﴿nurīdu﴾ came: that is, in the future, We wish to bestow favour upon them in the future and make them imams.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, that is it. Yes indeed, He bestows favour upon them with faith, leadership, and the inheritance of these people.

* In these noble verses:
* First: a demonstration of the greatness and exaltedness of the Qur'an. In what way?
* Student: By pointing to it.
* Shaykh: By pointing to it with the distal demonstrative; ﴿Those are the verses of﴾ [Al-Qasas 2].
* Second: that this Qur'an is written, as shown by His words ﴿the Book﴾. And what do we know of its being written? Three matters. What are they? In the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), in the mushafs, and in the scrolls in the hands of the angels.
* And among the benefits also: that this Qur'an is a clear manifestation and explainer of matters, as shown by His words ﴿the clear﴾. So it is a manifest and explanatory guide to matters.
Does the omission of the object in ﴿al-mubin﴾ (the clear) indicate the generality of the Qur'an's clarifying everything or not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: The omission of the object is one of the exegetical rules: that omitting the object indicates generality. ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [Ad-Duha 7]: He did not say "guided you," why? Because Allah guided him and guided through him. ﴿And He found you in need and enriched you﴾ [Ad-Duha 8]: He did not say "enriched you"...
Good, so the omission of the object in His words ﴿al-mubin﴾ indicates that it clarifies everything, and His words confirm this: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [An-Nahl 89]. Clear?
So what problem in religion can we take from?
* Student: From the Qur'an or the Sunnah.
* Shaykh: From the Qur'an, and the Qur'an directs us to adopt the Sunnah: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [Al-Hashr 7]. Then no problem remains in this world without its solution being found in the Book and the Sunnah. But failure to understand them has causes: either a followed desire or ignorance. Either the person does not want the truth and wants a desire, and searches the Book and the Sunnah perhaps to find what justifies what he has adopted. For example, a person who wants to justify socialism goes around the Qur'an and the Sunnah looking for something that supports this opinion; his aim is not the truth. What shows this is that if he found in the Qur'an and the Sunnah something contrary to it, he would abandon it and seek something else. Clear?
Likewise, all those who want to legislate laws or matters of jurisprudence or anything else, if they only return to the Book and the Sunnah in order to justify their positions, then if they see what contradicts them they close their eyes, and if they see what points to them, even to refute them, they open their eyes wide. Such people, in most cases, are not granted success.
But, as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, said in al-'Aqidah al-Wasitiyyah, a saying that passed by us before, a great saying, and it is: "Whoever reflects upon the Qur'an seeking guidance from it, the way of truth will become clear to him." This saying, in truth, its weight is heavy: "Whoever reflects upon the Qur'an seeking guidance from it." Two things: reflection and seeking guidance. Reflection is the act, and seeking guidance is the good intention. "The way of truth will become clear to him" is the answer to the condition, and the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, asserted it definitively, because there is no doubt about it in the Qur'an.
So the Qur'an clarifies all matters, either from the Qur'an itself or by what it directs to, which is by referring to what? The Sunnah.
Sometimes issues confront us that we search for in the books of the jurists, Hanbali jurists, Shafi'i jurists and others, and we do not find them. We return to the Qur'an and the Sunnah and find them present, and they become clear to us. Clear?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Returning to the Book and the Sunnah benefits a person in truth with two great benefits. First: tranquillity and stability, because following the words of the scholars, although a person may feel some reassurance in them, his tranquillity in them is not like his tranquillity when the Book and the Sunnah indicate it.
The second: he is able to convince others and reassure others. Correct or not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Because if someone said to you, "Well, (...) why do we say this is forbidden?" It is forbidden because Allah says it is forbidden, or because the Messenger ﷺ says it is forbidden; then he is reassured. But if you say to him, "Because it is in such-and-such a book it is forbidden," did that book come by revelation? No.
So this benefit: tranquillity and convincing others by returning to the Book and the Sunnah. For this reason I love that our return always be to the Book and the Sunnah. This does not mean I say: discard the words of the scholars. No, the words of the scholars are keys to these treasures, and how many a person is not guided by the Book and the Sunnah except where those scholars entered.
So there is a difference between one who says: follow the Book and the Sunnah, and take the words of the scholars as keys for opening these treasures from the Book and the Sunnah, and one who says: follow the Book and the Sunnah and discard the words of the scholars, paying them no attention and counting them as nothing. This is not correct. Because some people now do not regard the words of the scholars as anything at all, and never return to them. This is not correct. The truth is always between two extremes. Yes indeed.
So the Qur'an is a path to everything.
* Also in it: evidence that stories are called recitation (tilāwah). A person narrates a story, and it is said: "He recited it to them," from the words of the Exalted: ﴿We recite to you from the news﴾ [Al-Qasas 3].
* And among the benefits: the importance of the story of Musa with Fir'awn. For this reason Allah the Exalted undertook to recite it to His Prophet ﷺ, because of its importance, and the clarification of its benefits and their abundance. And it is not that you have time for us to say: gather the story from all its aspects and derive the benefits from it. We followed this method with students of a secondary institute. We taught in the secondary school at an institute, and the prescribed text for them was Surah Ghafir. Surah Ghafir contains the story of Musa, and we asked them to derive benefits from it. But the students were active then; they are not like the present time, this may have been about twenty years ago.
In any case, this story, the story of Musa and Fir'awn, is one of the most important stories, and for this reason Allah the Exalted repeats it in the Qur'an in different styles. Here He says: ﴿We recite to you from the news of Musa﴾.
* And also in it: evidence for the second benefit: that what Allah has informed of is true. All that Allah has informed of concerning these stories is true. It was previously said: when truth is attributed to a report, it means truthfulness; when it is attributed to a ruling, it means justice.
* Among its benefits: these stories are a cause of faith.
* And among its benefits also: they are an increase in faith, a cause for one who has not believed to believe, and for one who has believed that his faith increase in firmness and quantity. What is the evidence that the one who has not believed benefits from them? The words of the Exalted: ﴿There has certainly been in their stories a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111]. Every person who possesses intellect and reason must take a lesson and benefit. Yes indeed.
* And among the benefits of the verse: a demonstration of what Fir'awn had of haughtiness and tyranny: ﴿Indeed, Fir'awn exalted himself in the land﴾ [Al-Qasas 4].
* And among its benefits: whoever exalts himself in the land and seeks superiority over creation resembles Fir'awn, inherits this from Fir'awn, and wretched is the man whose leader is Fir'awn.
* And among its benefits: that dividing the nation is a cause of its failure and humiliation. From where is this taken?
* Student: ﴿And He made its people into factions﴾ [Al-Qasas 4].
* Shaykh: ﴿And He made its people into factions﴾.
* And also among its benefits: the famous saying of the English: "Divide and rule" (farriq tasud), is it Pharaonic or not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Pharaonic, because he is the one who made (...) so that he could rule through it.
* And among the benefits of the verse: that the Children of Israel were from the people of Egypt, although originally they were from the people of al-Sham. From this benefit it follows: whoever settles in a land and dwells there, even if he was not originally from its people, is attributed to it and becomes one of its people.
And among its benefits: a demonstration of the severity of Fir'awn's oppression of the Children of Israel, in that he slaughtered their sons and spared their women. Why? It was said: because he was informed that a boy would be born among the Children of Israel who would be his destruction at his hands.
It was also said: because that is the way to humiliate a nation; for when the men are gone and the women remain, they become slave-girls to the one who enslaves them, without doubt, having no guardian or defender.
* And among the benefits in the verse: that this action (high-handedness in the land, arrogance toward creation, and striving among them by division) is corruption. From where is this taken?
* Student: ﴿Indeed, he was of the corrupters﴾ [Al-Qasas 4].
* Shaykh: From His words: ﴿Indeed, he was of the corrupters﴾.
The opposite of that: the one who is humble toward the truth and toward creation, who unites the nation and restrains his aggression, is one of the reformers, because things are made clear by their opposites. If these matters are corruption, their opposite is reform.
* Among the benefits of the verse: affirmation of Allah's will in His words ﴿and We wish﴾. The proof of the affirmation of will from His words ﴿and We wish﴾, although "wish" (nurīdu) is a verb and not a noun, we say: because the verb indicates an event and its time. So from where is nurīdu derived?
* Student: From the will (irādah).
* Shaykh: From the will. "Nurīdu" is derived from "irādah." Accordingly, we say it indicates the affirmation of will for Allah. The Mu'tazilah affirmed the will?
* Student: They denied it.
* Another student: (...).
* Shaykh: They denied it. The Ash'aris affirmed the will; they said Allah the Exalted has will, because the specification of night being night and day being day, heat being heat and cold being cold, indicates the affirmation of will, since this specification does not occur except by will. Did you understand?
And they, as we have known before, derive the affirmation of the attributes from reason alone, and whatever contradicts their reason must be interpreted and turned to what agrees with reason.
This has passed before, but there is no harm in repeating it: it has passed that this is a corrupt method, contrary to the Qur'an: ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 71]. Imam Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "I wish I knew with what the Book and the Sunnah are to be weighed; whenever a man more eloquent comes to us, do we follow him and abandon the saying of the other?!" Does this make sense or not?
* Student: It does not make sense.
* Shaykh: It does not make sense.
So we say: affirming Allah's attributes by rational methods and denying what reason does not indicate is in truth transgression and a corrupt path. Moreover, we say: we can affirm by the method of reason what you denied, just as you affirmed what you affirmed by the method of reason; indeed, ours is more effective and more conclusive.
The manifestation of the attribute of mercy in creatures is more evident than the manifestation of the attribute of will.
* Student: Kindness.
* Shaykh: Yes, kindness to creatures through provision, sustenance, and provision of all that they enjoy; this is apparent to everyone, is it not? But that this is heat and that this is cold indicates the will; the indication of this upon the will is less evident than the indication of blessings upon mercy, without doubt, is it not?
Likewise, His support of the obedient and His forsaking of the disobedient indicates love and hatred, does it not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Were it not that He loves these, He would not support them; and were it not that He hates those, He would support them. This is well known: even a person, if he begins to hate someone, does not support him, and if he begins to love him, he supports him. So His support of these and His humiliation of those indicates the affirmation of love and hatred, and they deny that and say: reason does not indicate it.
So, praise be to Allah, the truth is clear. There is nothing that these people claim reason denies or does not affirm except that we find reason affirms it just as the Law affirmed it.
* Also there is evidence... one of the benefits of the verse: the perfection of Allah's power, the Mighty and Majestic. Its aspect is that these weak people were made imams and inheritors of these tyrants, is that not so? Good. Did He make them inheritors by their own power or by the power of Allah alone?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: In truth (...); that is, the Muslims of this nation inherited the lands of the Romans and the lands of the Persians through their own action and jihad. But the inheritance of the Children of Israel of the lands of Fir'awn was without any cause from them; rather it was purely from Allah the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason He said: ﴿and We make them the inheritors﴾. So it was purely by the act of Allah, glorified and exalted is He.
* It is derived from this, as I said a little while ago, the perfection of Allah's power, the Mighty and Majestic, and that Allah makes easy for His servants victory which was not within their capacity or their calculation.

* Another benefit of the verse: whoever is oppressed for upholding the truth will certainly end up with the outcome. Everyone who is oppressed for upholding the truth will certainly end up with the outcome, because His words, ﴿And We wish to bestow favor upon those who were oppressed in the land﴾, although they are in the context of the Children of Israel, include others as well. Is the generality verbal, if we say ﴿those who were oppressed in the land﴾ applies at any place and time? Or is it a generality of meaning, by analogy of others to them? The indications of generality are either verbal or semantic, and sound analogy (qiyas) is a semantic indication of what is analogized. So we say: ﴿those who were oppressed in the land﴾, if we take them to be the Children of Israel only, then are those who are oppressed for standing up for the truth from others like them, or not?
* Student: Like them.
* Shaykh: Like them, because God says: ﴿the Sunnah of God that has passed before, and you will not find any change in the Sunnah of God﴾ [Al-Fath 23]. The Sunnah of God in creation is one, because He, glorified and exalted, has no lineage with anyone that He would show consideration for it, nor any noble descent that He would show consideration for it: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you﴾ [Al-Hujurat 13].
So we say: this verse is evidence that whoever is oppressed on the path of truth, meaning for standing up for the truth, then the outcome is for him.
Here you may object to me that some people were oppressed for the truth and were killed or expelled or the like, so where is the outcome that is supposed to be theirs?
We say: the outcome is not only for the physical person, but for the conceptual person. The doctrine of this man must be supported. Now look at those who preceded us among the scholars: every scholar who was harmed for the truth, whether he was killed or not, you will find that his writings remain and spread more than others, far more than others, and this is clear to whoever reflects on it.
So victory is for the speaker during his lifetime, or for his doctrine after his death. The person who strives for God does not want to remain himself. What concerns him? That this truth he stood for remains. It does not matter to him whether he remains or not, if he is calling to God. As for the one who calls to himself, and we ask God to protect us all from that, he is the one who says, when he is killed or harmed, that he has not been victorious. But the one who calls to God is concerned only that this call prevails, and for this reason he fights for it and for its sake.
* Student: (...) How about his enemy, who in turn reads this story and says: there must be the victory of God?
* Shaykh: Yes, but the victory of the truth must come through its causes. If matters are beyond you, victory comes from God without a cause. But as long as you are commanded to a specific path, you may not be victorious because you oppose it, you may not be given victory because of your opposition and your shortcoming. A person does not mean that whoever has a good intention will have good action and be victorious. No, the matter may differ. For this reason these matters are among the most subtle issues, and we have spoken about them much, because these issues are extremely subtle. A person moves like a ball in the sea: the winds turn it, and sometimes a violent wind carries it miles away. Therefore a person must be balanced, not reckless. If he is reckless and then victory goes against him, the calamity is from himself.
* Another benefit of the verse: the virtues of the Children of Israel and their distinguished qualities, because of His words: ﴿and We will make them leaders﴾. Here it may be difficult for a person: God says here ﴿and We will make them leaders﴾, while in many verses He censures the Children of Israel?
We say: God, glorified and exalted, has explained the reason for making these people leaders. He said in Surah As-Sajdah (Alif Lam Mim Tanzil): ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and were certain of Our signs﴾ [As-Sajdah 24]. So when they were characterized by these two qualities, patience and certainty, they were leaders. Shaykh al-Islam took from this verse a principle, saying: through patience and certainty one attains leadership in religion. But when patience and certainty were lacking among them, what did they become?
* Student: Monkeys.
* Shaykh: They became the opposite, yes. They became ﴿apes, despised﴾, and verses came censuring them. So the verses do not contradict one another, but there are things that cause the rulings of some verses to change, because the cause is absent.
* Another benefit of the verse: when Muslims conquer the lands of the disbelievers, they come to own them. From where do we take this?
* Student: ﴿and We will make them the inheritors﴾.
* Shaykh: From His words: ﴿and We will make them the inheritors﴾. And an inheritor owns what he inherits, right? The inheritor owns what he inherits. So God makes them fully inheritors. For this reason the scholars said: the lands become owned property.
* Another benefit of the verse: lands are not purely spoils of war. Here He said ﴿We will make them the inheritors﴾, although the Messenger ﷺ said: "Booty has been made lawful for me, and it was not made lawful for anyone before me" [Agreed upon; Al-Bukhari (335) and Muslim (521/3), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah]. Look now at this claim I am making. See whether it is correct or not.
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: I think it is not correct, because God made the Children of Israel inherit their land and their wealth, the land and wealth of the people of Pharaoh. God said in Surah Ash-Shu'ara: ...
* Student: ﴿Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 59].
* Shaykh: No, before it: ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs (57), and treasures and a noble station (58). Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 57-59]. There is no doubt that the treasures are spoils, and He says: ﴿We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾. So how do we answer the hadith?
The answer is that we say: these people did not inherit them through fighting. Spoils, as is well known, are what is taken through fighting the enemies. These people did not inherit them by fighting, but by the power of God, mighty and majestic, which they had no way to reach. On this basis, the statement of the Messenger ﷺ, "Booty has been made lawful for me, and it was not made lawful for anyone before me," is not contradicted.
* Student: The houses and lands that (...)?
* Shaykh: Houses and lands are treasures too.
* Student: So they fall under (...)?
* Shaykh: No, I said: the claim. Did I claim whether it is correct or not?
* Student: On (...).
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: Yes, lands have value, yes. Lands have value, yes.
* Student: Do they enter into the spoils?
* Shaykh: We said that spoils are movable things. Then we refuted this and said that the Children of Israel were given the lands and were given the treasures, and treasures are movable things, right?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: And we raised this objection against the statement of the Messenger ﷺ: "Booty has been made lawful for me, and it was not made lawful for anyone before me."
Suppose you say: lands are not among the spoils, but treasures are among the spoils. We answer this: the Children of Israel's possession of the land and treasures of the family of Pharaoh was without fighting, and the spoils that are owned are those obtained through fighting. This is what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "it was not made lawful for anyone before me."
* Student: Were there spoils, Shaykh, in earlier times?
* Shaykh: In what came before?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: There were spoils, but they were not lawful for the fighters.
* Student: And what was their status?
* Shaykh: Their status was that they were gathered, then fire would descend upon them from heaven and burn them. Furthermore, if there was some misappropriation (ghulul) in them, the fire did not descend. Glory be to God the Mighty! It would not descend, so that nothing would be lost. If something was lost, the fire would descend and burn them.
* Student: What is the wisdom in burning the spoils (...)?
* Shaykh: The wisdom is to cut off attachment to them completely, because if they remained, people would trade them, buy and sell them, benefit from them, and they would come to own them.
* Student: And this nation is the last of the nations.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: So if, for example, it were forbidden from the spoils, that would be better, because its faith is stronger.
* Shaykh: No, this is not correct, that is not the reason. But God, glorified and exalted, has supported this nation with things so that it may be assisted by them. There is no objection to a person who is more excellent being supported with things to reach virtue. Did not the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, have his past and future sins forgiven by God? Yet he still asks God's forgiveness. And we too are commanded to send blessings upon him, although God says: ﴿Indeed, God and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [Al-Ahzab 56]. Yes indeed. Reaching perfection does not require that a person abandon striving by means.
* Student: The Prophet gave a reason, Shaykh: he saw our weakness and inability, so he made them lawful for us.
* Shaykh: Yes, that is it. Even the Messenger said: "My provision has been placed under the shade of my spear" [Ahmad (5114), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar], in order to help us in this.
* Student: (...) the story of the one who found the misappropriation?
* Shaykh: But the problem is that Ibrahim says: how can they be made lawful for us while we are the best of nations? Why is the matter not left to our merits and virtues?
We say: this is from the blessing of God. It is from the completion of God's blessing that we reach the level of perfection, and these spoils are made lawful so that we may be assisted by them in (...).
* From the benefits of the noble verse: empowerment in the land, a person's establishment in the land, is one of God's blessings upon us, because of His words: ﴿and We will establish them in the land﴾ [Al-Qasas 6]. Right? Because this is among what God bestowed upon the Children of Israel, that He empowered them in the land. So a person being empowered in the land, whether this empowerment is through authority, the authority of a ruler, or through the authority of the Qur'an.
Note, O people, that empowerment in the land does not mean that a person rules over people so as to be a sultan over them. No, among empowerment in the land is that God empowers him so that his word becomes authoritative over the believers.
For example, Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah: was he empowered in the land or not? He was empowered in the land more greatly than the rulers of his time. The empowerment of the rulers of his time ended with their deaths, but God's empowerment of this man, so that his word remained respected among people up to now, is what is lasting. So although empowerment in the land may first come to mind as the empowerment of a ruler, we should say: empowerment of what? Of the Qur'an. In other words, whoever stands up for the truth, his word will have authority and strength. This is also supported by the hadith: "When God loves a servant, He places acceptance for him on earth" [Agreed upon; Al-Bukhari (3209) and Muslim (2637/157), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. That means he will have acceptance and his word will have effect. This is among the empowerment of God in the land.
* Another benefit of the verse: its circumstances are what we mentioned. But His words: ﴿and We will show Pharaoh﴾ [Al-Qasas 6] are among the examples of the power of God, mighty and majestic.
* From its benefits: Pharaoh and his people were wary of the Children of Israel, so God showed them what they were wary of. Here there is a difficulty: how did God show them what they were wary of, when they perished?
* Student: When drowning overtook him, he said: ﴿I believe that there is no god except the one in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am among the Muslims﴾ [Yunus 90].
* Shaykh: Did you mean ﴿and We will show Pharaoh﴾?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: ﴿and Haman and their soldiers, what they were wary of﴾ [Al-Qasas 6].
* Student: Their soldiers were with them. Those who drowned, all of them (...)
* Shaykh: Yes, but I say: whoever drowned did not know (...)
* Student: He knew. When they drowned, all of them (...), each person and each individual knew that the Children of Israel had (...)
* Shaykh: You mean at the moment his soul departed, for example?
* Student: At the last moment.
* Shaykh: Alright, at the last moment he knew.
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: Yes, is that so? This is the basic meaning. Some said that ﴿and We will show Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers what they were wary of﴾ does not mean destruction. What is meant by ﴿what they were wary of﴾ is the contest of the family of Pharaoh. When Moses was sent, the Children of Israel became strong, and the story of the magicians is clear in this. When they gathered and the people gathered on their day of festival, at mid-morning, in the brightest part of the day, the defeat fell upon whom? Upon the family of Pharaoh. They were defeated physically and morally, right? They were defeated physically when the staff of Moses, peace be upon him, began to swallow what they were faking. And they were defeated morally when the magicians themselves believed and declared before the assembly that Pharaoh had compelled them to do magic, and they made clear that the true Lord is the Lord of Moses and Aaron, glory be to Him and exalted. This is a moral defeat, in addition to the physical defeat. Did this not enrage the family of Pharaoh?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: It enraged Pharaoh, Haman, and their soldiers with a great rage.
So we can answer this with two answers:
The first is what you mentioned: that each person, in the last moment of his life, becomes clear to him that he is a loser and that the Children of Israel are the victors.
The second is that we say: God, exalted is He, showed them the contest of the Children of Israel against them and the Children of Israel's triumph over them in that great gathering: ﴿Your appointment is the day of adornment﴾ [Ta-Ha 59]. ﴿The day of adornment﴾ is the day of festival on which people adorn themselves. ﴿and that the people be gathered﴾, they assemble. ﴿in the morning﴾ [Ta-Ha 59], at mid-morning, in the brightest part of the day.
This appointment was from Moses, and it was he who proposed it, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, was certain that God would give him victory. This gathering took place on this day, and it became in reality a day of festival for the Children of Israel and a day of evil and misfortune for Pharaoh, similar to what Abu Jahl said: we will not return until we reach Badr, slaughter camels, drink wine, have singing girls play for us, and the Arabs hear of us, so they will always fear us. (...) True, the Arabs and the non-Arabs also heard of this battle, but were the singing girls singing for them, or against them? For them or against them?
* Student: Against them.
* Shaykh: Against them in reality. They heard what revealed their disgrace and, God forbid, their arrogance, until God, exalted is He, honored Islam and the Muslims in (...)
* Student: (...) ﴿And indeed we are a cautious multitude﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 56].
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: There was fear in what they were wary of.
* Shaykh: Yes, this supports the second answer.
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Do you see that there is no objection to us (...) going on a little. The point is the benefit, yes.
* Student: The benefit (...) that He made every battle (...) to make them leaders?
* Shaykh: Yes. The word "jaʿl" (making) has multiple meanings in reality. All its meanings return to "taṣyīr" (causing to become) in reality. All its meanings, with respect to God, mighty and majestic, return to causing to become. But causing to become means turning what is non-existent into something existent.

(...) ﴿And We inspired﴾ Revelation (wahy) linguistically means informing swiftly and secretly, as in the words of Allah: ﴿So he inspired to them to glorify [Allah] morning and evening﴾ [Maryam 11]. It is applied to several meanings, among them:
Legislative revelation, which is the revelation of prophethood or messengership; inspiration (ilham), which is what Allah, blessed and exalted, casts into the soul of the one inspired; and the revelation of sleep, for true dreams are a part of forty-six parts of prophethood [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6983) and Muslim (2263/6), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]].
Consider this verse: ﴿And We inspired to the mother of Moses: Suckle him﴾. Revelation of prophethood or messengership is superior to this, because what was revealed to her was not a law... that you suckle him... to the end.
Moreover, the correct view is that no woman was ever sent as a prophet: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed﴾ [Yusuf 109].
So the revelation here is either inspiration or a dream. Inspiration is not a strange thing: that a woman be inspired with what is in her interest. Allah, the Exalted, inspired the bee, and (...) the children of Adam what is in their interest: ﴿And your Lord inspired to the bee: take for yourself among the mountains houses﴾ to the end [An-Nahl 68].
Hence the author said: (﴿And We inspired﴾ is inspiration of inspiration or dream).
(Or) here is for variation, indicating the variation of scholarly opinion on this issue: some scholars say the revelation is inspiration, and some say it is revelation through dream. The important point is that it is not revelation of messengership or prophethood.
His words: ﴿to the mother of Moses﴾ mean the one who bore him, and this is the basic meaning of "mother": ﴿Their mothers are none but those who bore them﴾ [Al-Mujadila 2]. As for a foster mother, she is not mentioned unqualified but qualified. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [An-Nisa 23], then He said: ﴿and your mothers who have nursed you﴾ [An-Nisa 23]. So the foster mother is not included in the unqualified term "mother"; rather it must be qualified.
Are you with us?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: And what did we say?
* Student: We said: the foster mother (...).
* Shaykh: Upon unqualified use.
* Student: Upon unqualified use (...).
* Shaykh: Good. I established this only so that it becomes clear that Allah's words ﴿and the mothers of your wives﴾ [An-Nisa 23] refer to the mother who bore, not the mothers of nursing.
He says: (﴿And We inspired to the mother of Moses﴾, and he is the child mentioned, and none knew of his birth except his sister).
(...) the child mentioned?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) and he is the child mentioned?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Or the one mentioned in the verse?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Good, and he is the child mentioned, because there is no mother without a child.
His words: (and none knew of his birth except his sister). This is among the Israelite narrations which are neither confirmed nor denied, for what tells us that none knew of it except his sister? We have no one to show us this.
His words: ﴿that suckle him﴾. ﴿أَنْ﴾ here is explanatory (tafsiriyyah). The rule for the explanatory "an": it occurs after something that carries the sense of speech but not its letters. Every "an" that occurs after something carrying the meaning of speech without its letters is explanatory: ﴿And We inspired to the mother of Moses that suckle him﴾. Similar to the words of Allah: ﴿So We inspired to him: construct the ship﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 27], and similar examples are many.
﴿that suckle him; then when you fear for him﴾. This is evidence that there was fear of Pharaoh's people, who seized children. Hence He said: ﴿when you fear for him, then cast him into the yamm﴾. He explained (yamm) as (the sea), then explained (the sea) as (i.e., the Nile). Al-yamm is the sea, as Allah said: ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and threw them into the yamm﴾ [Al-Qasas 40]; meaning the sea. The sea here means the Nile, and it was called a sea though it is a river because of its abundance and vastness.
﴿then cast him into the yamm and do not fear﴾. His words ﴿when you fear﴾ is the conditional verb, and the answer of the condition is ﴿cast him into the yamm﴾. It is strange that one for whom one fears is cast into what leads to his destruction; for casting him into the sea, what does it mean? Hastening his destruction, since it is known that he dies if cast into the sea. This is among the signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that Musa is cast into a place of fear and does not die, then lives in the embrace of Pharaoh, who was tracking the sons of Israel, killing their sons and sparing their women. These are signs showing the perfection of Allah's power, and that when Allah protects anyone, the causes leading to destruction have no effect and no influence, and Allah's power is above causes; hence fire undoubtedly burns, yet it became coolness and peace for Ibrahim.
﴿when you fear for him, cast him into the yamm and do not fear﴾. What is ﴿تَخَافِي﴾ (do not fear)? The author said: (drowning him), so the object of ﴿تَخَافِي﴾ is omitted, and he estimated it by his words: (drowning him), which is clear.
(﴿And do not grieve﴾ over his separation). He said: (over his separation), because grief concerns the past and fear concerns the future: whatever troubles a person, if it is future it is fear, and if it is past it is grief. Here Allah said to her: ﴿do not fear and do not grieve﴾, for the matter will be contrary to what you expect. Hence He said: ﴿We will surely return him to you and make him of the messengers﴾. ﴿إِنَّا رَادُّوهُ﴾: He did not say "We will return him," so that the sentence would be nominal, and a nominal sentence indicates firmness and stability.
His words: ﴿إِنَّا﴾ (...) with the plural pronoun for exalting (Allah).
His words: ﴿رَادُّوهُ إِلَيْكِ﴾ means: those who will bring him back. Allah, blessed and exalted, did not specify the period of her separation from him, but it is apparent that it was not long, as will come at the end of the story.
His words: ﴿وَجَاعِلُوهُ مِنَ الْمُرْسَلِينَ﴾ are glad tidings above the first glad tidings: that this child will be among the messengers, that is, among those whom Allah, blessed and exalted, sent and honored with messengership.
This verse contains a command and a prohibition; where are they? Are there two commands and two prohibitions and two glad tidings, or not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Two commands, two prohibitions and two glad tidings. The two commands: ﴿suckle him﴾ and ﴿cast him﴾; the two prohibitions: ﴿do not fear and do not grieve﴾; the two glad tidings: ﴿We will return him to you and make him of the messengers﴾.
(So she suckled him for three months without him crying, and she feared for him, so she placed him in a chest coated with pitch on the inside, prepared for him within it, closed it and cast it into the Nile at night).
His words: (she suckled him for three months): nothing in the verse indicates this. What is certain is that she obeyed Allah's command: she suckled him, and when she feared for him she cast him.
The author's statement that she (placed him in a chest) — from where did he take this?
From another verse: ﴿Cast him into the chest, then cast it into the yamm﴾ [Ta-Ha 39]. This is Allah's guidance to her, for He did not command her (...) to throw him (...) into the sea; rather He commanded her to place him in a chest so that it would be a protection for him. A chest is usually made of wood, and wood normally floats on water. If it is made with pitch, it also prevents water from entering it, for if water enters it and seeps into the wood, it becomes heavy and then sinks.
As for his words: (and she cast him into the Nile at night), from where did he take (at night)? It may be derived from His words later: ﴿And the heart of Musa's mother became empty﴾ [Al-Qasas 10], that she cast him at night, then she kept fretting over him and being concerned for him until she thought of nothing else, as will come.
Moreover, what supports this is that the woman feared for him, and if she feared for him it is customarily unlikely that she would take him out by day and cast him before people; so it must have been at night. Thus this ruling that it was (at night) is derived from the verse and from custom, as this would only happen at night.
He said: (﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up﴾, in the chest, at dawn of the night ﴿the family of Pharaoh﴾).
﴿فَالْتَقَطَهُ﴾: He did not say "took him," because he became like a foundling abandoned child. The scholars say the laqit (foundling) is an abandoned child who was cast out, called laqit; hence He said ﴿picked him up﴾ and did not say "took him"; why? Because the laqit is an abandoned child; these people took this chest.
As for ﴿آلُ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾, the author said: (his helpers); "his family" means his helpers, and it is possible that "his family" means his relatives.
In any case, the important point is that he was taken by someone affiliated with Pharaoh, who was the king.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, picking up is also done intentionally, for the one who picks up an abandoned foundling, for example in the street or an abandoned one in a mosque, wants to take him; but here it may suggest that it was something he found by chance. However, the scholars say that picking up originally refers to an abandoned child.
He said: (﴿the family of Pharaoh﴾ placed him before them) (placed him before them), that is, before Pharaoh, and they did not know what was in it, and perhaps they thought what was in it was some property.
(And it was opened, and Musa was taken out of it, while he was sucking milk from his thumb). This (...); his sucking milk from his thumb means he was nursing himself from himself; (...). The custom is that a person must open a closed thing and look at what is in it.
As for his sucking milk from his thumb, this is among the Israelite matters which are neither confirmed nor denied; (...) it is said to be denied, and that this is far from custom.
His words: (﴿so that it would be for them﴾ in the outcome of the matter). The pronoun in ﴿لِيَكُونَ﴾ refers to whom? To Musa, and the pronoun in ﴿لَهُمْ﴾ refers to ﴿آلُ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾, and Pharaoh himself is included in ﴿آلُ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾.
His words: ﴿لِيَكُونَ﴾: the author said (in the outcome of the matter), indicating that the lam here is for consequence (lam al-'aqibah), not for causation; for if they had perceived that he would become an enemy and a grief to them, they would have killed him, but the outcome was that it was so. As for what Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, held, that the lam here is for causation in view of Allah's knowledge, it has a basis: meaning ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he would be an enemy and grief for them﴾ in Allah's knowledge, not as a cause of the picking up. This has a basis, but the closer view is what the author and others held, that the lam here is for consequence, not causation.
The lam that enters the present-tense verb is divided into two kinds: extra (zā'idah) and non-extra. The non-extra one is for causation, for consequence, and for emphasizing negation; this is the non-extra. The extra one is that which generally occurs after the verb of will, such as the words of Allah: ﴿Allah only wants to make clear to you﴾ [An-Nisa 26], ﴿Allah only wants to remove from you the impurity﴾ [Al-Ahzab 33]; the lam here is extra, because if you removed it and estimated "that" (an): ﴿Allah only wants that He remove﴾, ﴿Allah only wants that He remove from you﴾, the sentence is complete, or not?
* Student: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: It is complete, the sentence is complete.
The non-extra lam is for causation, like: "I came in order to learn," meaning in order that I learn. It is for emphasizing negation, such as the words of Allah: ﴿Allah would not forgive them﴾ [An-Nisa 137]; therefore the grammarians call it the lam of denial (lam al-juhud), the lam of negation, as it emphasizes negation.
The third is for consequence, like this verse: ﴿so that it would be for them an enemy and grief﴾.
* Student: After kana?
* Shaykh: After "kana," whether it is a present verb or a past verb.
His words: (﴿so that it would be for them an enemy﴾ who kills their men) ﴿and grief﴾ (who enslaves their women). This is open to question; rather the apparent meaning is that he is an enemy for what occurs at his hands of grave harm to the family of Pharaoh.
﴿وَحَزَنًا﴾: because he would grieve them by the great victories that would appear to them, and the most profound of them: when he triumphed on the day of the adornment (zīnah), for he triumphed over them with a decisive, dazzling triumph, and they incurred from this a grief known only to Allah, glorified and exalted. We do not know that Musa ﷺ killed the men of Pharaoh's family, nor that he enslaved their women; what is known is that Allah, glorified and exalted, drowned them by His action.
(And in a reading with a damma on the ḥāʾ and sukūn on the zāy, there are two dialects for the verbal noun, and it here means the active participle of ḥazanahu like aḥzanahu). (...).
Alright, ﴿حَزَنًا﴾: he says (And in a reading): is it a Sab'i (canonical seven) reading or a shadhdh (irregular) one?
* Student: Sab'i.
* Shaykh: Sab'i; because you know the author, when he says (in a reading) he means canonical, and when he says (it was read) it is for the irregular.
He said: (with a damma on the ḥāʾ and sukūn on the zāy), ﴿لِيَكُونَ لَهُمْ عَدُوًّا وَحُزْنًا﴾ [Al-Qasas 8], ﴿حُزْنًا﴾ and ﴿حَزَنًا﴾ have the same meaning, and they are two dialects for the verbal noun.
From where is it derived? He says: from (ḥazina like aḥzana), (ḥazanahu like aḥzanahu).
What is the meaning of (ḥazanahu like aḥzanahu)?
It means that (ḥazina), which is not augmented by a hamzah, is like (aḥzanahu), augmented by a hamzah, in terms of transitivity.
His words: (and it here means the active participle): what does "means the active participle" mean?
* Student: ḥāzin (causing grief).
* Shaykh: That is, in the sense of ḥāzin, meaning muḥzin (causing grief).
Why did the author interpret it this way? Because ḥazan is a feeling within the soul, and would Musa ﷺ be a feeling within their souls?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: No, but he is the one who introduces this feeling, grief, into their souls; accordingly ﴿وَحَزَنًا﴾ means ḥāzinan (causing grief).
The verbal noun always comes in the sense of the active participle and always in the sense of the passive participle: it is said "fulan ʿadl, riḍā" (so-and-so is just, satisfactory), and it is also said "fulan thiqah" (so-and-so is trustworthy); ʿadl, riḍā and thiqah are verbal nouns in the sense of the active participle ʿādil, and riḍā in the sense of marḍī, and thiqah in the sense of mawthūq, in the sense of both active and passive participles.
His words, ﷺ: «Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697), and Muslim (1718/17), with his wording, from ʿĀʾishah.]]; this is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle.
﴿فَالْتَقَطَهُ آلُ فِرْعَوْنَ لِيَكُونَ لَهُمْ عَدُوًّا وَحَزَنًا﴾.
What is the enemy? The jurists have defined the enemy by a definition that is a ruling in reality: they said the enemy is one whose misfortune of a person pleases him or whose joy distresses him; so he is his enemy. Every person who is pleased when you are harmed and grieved when you are pleased is an enemy; and every person who is pleased when you are pleased and grieved when you grieve is a friend (walī), because the enemy's opposite is the friend.
He said: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were sinners﴾.
This sentence is a justification for His words ﴿so that it would be for them an enemy and grief﴾, as if it were said: why would he be an enemy and grief to them? So He explained that the cause of that is the error of these: Pharaoh the king, Haman his minister, their soldiers, their followers who comply with their orders; the root of "junūd" is the plural of jund, and jund are a person's helpers.
He says: (﴿they were sinners﴾ from sin, meaning disobedient, so they were punished at his hands).
What is the difference between khāṭi' and mukhṭi'? What is the difference between khāṭi' and mukhṭi'?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, meaning: whoever commits error deliberately is khāṭi', and whoever commits it without intent is mukhṭi'; therefore the khāṭi' is culpable and the mukhṭi' is not culpable. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿a lying, sinful forelock﴾ [Al-'Alaq 16], right?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: And the mukhṭi' bears no sin: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or err﴾ [Al-Baqarah 286]. And the verb from khāṭi' is khaṭiʾa, and from akhṭa' is mukhṭi'; this is the difference.
So the words of Allah, glorified and exalted, ﴿khāṭi'īn﴾ mean those who fall into error deliberately and intentionally; therefore the author said: (meaning disobedient, so they were punished at his hands).
(﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said﴾ and she had resolved with his helpers to kill him), meaning to kill Musa, (she said: ﴿A comfort of the eye for me and for you﴾).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 7–10 (part 2 of 4):

In my copy it is written ﴿قُرَّتُ﴾ with a open taa (tāʾ maftūḥa), whereas the rule is the taa marbuta (tāʾ marbūṭa), and it is with the taa marbuta in the rest of the verses: ﴿رَبَّنَا هَبْ لَنَا مِنْ أَزْوَاجِنَا وَذُرِّيَّاتِنَا قُرَّةَ أَعْيُنٍ﴾ [al-Furqan 74], with the taa marbuta, and it does not come with an open taa except in this place in the Qur'an. It is mentioned in the Qur'an in two other places besides this, and all of them are with the taa marbuta. If it is asked: what is the difference? We say: this is written according to the 'Uthmani script (al-rasm al-'Uthmani, the Uthmanic orthography), this is how the Companions (raḍiya Allāhu 'anhum) wrote it.

As for His words ﴿قُرَّتُ عَيْنٍ﴾: first, ﴿قَالَتِ﴾ directs the address to whom? To Pharaoh. And the author estimated ﴿قُرَّتُ﴾ as (huwa, "he"), to show that it is the predicate of an omitted subject.

And His words ﴿قُرَّتُ عَيْنٍ﴾ are derived from al-qarr (coolness) or from al-qarar (settledness); meaning: my intent is this or this, and it is valid from both together: from al-qarr, which is cold, because when the eye becomes cool it is a sign of joy, and for this it is said: the tears of joy are cold, and the tears of grief are hot; it is said: he weeps over him with hot tears, meaning from grief.

So we say: "coolness of the eye" is a metaphor for its coldness, and the coldness of the eye is a sign of joy.

It was also said: it is from qarra bi-al-makan, meaning settledness and absence of agitation; because when a person is afraid, his eye begins to roam from here and from here, it stares, roams and looks around, but this is a proof that it is steady, and its steadiness is a proof that it was not frightened.

﴿قُرَّتُ عَيْنٍ لِي وَلَكَ لَا تَقْتُلُوهُ عَسَى أَنْ يَنْفَعَنَا أَوْ نَتَّخِذَهُ وَلَدًا﴾.

Her words ﴿لَا تَقْتُلُوهُ﴾ indicate that they had intended to kill him, otherwise her words ﴿لَا تَقْتُلُوهُ﴾ would have no purpose.

Her words ﴿لِي وَلَكَ﴾: did it happen as she expected?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: As far as she is concerned, yes; there is no doubt that the matter happened as she expected, and this child became a coolness of the eye for her and an elevation for her in this world and the Hereafter. As for Pharaoh, no; he did not become a coolness of the eye for him, rather he was an enemy to him and a grief. And among the strange interpretations is that some said: ﴿قُرَّتُ عَيْنٍ لِي﴾ and stop, ﴿وَلَكَ لَا﴾ and stop also!! And ﴿تَقْتُلُوهُ﴾ is a new sentence!! This is in reality a manipulation of the Qur'an; because if it were as they say, Allah the Exalted would have said: (taqtulūnahu); since the deletion of the nūn here has no known reason except the prohibition, how can the speech of Allah be interpreted by such cold interpretations?! But we mention it because it has been said, and even though it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (raḍiya Allāhu 'anhumā) [[See Tafsir al-Samarqandi, Bahr al-'Ulum (2/599).]], this is far from Ibn 'Abbas, because of what it contains of disjointing the speech, scattering it and its parts not fitting together, and because the nūn in the verb ﴿تَقْتُلُوهُ﴾ is deleted, which indicates that ﴿لَا﴾ governs it.

But she, may Allah be pleased with her, the wife of Pharaoh, either said that as a means of calming him ﴿قُرَّتُ عَيْنٍ لِي وَلَكَ﴾ in order to calm and gladden him, or she said it believing it, but whoever believes something does not necessarily have the matter in accordance with what he believed; Allah the Exalted may contradict a person's belief for a wisdom He intends, and there is no obstacle to her saying that while believing that he would be a coolness of the eye for him and for her too.

And her words support this: ﴿عَسَى أَنْ يَنْفَعَنَا أَوْ نَتَّخِذَهُ وَلَدًا﴾.

﴿عَسَى﴾ expresses hope; and ﴿يَنْفَعَنَا﴾ in service. ﴿أَوْ نَتَّخِذَهُ وَلَدًا﴾: we adopt him. It was said: Pharaoh had no child from his wife, so she said: ﴿أَوْ نَتَّخِذَهُ وَلَدًا﴾. And it is known that there is a difference between the two matters; for their benefit from him does not make them feel tender toward him as they feel toward a child, isn't that so?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: A servant, to a person, he orders him and forbids him, and there is not in his heart for him the mercy, compassion and tenderness that there is for a child; and for this she said: ﴿أَوْ نَتَّخِذَهُ وَلَدًا﴾, and this is a move from the lower to the higher.

So we are not deprived of this child: either we take him as a servant from whom we benefit, or we take him as a son in whom we take pride and who will hold the rank of a child for us.

Is there a third possibility?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, there is a third possibility: that he neither benefits them nor do they take him, but this cannot be said in this context, because she wants to encourage them to keep him, and encouragement to keep him mentions only desirable qualities, namely that he benefits or is taken as a son.

He said: ﴿وَهُمْ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾.

Yes, ﴿وَهُمْ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾: is this a sentence from the speech of Allah or from her speech?

The apparent reading is that it is from the speech of Allah; meaning ﴿وَهُمْ﴾, i.e., the family of Pharaoh, including the woman, ﴿لَا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ of the outcome of this child's affair; for if they had perceived the outcome of his matter they would have accepted her advice, or not? They did not accept it, but Allah the Exalted blinded them to that.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: It indicates that she...?
* Student: Barren.
* Shaykh: Barren? I say: it has been said; it was said that he had no child from her.
* Student: Meaning if she had a child (...).
* Shaykh: It is not necessarily so in reality, because a person may adopt someone in addition, so as long as there is nothing clear, we do not affirm it; we say: perhaps it is this.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No. Some say: ﴿وَهُمْ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ refers to the family of Pharaoh, who do not perceive what the woman intends; it is as if Allah the Mighty and Majestic inspired the woman with the outcome of this man, while they do not perceive it; but the closer view is that it is from the speech of Allah the Exalted.
* Student: Was this speech of Pharaoh's wife after she became a Muslim or before she accepted Islam?
* Shaykh: No, before she accepted Islam, (...).
* Student: Meaning she was previously upon the creed of Pharaoh?
* Shaykh: (...) upon the creed of Pharaoh; that is, she did not return to..., but the apparent view is that she was upon his creed, because she was his wife and must have been obedient to him.

He said: (﴿﴿لَا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ ﴾ of the outcome of their affair with him), and this is clear.

Then Allah the Exalted said: (﴿﴿وَأَصْبَحَ فُؤَادُ أُمِّ مُوسَى﴾ ﴾ when she knew of his being picked up ﴿﴿فَارِغًا﴾ ﴾ from everything other than him). Allahu Akbar!

﴿وَأَصْبَحَ﴾ is based on the premise that she cast him at night. The word (aṣbaḥa) comes in the sense of (ṣāra, "became"), regardless of time; in the Arabic language (aṣbaḥa) comes in the sense of ṣāra, and it comes in the sense of ṣāra in the sense of morning; one says for example: the water became ice (ṣāra al-mā'u thalj). In colloquial language now people always say: "aṣbaḥa kadhā" and "aṣbaḥa kadhā", meaning he has moved to this, just as morning is a transition from night to day.

But here it is not far that in the morning of that night, whisperings and anxious thoughts overcame her until her heart became empty of everything, thinking of nothing except this child; and this, I mean that the intended meaning of the morning here is entering the morning, is more appropriate than making it mean ṣāra; because, as you know, a thing is grieved over when it is lost, but if time lengthens it may be forgotten, events cause one to forget it; so the apparent meaning of (aṣbaḥa) is: on that night.

﴿وَأَصْبَحَ فُؤَادُ﴾: what is al-fu'ad?
* Student: The heart.
* Shaykh: The heart.
﴿أُمِّ مُوسَى فَارِغًا﴾; he says: (mimmā siwāhu, "from what is other than him").

As for the author's words: (when she knew of his being picked up), this is not certain that she knew, because as soon as she cast him she would be whispering about him.

(﴿﴿إِنْ﴾ ﴾ is a lightened form of the heavy (inna), and its noun is omitted; i.e., she ﴿﴿كَادَتْ لَتُبْدِي بِهِ﴾ ﴾ i.e., that he is her son ﴿﴿لَوْلَا أَنْ رَبَطْنَا عَلَى قَلْبِهَا﴾ ﴾) and so on.

He says: ﴿إِنْ كَادَتْ﴾. The author parsed ﴿إِنْ﴾ as a lightened form of the heavy (inna). Ibn Malik says:

And (inna) is lightened, so its action is rare, and the lām is obligatory when it is not neglected; and sometimes it is dispensed with when clear, as in: "the speaker intended them, relying on it"; and the verb, if it is not an abrogating one, you will rarely find it joined by (in) which is connected...

So the verse follows the classical language: is (kāda) an abrogating (nāsikh) verb or not?
* Student: Abrogating.
* Shaykh: Abrogating; (kāda) is abrogating, yes.

And here the lām in ﴿لَتُبْدِي بِهِ﴾: is it obligatory or permissible?
* Student: Obligatory.
* Shaykh: The view of the majority is obligatory? Good. Suppose we delete it and say: ﴿إِنْ كَادَتْ﴾ tubdī bihi?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Can it not be in the sense of (mā)? That is: mā kādat tubdī bihi?
* Student: They said: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, the origin is the lām.

The lām becomes obligatory when its omission would cause confusion, because if you delete it, it would be confused with the negative (in); whereas if you make it obligatory there is no confusion, since the lām of emphasis does not come with negation. What is your opinion on this?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but the meaning differs; ﴿إِنْ كَادَتْ لَتُبْدِي بِهِ﴾ means that her disclosure of it was close, but (mā kānat latubdī bihi) means it was impossible.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is permissible, because the context indicates the meaning, namely His words: ﴿لَوْلَا أَنْ رَبَطْنَا عَلَى قَلْبِهَا﴾; because this sentence does not suit (in) being negative; meaning: she was not about to disclose it, were it not that We bound her heart; because binding the heart requires concealment, not clarification?
* Student: Concealment.
* Shaykh: It requires concealment, and it is not suitable to say: she did not almost reveal it "were it not that We bound"; because "were it not that We bound" implies that she would not reveal it. So on this basis the lām here is permissible. This is permissible from the standpoint of grammatical craft; but from the standpoint of Qur'anic recitation, deleting it is not permissible, and the reason? Because the speech of Allah cannot (...), neither by deficiency nor by addition.

﴿إِنْ كَادَتْ لَتُبْدِي بِهِ﴾: tubdī means tuẓhir, reveal; ﴿بِهِ﴾ means: with Musa.

As for the author's words: (i.e., that he is her son), it is based on his view that she reached the family of Pharaoh; and were it not that Allah bound her heart, she would have said: this is my son. There is no doubt that this is far from the story and far from the meaning.

Rather, ﴿إِنْ كَادَتْ لَتُبْدِي بِهِ﴾ means: she would have disclosed what she had done with him, meaning she would tell people: "By Allah, I did such and such, and I cast my son into the river," and so on; is it not so?

He said: ﴿إِنْ كَادَتْ لَتُبْدِي بِهِ﴾ because it is well known that when a person is grieved by something, he eases the pain of grief upon himself by speaking of it to someone among the people connected to him; that is why you find a person's chest tight with something until he talks about it, is it not so? This is a known matter. So she, were it not that Allah bound her heart, would have revealed that matter; she did not, and said: "This is my son"; she would have disclosed the matter that had happened from her, namely that she placed him in a chest and cast him into the river. If she had done this, the matter would have spread as people say: "news flies," because news is kept hidden as long as it is not revealed; once it is revealed to one person it branches out; so had she disclosed it even to the nearest of people to her, the matter of the infant would have come out and he would have been thrown away. But Allah the Exalted bound her heart.

For this He said: (﴿﴿لَوْلَا أَنْ رَبَطْنَا عَلَى قَلْبِهَا﴾ ﴾ with patience, i.e., We calmed it).

Binding upon something means tightening a bond upon it; note that ﴿رَبَطْنَا عَلَى قَلْبِهَا﴾ is more eloquent than "We calmed her heart," because binding upon it means it cannot move; this is more forceful. Allah the Exalted bound her heart such that she was patient and did not tell anyone what had happened.

But what happened was: ﴿قَالَتْ لِأُخْتِهِ قُصِّيهِ﴾, and it was already mentioned that the author says: (none knew of his birth except his sister).

(﴿﴿لَوْلَا أَنْ رَبَطْنَا عَلَى قَلْبِهَا لِتَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ﴾ the believers in Allah's promise; and the response of (lawlā) is indicated by what precedes it).

His words ﴿رَبَطْنَا عَلَى قَلْبِهَا﴾: i.e., We tightened it with binding, and what is meant is steadying.

His words ﴿لِتَكُونَ﴾: the lām is for causation. Where is the caused?
* Student: The binding of the heart.
* Shaykh: The binding of the heart; meaning: Allah bound her heart for this purpose, ﴿لِتَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾.

His words ﴿لِتَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾: what is meant is not new faith, because she was undoubtedly a believer; and the clearest proof that she was a believer is that she was a woman who cast her son into the river out of trust in what?
* Student: In the promise.
* Shaykh: In the promise of Allah the Mighty and Majestic; but what is meant here by faith is faith in addition to its basis, the increased faith, meaning firmness and certainty: ﴿لِتَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾, and this is what happened.

In the story there are great benefits and virtues of the mother of Musa.

...The verse: revelation is divided, or applied, in three senses.
* Student: Either by sharia, legislated (...).
* Shaykh: Revelation by sharia.
* Student: The second: either revelation of inspiration.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Meaning if revelation came down upon..
* Shaykh: First: revelation by sharia. Second?
* Student: Second: (...) either revelation...
* Shaykh: Revelation of dream.
* Student: Or revelation... meaning a person (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, or revelation of inspiration.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Meaning: or revelation of inspiration, is that right?
Good. An example of the first: revelation by sharia?
* Student: The revelation to the prophets.
* Shaykh: As His saying, the Exalted: ﴿إِنَّا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ كَمَا أَوْحَيْنَا﴾; who will recite the verse?
* Student: His saying the Exalted: ﴿إِنَّا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ كَمَا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى نُوحٍ وَالنَّبِيِّينَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ﴾ [al-Nisa 163].
* Shaykh: Good, and so on; this is revelation by sharia.
The second category: revelation of inspiration; its example?
* Student: (...).
* Another student: ﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا وَمِنَ الشَّجَرِ وَمِمَّا يَعْرِشُونَ﴾ [al-Nahl 68], and this verse as well.
* Shaykh: And this verse: ﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى أُمِّ مُوسَى أَنْ أَرْضِعِيهِ﴾ [al-Qasas 7]. Good, this verse has a second possibility. And revelation of dream.
* Student: A dream, like His saying the Exalted: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And His saying the Exalted: ﴿قَدْ صَدَّقْتَ الرُّؤْيَا﴾ [al-Saffat 105].
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And the saying of the Messenger, peace be upon him: "The good dream..."
* Shaykh: "is a part..."
* Student: "of forty-six parts of prophethood"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6989), and Muslim (1774/8), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raḍiya Allāhu 'anhu.]].
* Shaykh: Yes, and this verse, according to one view: ﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى أُمِّ مُوسَى﴾, some say: revelation of dream.
In this verse: ﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى أُمِّ مُوسَى﴾, there are two commands, two prohibitions and two reports?
* Student: Two commands: ﴿لَا تَخَافِي﴾.
* Shaykh: No, ﴿وَلَا تَخَافِي﴾: is this a command or a prohibition?!
* Student: Two commands: ﴿أَنْ أَرْضِعِيهِ﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿أَنْ أَرْضِعِيهِ﴾, yes.
* Student: ﴿أَلْقِيهِ فِي الْيَمِّ﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿أَلْقِيهِ فِي الْيَمِّ﴾.
* Student: And the two prohibitions: ﴿لَا تَخَافِي وَلَا تَحْزَنِي﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And the two glad tidings: ﴿إِنَّا رَادُّوهُ إِلَيْكِ وَجَاعِلُوهُ مِنَ الْمُرْسَلِينَ﴾ [al-Qasas 7].
* Shaykh: Yes, correct, complete?

In this verse he says: ﴿إِنَّا رَادُّوهُ﴾, plural, while Allah is one; what?
