As for the author's words: (i.e., that he is her son), it is based on his view that she reached the family of Pharaoh; and were it not that Allah bound her heart, she would have said: this is my son. There is no doubt that this is far from the story and far from the meaning.

Rather, ﴿إِنْ كَادَتْ لَتُبْدِي بِهِ﴾ means: she would have disclosed what she had done with him, meaning she would tell people: "By Allah, I did such and such, and I cast my son into the river," and so on; is it not so?

He said: ﴿إِنْ كَادَتْ لَتُبْدِي بِهِ﴾ because it is well known that when a person is grieved by something, he eases the pain of grief upon himself by speaking of it to someone among the people connected to him; that is why you find a person's chest tight with something until he talks about it, is it not so? This is a known matter. So she, were it not that Allah bound her heart, would have revealed that matter; she did not, and said: "This is my son"; she would have disclosed the matter that had happened from her, namely that she placed him in a chest and cast him into the river. If she had done this, the matter would have spread as people say: "news flies," because news is kept hidden as long as it is not revealed; once it is revealed to one person it branches out; so had she disclosed it even to the nearest of people to her, the matter of the infant would have come out and he would have been thrown away. But Allah the Exalted bound her heart.

For this He said: (﴿﴿لَوْلَا أَنْ رَبَطْنَا عَلَى قَلْبِهَا﴾ ﴾ with patience, i.e., We calmed it).

Binding upon something means tightening a bond upon it; note that ﴿رَبَطْنَا عَلَى قَلْبِهَا﴾ is more eloquent than "We calmed her heart," because binding upon it means it cannot move; this is more forceful. Allah the Exalted bound her heart such that she was patient and did not tell anyone what had happened.

But what happened was: ﴿قَالَتْ لِأُخْتِهِ قُصِّيهِ﴾, and it was already mentioned that the author says: (none knew of his birth except his sister).

(﴿﴿لَوْلَا أَنْ رَبَطْنَا عَلَى قَلْبِهَا لِتَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ﴾ the believers in Allah's promise; and the response of (lawlā) is indicated by what precedes it).

His words ﴿رَبَطْنَا عَلَى قَلْبِهَا﴾: i.e., We tightened it with binding, and what is meant is steadying.

His words ﴿لِتَكُونَ﴾: the lām is for causation. Where is the caused?
* Student: The binding of the heart.
* Shaykh: The binding of the heart; meaning: Allah bound her heart for this purpose, ﴿لِتَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾.

His words ﴿لِتَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾: what is meant is not new faith, because she was undoubtedly a believer; and the clearest proof that she was a believer is that she was a woman who cast her son into the river out of trust in what?
* Student: In the promise.
* Shaykh: In the promise of Allah the Mighty and Majestic; but what is meant here by faith is faith in addition to its basis, the increased faith, meaning firmness and certainty: ﴿لِتَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾, and this is what happened.

In the story there are great benefits and virtues of the mother of Musa.

...The verse: revelation is divided, or applied, in three senses.
* Student: Either by sharia, legislated (...).
* Shaykh: Revelation by sharia.
* Student: The second: either revelation of inspiration.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Meaning if revelation came down upon..
* Shaykh: First: revelation by sharia. Second?
* Student: Second: (...) either revelation...
* Shaykh: Revelation of dream.
* Student: Or revelation... meaning a person (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, or revelation of inspiration.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Meaning: or revelation of inspiration, is that right?
Good. An example of the first: revelation by sharia?
* Student: The revelation to the prophets.
* Shaykh: As His saying, the Exalted: ﴿إِنَّا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ كَمَا أَوْحَيْنَا﴾; who will recite the verse?
* Student: His saying the Exalted: ﴿إِنَّا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ كَمَا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى نُوحٍ وَالنَّبِيِّينَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ﴾ [al-Nisa 163].
* Shaykh: Good, and so on; this is revelation by sharia.
The second category: revelation of inspiration; its example?
* Student: (...).
* Another student: ﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا وَمِنَ الشَّجَرِ وَمِمَّا يَعْرِشُونَ﴾ [al-Nahl 68], and this verse as well.
* Shaykh: And this verse: ﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى أُمِّ مُوسَى أَنْ أَرْضِعِيهِ﴾ [al-Qasas 7]. Good, this verse has a second possibility. And revelation of dream.
* Student: A dream, like His saying the Exalted: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And His saying the Exalted: ﴿قَدْ صَدَّقْتَ الرُّؤْيَا﴾ [al-Saffat 105].
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And the saying of the Messenger, peace be upon him: "The good dream..."
* Shaykh: "is a part..."
* Student: "of forty-six parts of prophethood"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6989), and Muslim (1774/8), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raḍiya Allāhu 'anhu.]].
* Shaykh: Yes, and this verse, according to one view: ﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى أُمِّ مُوسَى﴾, some say: revelation of dream.
In this verse: ﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى أُمِّ مُوسَى﴾, there are two commands, two prohibitions and two reports?
* Student: Two commands: ﴿لَا تَخَافِي﴾.
* Shaykh: No, ﴿وَلَا تَخَافِي﴾: is this a command or a prohibition?!
* Student: Two commands: ﴿أَنْ أَرْضِعِيهِ﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿أَنْ أَرْضِعِيهِ﴾, yes.
* Student: ﴿أَلْقِيهِ فِي الْيَمِّ﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿أَلْقِيهِ فِي الْيَمِّ﴾.
* Student: And the two prohibitions: ﴿لَا تَخَافِي وَلَا تَحْزَنِي﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And the two glad tidings: ﴿إِنَّا رَادُّوهُ إِلَيْكِ وَجَاعِلُوهُ مِنَ الْمُرْسَلِينَ﴾ [al-Qasas 7].
* Shaykh: Yes, correct, complete?

In this verse he says: ﴿إِنَّا رَادُّوهُ﴾, plural, while Allah is one; what?
* Student: Meaning that Allah is one.
* Shaykh: He says ﴿إِنَّا رَادُّوهُ﴾ in plural?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: But how is Allah one, glorified and exalted, and He says ﴿إِنَّا رَادُّوهُ﴾?
* Student: Meaning Allah (...).
* Another student: This plural is for magnification; the magnification of Allah.
* Shaykh: This plural is for magnification; Allah, blessed and exalted, speaks of Himself in the form of magnification.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 28, verses 7–10 (part 3 of 4):**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up﴾ [Al-Qasas: 8]. Why "*iltaqatahu*" (picked him up) and not "*akhadhahu*" (took him)?

* Student: O Shaykh, I did not understand the question.
* Shaykh: The question is: why the expression *iltaqatahu* instead of *akhadhahu*?
* Student: (...).
* Another student: (...).
* Shaykh: We said that *iltiqat* (picking up) is specific to what? To human beings. *Iltaqatahu*, as the scholars say, and they call him *al-laqit* (the foundling). *Al-laqit* is specific to a human being. *Al-laqit* is a child who has been abandoned or a lost child. This is the expression. It may also be said, as the brothers said, that *iltaqatuhu* means *akhadhuhu*, that is, without any compensation and by way of seizure, as if he were a spoil they had taken.

The lam in His saying: ﴿so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾?

* Student: The lam is for consequence (*lam al-'aqibah*).
* Shaykh: The lam is for consequence. Why could it not be for causation (*ta'lil*)?
* Student: Because they did not pick him up in order that he would become an enemy to them, but the outcome was that.
* Shaykh: But the outcome was that, that is known. If they had known that he would be an enemy and a grief, they would have killed him. Yes.
Has anyone among the people of knowledge said otherwise?
* Student: (...) in Allah's knowledge.
* Shaykh: Yes, in Allah's knowledge. But what is the correct view?
* Student: That it is for consequence.
* Shaykh: That it is for consequence, not that it is a causal explanation of the act (...) *iltaqatahu*.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were sinners﴾. This is a causal explanation. This sentence is explanatory. Where is the thing being explained? ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief. Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were sinners﴾ [Al-Qasas: 8].

* Student: An explanatory sentence?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: The thing being explained?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: ﴿so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [Al-Qasas: 8].
* Shaykh: Yes. This explanation explains what precedes it. The purpose of the picking up was not that; that is, he would become an enemy and a grief because they are sinners.

Now, His saying: ﴿The heart of the mother of Musa became empty﴾ [Al-Qasas: 10]. Empty of what?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...). I am not asking why it was empty. I am asking: empty of what?
* Student: Of grief.
* Another student: Of everything except Musa.
* Shaykh: Yes, correct. Empty of the remembrance of everything; there was nothing in her heart except Musa. Clear?

Now, His saying: ﴿It almost revealed him﴾ [Al-Qasas: 10]. This *in*: what is this *in*?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is *in* of negation!
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What (...)? (...). ﴿This is none but a noble angel﴾ [Yusuf: 31], meaning: this is not but a noble angel.
* Student: She was close to revealing it (...).
* Shaykh: That is, she was not close to revealing it! When we brought evidence, we saw in it a possibility.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: This (...), yes.
* Student: (...) it is a lightened form of the heavy (*mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah*).
* Shaykh: And it cannot be a negation?
* Student: It cannot be a negation.
* Shaykh: What prevents it?
* Student: The presence of the lam, the lam (...) that distinguishes.
* Shaykh: Yes, what else?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. That is, there are two impediments: one verbal, which is the lam you mentioned.
* Student: And the second is semantic: that she "almost revealed it" (*kadat latubdi bihi*), and not (...), so she was close to revealing it, were it not that Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, strengthened her heart.
* Shaykh: Yes, this is the meaning. Where is the semantic evidence?
* Student: The semantic evidence is that Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, intends that she almost revealed it, (...) reveal it.
* Shaykh: There is no semantic evidence in the context, that is, from the context of the verse?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, all right.
* Student: His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿Had We not fortified her heart﴾ [Al-Qasas: 10].
* Shaykh: Yes, good. And does fortifying imply that (...)?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Good.

* * *

Let us now take the benefits. Some benefits are derived from these verses:

* First: from the first verse, His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿And We inspired to the mother of Musa﴾ [Al-Qasas: 7]. It shows Allah's honouring of the mother of Musa through this inspiration.
* Among its benefits also: Allah's care for Musa. Yes.
* It also shows that prophets, like other human beings, need nourishment, as in His saying:
* Student: ﴿Suckle him﴾.
* Shaykh: As in His saying: ﴿Suckle him﴾.
* It may also be derived from it that breastfeeding is obligatory, if we take the command as obligatory and not as guidance. But what do the legal principles require? They require the obligation of breastfeeding and the rescue of a person whose life is protected.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the strength of the faith of the mother of Musa, and this is one of her virtues. How? By placing him in the river, although he is her son. This is something that only a truly faithful person would do.
* Among the benefits of the verse: we have mentioned Allah's honouring of the mother of Musa, which is derived in fact from several aspects: from this revelation and inspiration, from His reassurance in His saying: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve﴾, and from His giving her good news that he will be returned to her and that He will make him one of the messengers.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the demonstration of Allah, may He be exalted's power, that this child who was cast into the river, and the river is a place of destruction, or not? Allah preserved him, and he remained, and at the end of his affair he became one of the messengers.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that one should reassure the grieved by giving him good news about his future, because He says: ﴿Indeed, We will return him to you and make him one of the messengers﴾.
* In it: the affirmation of prophethood for Musa as well, or not? The affirmation of messengerhood for Musa, by His saying: ﴿and make him one of the messengers﴾.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ and so on to the end [Al-Qasas: 8].

* Among the benefits of this verse, first: that the followers and entourage of a man are his family, by His saying: ﴿the family of Pharaoh﴾. You know that the author explained it by saying: (the helpers of Pharaoh).
* Among its benefits also: that however much a person may rise in arrogance and haughtiness, he does not know the future. From where is this taken? From the fact that the family of Pharaoh did not know that this child would become an enemy and a grief to them.
* Among its benefits: that the believers are enemies to the disbelievers, by His saying: ﴿so that he might become for them an enemy﴾; and that they are also a grief to them. This is clear: the Muslims are enemies to the disbelievers and are also a grief to them. There is no doubt that they are harmed by what pleases them, and vice versa.
* Among the benefits of the verse also: that a person may strive for that which will be his own destruction, because these people strove for that which was their own destruction. They picked up this child who would become an enemy and a grief to them.
* Among its benefits: the demonstration of Allah, may He be exalted's power, that this boy or child, whose sons the Children of Israel were killing, where was he raised? In the lap of Pharaoh, in his house. Although Pharaoh was searching for the sons of the Children of Israel in order to kill them, Allah, may He be glorified, said, in the language of the situation: "This one whose sons of the Children of Israel you kill (and this is from (...)) will live in your lap." This is one of the greatest proofs of Allah, may He be glorified's power, and that a person should not rely on material causes, for Allah, may He be exalted, changes things.
* Among its benefits: that Pharaoh, Haman and their soldiers were upon falsehood, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were sinners﴾ [Al-Qasas: 8]. There is a difference between *khati'* (one who sins) and *mukhti'* (one who errs): the *khati'* is the one who commits sin deliberately, and the *mukhti'* is the one who commits it without intent, out of ignorance.
* In this verse there is evidence that Haman, the minister of Pharaoh, had great authority in the kingdom of the family of Pharaoh, by His saying: ﴿and their soldiers were sinners﴾. In several verses Allah attributes the soldiers to Pharaoh alone, because Pharaoh is the reference point for these soldiers, and it is attributed to him alone. And, considering that Haman had influence because he was a minister, I do not know whether he was a minister of the interior or of foreign affairs.
* Student: Minister of foreign affairs.
* Shaykh: All of them, apparently. A minister in all his affairs. He is a minister, and a minister normally acts in the domain for which he has been appointed.
* Among the benefits of the following verse:
* First: the demonstration of the virtue of the wife of Pharaoh, from her saying: ﴿Do not kill him﴾ [Al-Qasas: 9].
* In it also: evidence of her insight (*firasah*), because she expected that he would benefit them, but what she expected did not happen in every respect. It benefited whom? It benefited her, but it harmed Pharaoh.
* In it also: evidence for what has been said: "Affliction is entrusted to speech," and optimism is likewise; because with regard to the wife of Pharaoh, she said: ﴿A comfort of the eye for me and for you﴾, so she was optimistic about him, and that came about for her, and he became a comfort of the eye.
* In it also: evidence that a person should adopt the methods that achieve the intended goal, by her saying: ﴿A comfort of the eye for me and for you; do not kill him; perhaps he will benefit us﴾. Whether she expected that or not, this statement from her must be a cause for Pharaoh's agreement to what she requested.
* Among its benefits: that it shows Pharaoh had resolved to kill Musa. From where is this derived? From her saying: ﴿Do not kill him﴾. So it appears that he had resolved upon it. Yes.
* Among its benefits also: the limitation of a human being's knowledge, however high he rises in his exaltation and arrogance, by His saying: ﴿while they did not perceive﴾.
* And is the permissibility of adoption derived from it? Is the permissibility of adoption derived from it?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...). Let us see whether this is established from the verse or not.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿Or we may take him as a son﴾. Or it may be said that the meaning of ﴿or we may take him as a son﴾ is like a child in our house, in honour, and that ﴿perhaps he will benefit us﴾ [Al-Qasas: 9] is like a servant?
In any case, if what is meant in the verse by ﴿take him as a son﴾ is adopting him (*tabanni*), then this practice was abrogated (*nusikha*). It existed at the beginning of Islam and was then abrogated. If what is meant by ﴿take him as a son﴾ is that he would be like a son in honour without us employing him, then this does not indicate adoption, and it is a possibility.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, but my point is that adoption was well known among them. Is this what is meant by the verse, and was adoption well known among them or not?

Then Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And the heart of the mother of Musa became empty. It almost revealed him﴾ [Al-Qasas: 10].

* Among the benefits of this verse: that a person may have a state when affliction descends that is different from his state before it descended. Do you understand this benefit?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: That when affliction descends upon a person, his state may change. From where?
* Student: ﴿And the heart of the mother of Musa became empty﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿The heart of the mother of Musa became empty﴾, although at first she had tranquillity. That is why she placed him in the chest and cast him into the river, and this is the utmost of tranquillity. But now her heart became empty, anxious, as if there were nothing in the world except her son. This is the reality: a person has a state before affliction descends and a state after it descends. For this reason, a person should not expose himself to affliction.

It is related that Sahnun, one of the companions of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, was at the utmost of contentment with Allah's decree and (...) worship and ... and so on. One day he said a line of poetry, but I only remember its meaning, only its meaning comes to mind. The meaning of the line is: "I am patient, so test me however you wish." He was then afflicted with difficulty in urinating; he could only urinate with great exertion. He used to pass by the children in the Quranic schools and say: "Pray for your liar uncle." Because children's supplications are hoped to be answered. The point is that a person has a state before affliction, and after affliction his state changes.

Likewise, in matters of the Shariah: the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever hears of the Dajjal, let him keep far from him, for a man may come to him while he is a believer, or thinking he is a believer, and then he will continue to be with him until he destroys him."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4319) from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn, and its wording is: "Whoever hears of the Dajjal, let him keep far from him, for by Allah, a man will come to him thinking he is a believer, and so he follows him because of the doubts that he brings," or "because of the doubts that he brings."]] This is the reality: a person must guard himself against affliction.

It is also related from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that he said: "Let none of you humiliate himself." They said: "How does one humiliate himself?" He said: "By exposing himself to affliction that he cannot repel."[[Narrated by Ibn Majah (4016) from the hadith of Hudhayfah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It is not fitting for a believer to humiliate himself." They said: "And how does he humiliate himself?" He said: "By exposing himself to affliction that he cannot bear."]] This is the meaning of the hadith. The conclusion is that a person has a state before affliction exists and a state after it.

* Also in it: evidence that a person is not held accountable for what human nature inclines toward. What human nature requires is not something for which a person is held accountable. The reason is that the heart of the mother of Musa ought not to have been empty of the remembrance of Allah, may He be exalted, and of the Hereafter, yet it became empty, with nothing in it at all remembering anything except the remembrance of Musa. This is what human nature requires, because great matters that descend upon a person make him forget everything.
* Also in it: evidence of the virtue of the mother of Musa, may Allah be pleased with her, in that she did not reveal what was in her heart to anyone, by His saying: ﴿It almost revealed him, had We not fortified her heart﴾.
* In the verse: evidence that a person is in need of Allah, may He be exalted, in all his states, and especially when events descend; by His saying: ﴿Had We not fortified her heart﴾. A person is in need of Allah, may He be exalted, and were it not for Allah's help, a person would accomplish nothing: he would neither be patient in affliction nor thankful in ease.
* Also in it: evidence for the affirmation of causes and means, by His saying: ﴿so that she might be among the believers﴾.
Who denies causes and means?
* Student: The Jahmiyyah.
* Shaykh: The Jahmiyyah, and the Ash'aris as well. Even manifest, sensory causes they deny. They say: a thing happens *at* it, not *by* it. Even if you take a stone and strike glass with it and it breaks, they do not say that the glass broke *by* the stone, but that it broke *at* it. Yes. Although if you place the stone on the glass, on top of it, it does not break, does it? It does not break. If you place it on top of it, it does not break. But if you strike it with it, it breaks.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, yes. He says: the pain occurred when you struck, not *by* it. It was only (...).
* Student: The clearer example, O our Shaykh, for their shaykhs: whoever takes a medicine while sick, supplicating and saying: "O Allah, make my cure *at* it, not *by* it."
* Shaykh: Yes, yes, indeed. Based on their denial of causes. We ask Allah for well-being.

In his statement, ﴿so that she might be among the believers﴾, there is evidence that faith and perfection are more common among men, since He did not say "among the believing women." This is further shown by the Almighty's words about Mary: ﴿And she affirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was among the devout﴾ [At-Tahrim 12]. For this reason, a hadith states: "Many men attained perfection, but among women, none attained perfection except Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh."[[Agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh); al-Bukhari (3411) and Muslim (2431/70), from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with him).]] There is no doubt that faith is greater, firmer and more abundant in men. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, in a hadith: "I have not seen anyone more deficient in intellect and religion who takes away the reason of a resolute man more than one of you (women)."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (304), from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him).]] We have established this so that a person must show consideration toward women. A man must show consideration toward women, and they need care. Also, they need not to be granted everything they ask for, because they are deficient in intellect and deficient in religion, as the Prophet (ﷺ) described them.

* Also in the verse there is evidence for affirming al-qada' wal-qadar (divine decree and predestination). Where do we take it from?
* Student: ﴿Had We not strengthened her heart﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Had We not strengthened her heart﴾. This is from Allah's decree and predestination.

Now, can a name of Allah be derived from this verb, so that we call Allah "al-Rabit" (the One who binds)?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: No, it cannot be derived. Everything in the universe comes from Allah's action and decree, yet we do not derive a name from every single thing in the universe. Can we derive a name for Allah from everything in the universe? No, that is not possible. Allah's actions are varied and their types are many, and an action is not the same as a name. For this reason, we do not derive, for example, from ﴿They plot and Allah plots﴾ [Al-Anfal 30] that Allah is called "the Plotter." We do not derive from His words ﴿And He is their deceiver﴾ [An-Nisa 142] that Allah is called "the Deceiver," and we do not derive from ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 15] that He is "the Mocker." These actions are restricted in their types. It is correct to say: Allah mocks the hypocrites, Allah deceives the hypocrites, Allah plots against the plotters, and similar statements. The author said: (﴿so that she might be among the believers﴾ [Al-Qasas 10], those who affirm Allah's promise).

We should not interpret faith (iman) merely as affirmation (tasdiq). Rather, we should make it more comprehensive than that, meaning the steadfast affirmation that is shown through what is required of it.

(The response of ﴿lawla﴾ (if not / were it not) is indicated by what precedes it.) Where is ﴿lawla﴾?
* Student: ﴿Had We not strengthened her heart﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Had We not strengthened her heart﴾. What is its estimate? It would have disclosed it (﴿لَأَبْدَتْ بِهِ﴾). For this reason the author said that it is (indicated by what precedes it), and did not say that it is "what precedes it," but rather "indicated by it." Did you pay attention, brothers?

We have previously discussed whether such an expression requires a response (jawab) or not. We mentioned that some scholars say it does not require a response, because if you supplied a response the speech would be awkward. So it does not need a response. (Honor the student if he is diligent.) So this does not require a response. Yes, because if you answered it, saying: "Honor the student if he is diligent, then honor him," that would be unsound speech, an awkward statement. This meaning that we have mentioned was pointed out by Ibn al-Qayyim in his book At-Tibyan fi Aqsam al-Qur'an (The Clarification on the Divisions of the Qur'an).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 11–13 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him," so she watched him from a distance while they did not perceive.﴾ [al-Qasas: 11].

﴿She said to his sister﴾. The author says: (Maryam). Maryam... we say to the author: from where do you have that her name is Maryam?

* Student: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾ [Maryam: 28] (...).

* The Shaykh: That is not her. This is not Maryam, because the one you mentioned is Maryam the mother of 'Isa, and between her and Musa there are long ages.

In any case, this is from the Israelite reports (al-Isra'iliyyat), and specifying her name, if any benefit depended on it, Allah, blessed and exalted, would have made it clear. But what concerns us is not specifying the name. What matters is that we know this woman's relation to Musa's mother and to Musa as well. She is Musa's sister, so what is she in relation to Musa's mother?
If she has become a sister of Musa, what is her relation to Musa's mother?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, did you not understand my words? Did you understand the question? ﴿And she said to his sister﴾. Sister of whom?

* The Student: Sister of Musa.

* The Shaykh: Sister of Musa. If this woman has become a sister of Musa, what is her relation to Musa's mother? Do you see that the question is not (...).

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: What is she to Musa's mother?

* The Student: You mean a relative?

* The Shaykh: Yes, a relative of Musa's mother.

* The Student: A relative of Musa's mother.

* The Shaykh: Yes, what is she?

* The Student: (...) his wet-nurse.

* The Shaykh: What is this?! Alright, what (...)?

* Student: (...) her mother (...).

* The Shaykh: If she has become Musa's sister, her relation to Musa's mother is what?

* The Student: That she is her daughter.

* The Shaykh: Her daughter?

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Certainly?

* The Student: Yes, certainly.

* The Shaykh: No doubt still?

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Or her daughter?

* The Student: Or her maternal aunt.

* The Shaykh: Or..

* The Student: The apparent meaning of the verse: her daughter.

* The Shaykh: Alright, what is the apparent meaning?

* The Student: ﴿And she said to his sister﴾.

* The Shaykh: Alright, his sister.

* The Student: Musa's mother, that is, she said to Musa's sister.

* The Shaykh: Alright, Musa's sister from his father, is that not possible?

* The Student: The apparent (...).

* The Shaykh: (...) from the apparent.

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: What is the basis of the apparent meaning?

* The Student: He did not say: (...) to his sister from his father.

* Student: The basis of (...).

* The Shaykh: No, the apparent... In any case, what you say may be correct, meaning that if she were from the father or from the mother, had she been from his father or from his mother, it would have been specified. When it is unrestricted, brotherhood is taken in its complete sense, which is from both mother and father, although there is a possibility that she is from his mother or from his father. But the apparent meaning, as you have said, is that since it is unrestricted, it is interpreted as the most complete kind of brotherhood, which is full (shaqiqah) sibling.

She said: ﴿Follow him﴾, that is: (follow his track until you know his news).

Al-qass means: tracing the trail, that is, follow his trail and search for him.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿so she watched him﴾, that is: (she saw him). The sister went, and the apparent meaning of the noble verse, ﴿so she watched﴾, with the fa' indicating sequence and immediacy, is that she did not go far before she saw him.

His saying: ﴿from a distance﴾ (from a far place). ﴿Junub﴾ means far, and on this basis the qualified noun is omitted, and the sense is: from a far place, far from her, but she recognized that this was her brother.

(Stealthily) he says: (﴿so she watched him from a distance﴾ from a far place, stealthily). What is the meaning of stealthily? Furtively; that is, she did not keep her gaze fixed on him, for if she had kept her gaze fixed on him and approached him quickly, and signs of her intention had appeared, they would have sensed it. But she did not look at him in a way that they would perceive. She was glancing furtively, stealing a look, and this is clear, although there is no proof for it in the verses, it is obvious that it must have been so, because if she had seen him and gone to him, and kept staring, and the like, they would have become suspicious of this matter and held her back. But she watched him from a distance, stealing glances.

﴿while they did not perceive﴾ that she was his sister and that she was watching him. Who are the ones who ﴿did not perceive﴾? Who? The people of Pharaoh. They did not know. But the woman was clever; she kept looking from afar until she reached him, ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ that she was his sister or was watching him, because she did not display movements that would indicate that.

As for his saying: ﴿while they did not perceive﴾, what is the grammatical position of this clause?

* Students: A circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

* The Shaykh: A circumstantial clause of whom? Of the subject of ﴿watched﴾, meaning: and the state being that they did not perceive (...). A circumstantial clause is not required to be a description of its referent. That is why you say: Zayd came while the sun was rising. This clause is circumstantial, though it is not one of Zayd's attributes.

So here: she watched him while they did not perceive. If someone said: how do you make it a circumstantial clause of the subject of (watched), when it is not one of her attributes? We say: a circumstantial clause requires only the slightest connection.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We had forbidden to him the wet-nurses before﴾ [al-Qasas: 12].

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...), the child in reality began to become restless and cry, wanting to nurse, and perhaps they took him out seeking a nurse, and it so happened that his sister saw him.

* The Student: Yes, this was before the request for nursing took place.

* The Shaykh: That is, how is it ﴿so she watched him﴾?

* The Student: Before the request for nursing, when he requested nursing.

* The Shaykh: What is your proof?

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: There is no proof.

* Student: We say: this verse indicates the author's statement: (﴿And the heart of Musa's mother became empty﴾ when she knew of his being taken up).

* The Shaykh: That is, was (...) that you should follow him?

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: (...).

* Student: She sent her to (...).

* The Shaykh: Had she not sent her, (...) in the town.

* Student: She was certain of the good news, his mother (...).

* The Shaykh: There is no doubt that she was certain; otherwise, had she not been certain, she would not have cast him into the river. She ordered her to go out seeking to nurse him, because she knew he would surely return to her.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, no, (...).

He said: (﴿And We had forbidden to him the wet-nurses before﴾, that is: before his return to his mother).

His saying: ﴿We had forbidden﴾ means: We prevented, and tahrim linguistically means prevention, and from it (...).

* * *

His saying: ﴿to his sister﴾. The author specified her as Maryam. What do you say about this specification?

* Student: (...) it is not valid.

* The Shaykh: Yes, and ignorance of it does no harm.

What is the meaning of ﴿Follow him﴾?

* Student: That is: follow his trail.

* The Shaykh: Follow him or track him?

* The Student: That is: track his trail.

* The Shaykh: Track his trail; that is: seek him and follow him.

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Alright, his saying: ﴿so she watched him﴾, what is the meaning of ﴿watched him﴾?

* The Student: That is, she saw him.

* The Shaykh: Alright, the meaning of ﴿from a distance﴾?

* Student: From a far place.

* The Shaykh: A far place. ﴿while they did not perceive﴾?

* The Student: ﴿while they did not perceive﴾, that is: they did not know that she was following him and watching him.

* The Shaykh: Yes, and it is in a position of accusative?

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes. His exalted saying: ﴿And We had forbidden to him the wet-nurses﴾, what is the meaning of ﴿We had forbidden﴾?

* Student: Before his return, (...) We prevented him from nursing at a breast, and this is a decreed prohibition, Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: A decreed prohibition.
Is prohibition divided into two kinds?

* Student: A legislated prohibition, and a cosmic decreed prohibition.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The Student: The legislated is what is from the Sharia.

* The Shaykh: The object of the legislated is what?

* The Student: (...) the Sharia.

* The Shaykh: Yes, what is it connected to? That is, what is the legislated prohibition connected to?

* The Student: To the legislated rulings.

* The Shaykh: To the legislated rulings, and the decreed one to the cosmic rulings.
Alright, is there (...)?

* Student: The decreed (...).

* The Shaykh: No, other than it. Did we mention other than these two examples?

* Student: ﴿And it is forbidden upon a city which We have destroyed that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiya: 95].

* The Shaykh: Alright, and the second example?

* Student: ﴿Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 26].

* The Shaykh: ﴿He said, "Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land"﴾, that is, a decreed prohibition.

* The Shaykh: (...).

* * *

﴿to the people of a house﴾ [al-Qasas: 12], and she did not say: to his people. Of course, had she said: to his people, the matter would have become clear and they would have seized her, him and his people. Rather she said: ﴿to the people of a house﴾, indefinite, as if they did not know him, although she, or the people of the house, is his mother, Musa's mother.

﴿to the people of a house who will rear him for you﴾ (﴿the people of a house﴾ when she saw their compassion toward him). (When she saw their compassion) means: the compassion of the family of Pharaoh toward this child, and that they loved to find someone to undertake his upbringing and nursing, so she said: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household﴾.

(﴿who will rear him for you﴾ with nursing and otherwise). Kafl means undertaking the care of a child; undertaking a child's custody is called kafl, as in His saying: ﴿and Zakariyya took charge of her﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 37], and in another reading: ﴿and Zakariyya' took charge of her﴾. The meaning: I will direct you to a household who will undertake his custody in the most complete manner, as evidenced by her saying: ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾. The act came with a verb, and the intention came with a nominal clause: ﴿who will rear him﴾, because kafala is an act, and ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾, sincerity is based on intention in the heart.

The meaning of ﴿sincere﴾ is: pure, and the origin of nasih is purifying a thing from impurities, and from it His saying: ﴿O you who believe, repent to Allah with sincere repentance﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8], that is, pure from impurities, for Allah alone.

So ﴿sincere﴾: what is the meaning of nush? Purity from impurities, that is: they are wholly sincere to him. And is she truthful in her statement or not?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, truthful without doubt.

As for his saying: ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾, the pronoun in ﴿to him﴾ refers to this child. Without doubt it refers to this child. And if it refers to this child, then if someone says: what is the benefit of the family of Pharaoh being sincere to the people of this house toward him?

We say: the benefit of the family of Pharaoh in that is that they loved this child and wished for someone who would take care of his needs and his upbringing in the most complete way. Therefore...

Alright, the author says: (And she interpreted the pronoun in ﴿to him﴾ as the king, in answer to them, so she was answered). This is based on an Israelite story: when she said: ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾, it seems they raised a question and said: what made you know that they are sincere to him? So she said: I mean that they are sincere to the king. Who is the king? Pharaoh, meaning: and they are sincere to the king. This story is undoubtedly far from correct; rather it is not correct. What is meant is that ﴿to him﴾ refers to the child, and there is nothing that prevents the pronoun from referring to him. Nor is there any need to interpret it as the king, because they (the family of Pharaoh) love, that is, the family of Pharaoh loves whoever is sincere to him, so they are not asking about this matter. Yes, this interpretation by the author is unnecessary.

He says: (So she brought his mother, and he accepted her breast, and they were answered about his accepting it by her saying that her scent was pleasant and her milk was good, so he was permitted to be nursed by her in her house, and she returned with him, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We returned him﴾).

This account that the author mentioned also has no indication in the verse. And whoever says: she is the one who came, and he accepted her breast in front of the people, and she was accused of it, and she defended herself by saying that her breast had a pleasant scent and her milk was good, all of this has no basis.

The correct view is that when she said: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household who will undertake his custody for you and they are sincere to him﴾, they said, what did they say? They said: yes, direct us. So the story is very clear: direct us, so she directed them, and they brought him to his mother. This is more eloquent as a miracle and a sign: his mother, in her house, ordered his sister to go out seeking him, and his sister returned with him only to his mother. As for the claim that the mother went out, and that she put the breast to his mouth, and that she was accused of it and defended herself by saying she had a pleasant scent or pleasant milk, this is not correct, and such matters need not have known natural causes, because they are from the extraordinary, and extraordinary events are not something we need to fit to customary causes; rather they are above custom.

So we say: the matter proceeds according to what came in the noble Qur'an. The mother did not come; Allah did not mention that the mother came, rather He said: ﴿So We returned him to his mother﴾ [al-Qasas: 13].

﴿We returned him﴾, that is: Musa, (﴿to his mother that her eye might be comforted﴾ by meeting him).

﴿might be comforted﴾: it was mentioned before that it is derived either from qarr, which is coolness, or from qarar, which is stillness, and perhaps it includes both meanings: derived from qarar, the eye becomes still and cool.

﴿That her eye might be comforted﴾: here ﴿that﴾ is a particle of causation, and it is a verbal particle (masdariyyah) that puts the imperfect verb in the subjunctive, and for this reason ﴿might be comforted﴾ is in the subjunctive, and the sign of its subjunctive is a visible fatha on the qaf.

* Student: On the ra'.

* The Shaykh: On its end?

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: And the qaf (...).

* Student: The original.

* The Shaykh: This is the original, yes; because it is from qarra yaqarru, and not from qarra yaqirru.

(﴿That her eye might be comforted﴾ by meeting him ﴿and she would not grieve﴾ then). That is: she would not grieve over what had passed, rather the grief would leave her; the eye is comforted and grief leaves her.

(﴿And that she may know that the promise of Allah﴾ of returning him to her ﴿is true﴾). This also... there are three benefits: ﴿might be comforted﴾, ﴿and she would not grieve﴾, and the third: ﴿and that she may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾.

As for the first two, it is clear that her eye is comforted by his return and that she does not grieve, the grief leaves her. But as for his saying: ﴿and that she may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾, this cause had already preceded, for from the moment she cast him into the river she knew that the promise of Allah was true, and if it were not for her knowledge and certainty that the promise of Allah is true, she would not have cast him. So is the knowledge meant here the knowledge of certainty or the eye of certainty?

* The students: The eye of certainty.

* The Shaykh: The eye of certainty, or the truth of certainty if you wish. Her knowledge the first time was knowledge of the thing by report; her second knowledge was knowledge of the thing by its occurrence. There is a difference between a person's knowledge of a thing by report and his knowledge of it by its occurrence. That is why Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said, 'Have you not believed?' He said, 'Yes, but that my heart may be assured'﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. And it has come in a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The report is not like seeing with one's own eyes"[[Narrated by Ahmad (2446) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. So the conclusion is that His saying: ﴿and that she may know﴾ means knowledge of the thing after its occurrence, and as for her knowledge of it by report, that has already preceded, and had she not been confident in the first, she would not have acted.

His saying: ﴿and that she may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾, ﴿promise﴾: they mention that the wa'd (promise) is a promise of what gladdens, and the wa'id (threat) is a warning of what grieves; that is, a promise of good and a threat of evil. Is that so? They say that the evil is from (awada), and the good is from (wa'ada), so they say: awadahu, that is, with evil, and wa'adahu with good.

* Student: Regarding His saying: ﴿So that her eye may be comforted and she would not grieve﴾ [al-Qasas: 13], it is known that when a person's eye is comforted he forgets grief and is made glad.

* The Shaykh: Yes, but it is mentioned; the negation of grief here is to show that the comfort is complete, because the eye may be comforted with some grief still present.

Alright, the promise, what did we say its meaning is? The promise relates to what gladdens, and the threat to what distresses. So is the promise and the truth less than the threat, or are both (equal)?

* Student: Both.

* Another student: No, the threat may be left unfulfilled.

* Another student: The threat (...).

The Shaykh: It is true. The threat and the promise are both true. If we said that the threat is not true, it would follow that there is falsehood in the report of Allah, and that is impossible. But the threat may not be carried out, as a favour from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because it is His right. The threat is the right of Allah, and Allah, Blessed and Exalted, may overlook it, or not? As for the promise, whose right is it? It is the right of the one who is promised, and for this reason it cannot fail to be fulfilled. The poet said:

"Indeed I, whether I threaten him or promise him,
I break my threat and I fulfil my promise."

Because the promise is the right of the one promised, while the threat is the right of the one who threatens.

Let me give you an example. If I say to this man: "If you do such-and-such, I will give you a hundred dinars," what is this?

Student: A promise.

Shaykh: A promise or a threat?

Student: A promise.

Shaykh: Why?

Student: Because it is in (...).

Shaykh: Because it concerns good, yes. If he does what I said, I must fulfil it for him, because the right is his. But suppose I say to my son, for example: "If you do such-and-such, I will imprison you." Then he does it, but I pardon him. Is this permissible or not permissible?

Student: Permissible.

Shaykh: It is permissible, and it is a favour, especially when he pardons while he has the power to punish. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Whether you show good or conceal it, or pardon an evil, indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and All-Powerful﴾ [An-Nisa 149]. But pardoning in a state of incapacity is not praiseworthy.

In summary: the promise and the threat of Allah are both true. But since His promise is a right of the one promised, it must come to pass. And His threat, since it is His right, He may pardon, if He wills, out of generosity and favour, according to what His wisdom requires, glory be to Him.

Student: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾ [Al-A'raf 44]. This is a threat that was applied to a promise.

Shaykh: Yes, that is correct. It was called a promise, either because it is in contrast to (...), so it matches it, or because it is sometimes called that.

He says: ﴿And that you may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾. "True" here means "established." I think we have said that "true" in some contexts has one meaning and in other contexts another meaning. Which of the two meanings is this?

Students: It means "truthful."

Shaykh: Truthful, yes. When truth relates to reports, it means truthfulness, and in rulings it means justice. Accordingly, here it means truthfulness: ﴿And that you may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾, meaning it is truthful, and it cannot fail. For the failure of a promise is either due to the promiser lying or to his inability to carry it out. Both of these are impossible for Allah. There is no falsehood in His word and no incapacity in His action. For this reason, the servants of Allah, glory be to Him, end their supplications by saying: "Indeed You do not break Your promise."

He says: (﴿But most of them﴾, that is, the people, ﴿do not know﴾ this promise, nor that this is his sister.)

The author has restricted the verse, but in reality the verse is general, though most people do not know. That is, they do not possess knowledge that benefits them regarding Allah's promise. So the negation of knowledge here is either to establish ignorance or to negate beneficial knowledge. Most people do not know this, they do not know that the promise of Allah is true.

Student: ﴿Most of them﴾.

Shaykh: Yes, ﴿most of them﴾, meaning the people. I say: most people do not know that the promise of Allah is true, either because of their ignorance or because they do not benefit from this knowledge. The negation of a thing to negate benefit from it is established in the Qur'an: ﴿Do not be like those who say, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [Al-Anfal 21]. Allah, glory be to Him, constantly negates intellect or hearing from people, or things similar to that, because they do not benefit from them. So most people do not know. The author restricted this to the story of Musa, but the verse is general: most people do not know that the promise of Allah is true. I say: either they are ignorant of this, because they do not know what befits Allah's names and attributes, or they do not benefit from this knowledge. Those who do not strive to do good or to avoid evil are, in reality, like the ignorant of the truth that Allah's promise is true. For human nature and reason require that as long as you believe in something, whether it is a promise or a threat, you must strive for it according to the requirement of your faith. If you know that a person will die, and that a believer, when he dies, will find good, will be in Paradise and be saved from the Fire, is this true or not?

Students: True.

Shaykh: True. But the one who does not strive for this Paradise and is absorbed in striving for the perishing world, is this person in reality a knower that Allah's promise is true, or one who benefits from his knowledge?

Student: He did not benefit.

Shaykh: He did not benefit from it, he did not benefit from his knowledge. Had he benefited from it, he would not have missed this great opportunity.

Now, a person who knows that sin is a cause for entering the Fire, knows this, and knows that Allah's promise is true, yet he still dares to commit sins. We say: his knowledge here is deficient. For if he truly believed in that, he would avoid this thing. Thus the meaning of the saying of Allah, the Exalted, is fulfilled: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾.

May Allah have mercy on him, the author analysed the verse, saying: (﴿do not know﴾ this promise), meaning what Allah promised his mother of returning him to her, (nor that this is his sister). Accordingly, the pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ refers to the people of Pharaoh.

(And this is his mother, so he remained with her until she weaned him, and a wage was paid to her, a dinar per day.)

Breastfeeding was expensive at that time. As for his remaining with her until she weaned him, this is clear, for as long as he needed breastfeeding he would stay with her. As for (a wage was paid to her), this too is correct, for a wage was set for her, and they used to send her gifts and presents and honour her, because she was the one caring for this child whom they said would be ﴿a delight of the eye﴾ and ﴿perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾. For this reason it is narrated from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, concerning one who does his work well and takes a wage for it: "He is like the mother of Musa; she nurses her child and takes a wage for it." [1] This is one of the signs of Allah. Her son comes to her, she nurses him and is honoured because of him. What do you think if she had not done this, and had not thrown him into the river, and the people of Pharaoh had not picked him up? She would have remained fearful and anxious, and she would not have gained a wage, honour or esteem from these tyrants.

As for his saying (a dinar per day), this is not accepted, because our method in such matters is: what is established from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is accepted; what is not established from the reports of the Children of Israel, we withhold judgement on, and should not affirm it with such certainty. We may narrate it, but we do not affirm it.

He says (a dinar per day). Look, then he raised an objection: (she took it because it was the property of a combatant enemy). Glory be to Allah, the Most High, the Mighty! The notion of some scholars is strange. Did she take it because it was the property of a combatant enemy, or did she take it because it was a wage for nursing him?

A wage. There is no problem with that. But that she took a wage because it was the property of an enemy combatant, this has no basis, it has no basis. One cannot say, for example, that since Musa's mother was the only one he would accept breastfeeding from, her nursing him was an obligation upon her, and one may not take a compensation for an obligation, so the taking of compensation here becomes the taking of the property of an enemy combatant.

We say: even the property of an enemy combatant, if it comes by way of a contract, is it permissible to take it or not?

Student: It is not permissible.

Shaykh: No, it is not permissible. You take it only according to the terms of the contract. The dealing between you and the enemy combatants is like a safe-conduct; indeed, it is a safe-conduct in reality. So the correct view is that she took it because she was paid for her care and nursing of him.

Student: The service, (...).

Shaykh: That does not contradict it. Had she not taken it, there would have been a trial in that, and it would have been known that she was a relative of his or something similar. She took it because they believed she was not his mother, and they believed this child would belong to them.

Student: It is not permissible (...). If it were permissible outwardly, taking it inwardly would not be permissible.

Shaykh: It is permissible inwardly, because of her caring for him in their eyes.

The author says: (So she brought him to Pharaoh, and he was raised by him, as Allah the Exalted said, relating about him in Surah Ash-Shu'ara: ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child, and did you not remain among us for years of your life?﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 18]).

He was raised in the house of the king, and he rode the mounts of kings and wore the clothing of kings. Instead of being with his mother, where without doubt this would not have happened to him, he now became honoured and esteemed. This was by the subjugation of Allah, glory be to Him, for him.

Student: (...). It is not reported that Musa contacted his mother (...).

Shaykh: He contacted her?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: In any case he would visit her, because she was his mother.

Student: Because when he finished weaning, she returned to..

Shaykh: He was raised by Pharaoh, but he would come to his mother, because he would say: "This is my mother by nursing," and no one would object to his (...) his mother. No one would object that he went to her, because she was his mother through nursing.

Student: Did he not know the truth?

Shaykh: They did not know.

Student: Musa?

Shaykh: No, he knew the truth. He must have known, and his mother must have informed him too.

Student: The evidence?

Shaykh: The evidence is that she, when she cared for him and he grew up, he would certainly be in her custody constantly; meaning he would come to her, and of necessity she would be teaching him.

Student: No, perhaps not (...).

Shaykh: Never (...). For he feared for himself just as she feared for him. Never, there was no fear at all. As long as the man feared for himself, it is not possible (...).

Student: The naming, Shaykh, is it from her or from the people of Pharaoh?

Shaykh: The naming (...). It is possible that she named him that, or that it was from the people of Pharaoh. (...) the people of Pharaoh, how would they know whether she named him?

Student: A Hebrew name, I mean.

Shaykh: Yes, indeed, except that perhaps it was, for example, a mark of Allah's honour to him, that they named him with what his mother named him. I do not know, by Allah.

He says: (﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child, and did you not remain among us for years of your life?﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 18]) So the man remained with the king, honoured and esteemed.

---

[1] Abu Dawud narrated in al-Maraseel (332) from Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The example of those among my nation who fight and take a reward, that is, who strengthen themselves against their enemy, is the example of the mother of Musa: she nurses her child and takes her wage." Ibn Kathir cited it in his Tafsir without a chain of narration, in his commentary on Surah Ta-Ha verse 40 and Surah Al-Qasas verses 12-13, with the wording: "The example of the craftsman who works and seeks reward from Allah in his craft is like the mother of Musa: she nurses her child and takes her wage."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 11–13 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him," so she watched him from a distance while they did not perceive.﴾ [al-Qasas: 11].

﴿She said to his sister﴾. The author says: (Maryam). Maryam... we say to the author: from where do you have that her name is Maryam?

* Student: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾ [Maryam: 28] (...).

* The Shaykh: That is not her. This is not Maryam, because the one you mentioned is Maryam the mother of 'Isa, and between her and Musa there are long ages.

In any case, this is from the Israelite reports (al-Isra'iliyyat), and specifying her name, if any benefit depended on it, Allah, blessed and exalted, would have made it clear. But what concerns us is not specifying the name. What matters is that we know this woman's relation to Musa's mother and to Musa as well. She is Musa's sister, so what is she in relation to Musa's mother?
If she has become a sister of Musa, what is her relation to Musa's mother?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, did you not understand my words? Did you understand the question? ﴿And she said to his sister﴾. Sister of whom?

* The Student: Sister of Musa.

* The Shaykh: Sister of Musa. If this woman has become a sister of Musa, what is her relation to Musa's mother? Do you see that the question is not (...).

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: What is she to Musa's mother?

* The Student: You mean a relative?

* The Shaykh: Yes, a relative of Musa's mother.

* The Student: A relative of Musa's mother.

* The Shaykh: Yes, what is she?

* The Student: (...) his wet-nurse.

* The Shaykh: What is this?! Alright, what (...)?

* Student: (...) her mother (...).

* The Shaykh: If she has become Musa's sister, her relation to Musa's mother is what?

* The Student: That she is her daughter.

* The Shaykh: Her daughter?

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Certainly?

* The Student: Yes, certainly.

* The Shaykh: No doubt still?

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Or her daughter?

* The Student: Or her maternal aunt.

* The Shaykh: Or..

* The Student: The apparent meaning of the verse: her daughter.

* The Shaykh: Alright, what is the apparent meaning?

* The Student: ﴿And she said to his sister﴾.

* The Shaykh: Alright, his sister.

* The Student: Musa's mother, that is, she said to Musa's sister.

* The Shaykh: Alright, Musa's sister from his father, is that not possible?

* The Student: The apparent (...).

* The Shaykh: (...) from the apparent.

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: What is the basis of the apparent meaning?

* The Student: He did not say: (...) to his sister from his father.

* Student: The basis of (...).

* The Shaykh: No, the apparent... In any case, what you say may be correct, meaning that if she were from the father or from the mother, had she been from his father or from his mother, it would have been specified. When it is unrestricted, brotherhood is taken in its complete sense, which is from both mother and father, although there is a possibility that she is from his mother or from his father. But the apparent meaning, as you have said, is that since it is unrestricted, it is interpreted as the most complete kind of brotherhood, which is full (shaqiqah) sibling.

She said: ﴿Follow him﴾, that is: (follow his track until you know his news).

Al-qass means: tracing the trail, that is, follow his trail and search for him.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿so she watched him﴾, that is: (she saw him). The sister went, and the apparent meaning of the noble verse, ﴿so she watched﴾, with the fa' indicating sequence and immediacy, is that she did not go far before she saw him.

His saying: ﴿from a distance﴾ (from a far place). ﴿Junub﴾ means far, and on this basis the qualified noun is omitted, and the sense is: from a far place, far from her, but she recognized that this was her brother.

(Stealthily) he says: (﴿so she watched him from a distance﴾ from a far place, stealthily). What is the meaning of stealthily? Furtively; that is, she did not keep her gaze fixed on him, for if she had kept her gaze fixed on him and approached him quickly, and signs of her intention had appeared, they would have sensed it. But she did not look at him in a way that they would perceive. She was glancing furtively, stealing a look, and this is clear, although there is no proof for it in the verses, it is obvious that it must have been so, because if she had seen him and gone to him, and kept staring, and the like, they would have become suspicious of this matter and held her back. But she watched him from a distance, stealing glances.

﴿while they did not perceive﴾ that she was his sister and that she was watching him. Who are the ones who ﴿did not perceive﴾? Who? The people of Pharaoh. They did not know. But the woman was clever; she kept looking from afar until she reached him, ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ that she was his sister or was watching him, because she did not display movements that would indicate that.

As for his saying: ﴿while they did not perceive﴾, what is the grammatical position of this clause?

* Students: A circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

* The Shaykh: A circumstantial clause of whom? Of the subject of ﴿watched﴾, meaning: and the state being that they did not perceive (...). A circumstantial clause is not required to be a description of its referent. That is why you say: Zayd came while the sun was rising. This clause is circumstantial, though it is not one of Zayd's attributes.

So here: she watched him while they did not perceive. If someone said: how do you make it a circumstantial clause of the subject of (watched), when it is not one of her attributes? We say: a circumstantial clause requires only the slightest connection.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We had forbidden to him the wet-nurses before﴾ [al-Qasas: 12].

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...), the child in reality began to become restless and cry, wanting to nurse, and perhaps they took him out seeking a nurse, and it so happened that his sister saw him.

* The Student: Yes, this was before the request for nursing took place.

* The Shaykh: That is, how is it ﴿so she watched him﴾?

* The Student: Before the request for nursing, when he requested nursing.

* The Shaykh: What is your proof?

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: There is no proof.

* Student: We say: this verse indicates the author's statement: (﴿And the heart of Musa's mother became empty﴾ when she knew of his being taken up).

* The Shaykh: That is, was (...) that you should follow him?

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: (...).

* Student: She sent her to (...).

* The Shaykh: Had she not sent her, (...) in the town.

* Student: She was certain of the good news, his mother (...).

* The Shaykh: There is no doubt that she was certain; otherwise, had she not been certain, she would not have cast him into the river. She ordered her to go out seeking to nurse him, because she knew he would surely return to her.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, no, (...).

He said: (﴿And We had forbidden to him the wet-nurses before﴾, that is: before his return to his mother).

His saying: ﴿We had forbidden﴾ means: We prevented, and tahrim linguistically means prevention, and from it (...).

* * *

His saying: ﴿to his sister﴾. The author specified her as Maryam. What do you say about this specification?

* Student: (...) it is not valid.

* The Shaykh: Yes, and ignorance of it does no harm.

What is the meaning of ﴿Follow him﴾?

* Student: That is: follow his trail.

* The Shaykh: Follow him or track him?

* The Student: That is: track his trail.

* The Shaykh: Track his trail; that is: seek him and follow him.

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Alright, his saying: ﴿so she watched him﴾, what is the meaning of ﴿watched him﴾?

* The Student: That is, she saw him.

* The Shaykh: Alright, the meaning of ﴿from a distance﴾?

* Student: From a far place.

* The Shaykh: A far place. ﴿while they did not perceive﴾?

* The Student: ﴿while they did not perceive﴾, that is: they did not know that she was following him and watching him.

* The Shaykh: Yes, and it is in a position of accusative?

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes. His exalted saying: ﴿And We had forbidden to him the wet-nurses﴾, what is the meaning of ﴿We had forbidden﴾?

* Student: Before his return, (...) We prevented him from nursing at a breast, and this is a decreed prohibition, Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: A decreed prohibition.
Is prohibition divided into two kinds?

* Student: A legislated prohibition, and a cosmic decreed prohibition.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The Student: The legislated is what is from the Sharia.

* The Shaykh: The object of the legislated is what?

* The Student: (...) the Sharia.

* The Shaykh: Yes, what is it connected to? That is, what is the legislated prohibition connected to?

* The Student: To the legislated rulings.

* The Shaykh: To the legislated rulings, and the decreed one to the cosmic rulings.
Alright, is there (...)?

* Student: The decreed (...).

* The Shaykh: No, other than it. Did we mention other than these two examples?

* Student: ﴿And it is forbidden upon a city which We have destroyed that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiya: 95].

* The Shaykh: Alright, and the second example?

* Student: ﴿Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 26].

* The Shaykh: ﴿He said, "Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land"﴾, that is, a decreed prohibition.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: (...).

* * *

﴿to the people of a house﴾ [al-Qasas: 12], and she did not say: to his people. Of course, had she said: to his people, the matter would have become clear and they would have seized her, him and his people. Rather she said: ﴿to the people of a house﴾, indefinite, as if they did not know him, although she, or the people of the house, is his mother, Musa's mother.

﴿to the people of a house who will rear him for you﴾ (﴿the people of a house﴾ when she saw their compassion toward him). (When she saw their compassion) means: the compassion of the family of Pharaoh toward this child, and that they loved to find someone to undertake his upbringing and nursing, so she said: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household﴾.

(﴿who will rear him for you﴾ with nursing and otherwise). Kafl means undertaking the care of a child; undertaking a child's custody is called kafl, as in His saying: ﴿and Zakariyya took charge of her﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 37], and in another reading: ﴿and Zakariyya' took charge of her﴾. The meaning: I will direct you to a household who will undertake his custody in the most complete manner, as evidenced by her saying: ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾. The act came with a verb, and the intention came with a nominal clause: ﴿who will rear him﴾, because kafala is an act, and ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾, sincerity is based on intention in the heart.

The meaning of ﴿sincere﴾ is: pure, and the origin of nasih is purifying a thing from impurities, and from it His saying: ﴿O you who believe, repent to Allah with sincere repentance﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8], that is, pure from impurities, for Allah alone.

So ﴿sincere﴾: what is the meaning of nush? Purity from impurities, that is: they are wholly sincere to him. And is she truthful in her statement or not?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, truthful without doubt.

As for his saying: ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾, the pronoun in ﴿to him﴾ refers to this child. Without doubt it refers to this child. And if it refers to this child, then if someone says: what is the benefit of the family of Pharaoh being sincere to the people of this house toward him?

We say: the benefit of the family of Pharaoh in that is that they loved this child and wished for someone who would take care of his needs and his upbringing in the most complete way. Therefore...

Alright, the author says: (And she interpreted the pronoun in ﴿to him﴾ as the king, in answer to them, so she was answered). This is based on an Israelite story: when she said: ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾, it seems they raised a question and said: what made you know that they are sincere to him? So she said: I mean that they are sincere to the king. Who is the king? Pharaoh, meaning: and they are sincere to the king. This story is undoubtedly far from correct; rather it is not correct. What is meant is that ﴿to him﴾ refers to the child, and there is nothing that prevents the pronoun from referring to him. Nor is there any need to interpret it as the king, because they (the family of Pharaoh) love, that is, the family of Pharaoh loves whoever is sincere to him, so they are not asking about this matter. Yes, this interpretation by the author is unnecessary.

He says: (So she brought his mother, and he accepted her breast, and they were answered about his accepting it by her saying that her scent was pleasant and her milk was good, so he was permitted to be nursed by her in her house, and she returned with him, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We returned him﴾).

This account that the author mentioned also has no indication in the verse. And whoever says: she is the one who came, and he accepted her breast in front of the people, and she was accused of it, and she defended herself by saying that her breast had a pleasant scent and her milk was good, all of this has no basis.

The correct view is that when she said: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household who will undertake his custody for you and they are sincere to him﴾, they said, what did they say? They said: yes, direct us. So the story is very clear: direct us, so she directed them, and they brought him to his mother. This is more eloquent as a miracle and a sign: his mother, in her house, ordered his sister to go out seeking him, and his sister returned with him only to his mother. As for the claim that the mother went out, and that she put the breast to his mouth, and that she was accused of it and defended herself by saying she had a pleasant scent or pleasant milk, this is not correct, and such matters need not have known natural causes, because they are from the extraordinary, and extraordinary events are not something we need to fit to customary causes; rather they are above custom.

So we say: the matter proceeds according to what came in the noble Qur'an. The mother did not come; Allah did not mention that the mother came, rather He said: ﴿So We returned him to his mother﴾ [al-Qasas: 13].

﴿We returned him﴾, that is: Musa, (﴿to his mother that her eye might be comforted﴾ by meeting him).

﴿might be comforted﴾: it was mentioned before that it is derived either from qarr, which is coolness, or from qarar, which is stillness, and perhaps it includes both meanings: derived from qarar, the eye becomes still and cool.

﴿That her eye might be comforted﴾: here ﴿that﴾ is a particle of causation, and it is a verbal particle (masdariyyah) that puts the imperfect verb in the subjunctive, and for this reason ﴿might be comforted﴾ is in the subjunctive, and the sign of its subjunctive is a visible fatha on the qaf.

* Student: On the ra'.

* The Shaykh: On its end?

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: And the qaf (...).

* Student: The original.

* The Shaykh: This is the original, yes; because it is from qarra yaqarru, and not from qarra yaqirru.

(﴿That her eye might be comforted﴾ by meeting him ﴿and she would not grieve﴾ then). That is: she would not grieve over what had passed, rather the grief would leave her; the eye is comforted and grief leaves her.

(﴿And that she may know that the promise of Allah﴾ of returning him to her ﴿is true﴾). This also... there are three benefits: ﴿might be comforted﴾, ﴿and she would not grieve﴾, and the third: ﴿and that she may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾.

As for the first two, it is clear that her eye is comforted by his return and that she does not grieve, the grief leaves her. But as for his saying: ﴿and that she may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾, this cause had already preceded, for from the moment she cast him into the river she knew that the promise of Allah was true, and if it were not for her knowledge and certainty that the promise of Allah is true, she would not have cast him. So is the knowledge meant here the knowledge of certainty or the eye of certainty?

* The students: The eye of certainty.

* The Shaykh: The eye of certainty, or the truth of certainty if you wish. Her knowledge the first time was knowledge of the thing by report; her second knowledge was knowledge of the thing by its occurrence. There is a difference between a person's knowledge of a thing by report and his knowledge of it by its occurrence. That is why Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said, 'Have you not believed?' He said, 'Yes, but that my heart may be assured'﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. And it has come in a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The report is not like seeing with one's own eyes"[[Narrated by Ahmad (2446) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. So the conclusion is that His saying: ﴿and that she may know﴾ means knowledge of the thing after its occurrence, and as for her knowledge of it by report, that has already preceded, and had she not been confident in the first, she would not have acted.

His saying: ﴿and that she may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾, ﴿promise﴾: they mention that the wa'd (promise) is a promise of what gladdens, and the wa'id (threat) is a warning of what grieves; that is, a promise of good and a threat of evil. Is that so? They say that the evil is from (awada), and the good is from (wa'ada), so they say: awadahu, that is, with evil, and wa'adahu with good.

* Student: Regarding His saying: ﴿So that her eye may be comforted and she would not grieve﴾ [al-Qasas: 13], it is known that when a person's eye is comforted he forgets grief and is made glad.

* The Shaykh: Yes, but it is mentioned; the negation of grief here is to show that the comfort is complete, because the eye may be comforted with some grief still present.

Alright, the promise, what did we say its meaning is? The promise relates to what gladdens, and the threat to what distresses. So is the promise and the truth less than the threat, or are both (equal)?

* Student: Both.

* Another student: No, the threat may be left unfulfilled.

* Another student: The threat (...).

The Shaykh: It is true. The threat and the promise are both true. If we said that the threat is not true, it would follow that there is falsehood in the report of Allah, and that is impossible. But the threat may not be carried out, as a favour from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because it is His right. The threat is the right of Allah, and Allah, Blessed and Exalted, may overlook it, or not? As for the promise, whose right is it? It is the right of the one who is promised, and for this reason it cannot fail to be fulfilled. The poet said:

"Indeed I, whether I threaten him or promise him,
I break my threat and I fulfil my promise."

Because the promise is the right of the one promised, while the threat is the right of the one who threatens.

Let me give you an example. If I say to this man: "If you do such-and-such, I will give you a hundred dinars," what is this?

Student: A promise.

Shaykh: A promise or a threat?

Student: A promise.

Shaykh: Why?

Student: Because it is in (...).

Shaykh: Because it concerns good, yes. If he does what I said, I must fulfil it for him, because the right is his. But suppose I say to my son, for example: "If you do such-and-such, I will imprison you." Then he does it, but I pardon him. Is this permissible or not permissible?

Student: Permissible.

Shaykh: It is permissible, and it is a favour, especially when he pardons while he has the power to punish. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Whether you show good or conceal it, or pardon an evil, indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and All-Powerful﴾ [An-Nisa 149]. But pardoning in a state of incapacity is not praiseworthy.

In summary: the promise and the threat of Allah are both true. But since His promise is a right of the one promised, it must come to pass. And His threat, since it is His right, He may pardon, if He wills, out of generosity and favour, according to what His wisdom requires, glory be to Him.

Student: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾ [Al-A'raf 44]. This is a threat that was applied to a promise.

Shaykh: Yes, that is correct. It was called a promise, either because it is in contrast to (...), so it matches it, or because it is sometimes called that.

He says: ﴿And that you may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾. "True" here means "established." I think we have said that "true" in some contexts has one meaning and in other contexts another meaning. Which of the two meanings is this?

Students: It means "truthful."

Shaykh: Truthful, yes. When truth relates to reports, it means truthfulness, and in rulings it means justice. Accordingly, here it means truthfulness: ﴿And that you may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾, meaning it is truthful, and it cannot fail. For the failure of a promise is either due to the promiser lying or to his inability to carry it out. Both of these are impossible for Allah. There is no falsehood in His word and no incapacity in His action. For this reason, the servants of Allah, glory be to Him, end their supplications by saying: "Indeed You do not break Your promise."

He says: (﴿But most of them﴾, that is, the people, ﴿do not know﴾ this promise, nor that this is his sister.)

The author has restricted the verse, but in reality the verse is general, though most people do not know. That is, they do not possess knowledge that benefits them regarding Allah's promise. So the negation of knowledge here is either to establish ignorance or to negate beneficial knowledge. Most people do not know this, they do not know that the promise of Allah is true.

Student: ﴿Most of them﴾.

Shaykh: Yes, ﴿most of them﴾, meaning the people.
