I say: most people do not know that the promise of Allah is true, either because of their ignorance or because they do not benefit from this knowledge. The negation of a thing to negate benefit from it is established in the Qur'an: ﴿Do not be like those who say, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [Al-Anfal 21]. Allah, glory be to Him, constantly negates intellect or hearing from people, or things similar to that, because they do not benefit from them. So most people do not know. The author restricted this to the story of Musa, but the verse is general: most people do not know that the promise of Allah is true. I say: either they are ignorant of this, because they do not know what befits Allah's names and attributes, or they do not benefit from this knowledge. Those who do not strive to do good or to avoid evil are, in reality, like the ignorant of the truth that Allah's promise is true. For human nature and reason require that as long as you believe in something, whether it is a promise or a threat, you must strive for it according to the requirement of your faith. If you know that a person will die, and that a believer, when he dies, will find good, will be in Paradise and be saved from the Fire, is this true or not?

Students: True.

Shaykh: True. But the one who does not strive for this Paradise and is absorbed in striving for the perishing world, is this person in reality a knower that Allah's promise is true, or one who benefits from his knowledge?

Student: He did not benefit.

Shaykh: He did not benefit from it, he did not benefit from his knowledge. Had he benefited from it, he would not have missed this great opportunity.

Now, a person who knows that sin is a cause for entering the Fire, knows this, and knows that Allah's promise is true, yet he still dares to commit sins. We say: his knowledge here is deficient. For if he truly believed in that, he would avoid this thing. Thus the meaning of the saying of Allah, the Exalted, is fulfilled: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾.

May Allah have mercy on him, the author analysed the verse, saying: (﴿do not know﴾ this promise), meaning what Allah promised his mother of returning him to her, (nor that this is his sister). Accordingly, the pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ refers to the people of Pharaoh.

(And this is his mother, so he remained with her until she weaned him, and a wage was paid to her, a dinar per day.)

Breastfeeding was expensive at that time. As for his remaining with her until she weaned him, this is clear, for as long as he needed breastfeeding he would stay with her. As for (a wage was paid to her), this too is correct, for a wage was set for her, and they used to send her gifts and presents and honour her, because she was the one caring for this child whom they said would be ﴿a delight of the eye﴾ and ﴿perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾. For this reason it is narrated from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, concerning one who does his work well and takes a wage for it: "He is like the mother of Musa; she nurses her child and takes a wage for it." [1] This is one of the signs of Allah. Her son comes to her, she nurses him and is honoured because of him. What do you think if she had not done this, and had not thrown him into the river, and the people of Pharaoh had not picked him up? She would have remained fearful and anxious, and she would not have gained a wage, honour or esteem from these tyrants.

As for his saying (a dinar per day), this is not accepted, because our method in such matters is: what is established from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is accepted; what is not established from the reports of the Children of Israel, we withhold judgement on, and should not affirm it with such certainty. We may narrate it, but we do not affirm it.

He says (a dinar per day). Look, then he raised an objection: (she took it because it was the property of a combatant enemy). Glory be to Allah, the Most High, the Mighty! The notion of some scholars is strange. Did she take it because it was the property of a combatant enemy, or did she take it because it was a wage for nursing him?

A wage. There is no problem with that. But that she took a wage because it was the property of an enemy combatant, this has no basis, it has no basis. One cannot say, for example, that since Musa's mother was the only one he would accept breastfeeding from, her nursing him was an obligation upon her, and one may not take a compensation for an obligation, so the taking of compensation here becomes the taking of the property of an enemy combatant.

We say: even the property of an enemy combatant, if it comes by way of a contract, is it permissible to take it or not?

Student: It is not permissible.

Shaykh: No, it is not permissible. You take it only according to the terms of the contract. The dealing between you and the enemy combatants is like a safe-conduct; indeed, it is a safe-conduct in reality. So the correct view is that she took it because she was paid for her care and nursing of him.

Student: The service, (...).

Shaykh: That does not contradict it. Had she not taken it, there would have been a trial in that, and it would have been known that she was a relative of his or something similar. She took it because they believed she was not his mother, and they believed this child would belong to them.

Student: It is not permissible (...). If it were permissible outwardly, taking it inwardly would not be permissible.

Shaykh: It is permissible inwardly, because of her caring for him in their eyes.

The author says: (So she brought him to Pharaoh, and he was raised by him, as Allah the Exalted said, relating about him in Surah Ash-Shu'ara: ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child, and did you not remain among us for years of your life?﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 18]).

He was raised in the house of the king, and he rode the mounts of kings and wore the clothing of kings. Instead of being with his mother, where without doubt this would not have happened to him, he now became honoured and esteemed. This was by the subjugation of Allah, glory be to Him, for him.

Student: (...). It is not reported that Musa contacted his mother (...).

Shaykh: He contacted her?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: In any case he would visit her, because she was his mother.

Student: Because when he finished weaning, she returned to..

Shaykh: He was raised by Pharaoh, but he would come to his mother, because he would say: "This is my mother by nursing," and no one would object to his (...) his mother. No one would object that he went to her, because she was his mother through nursing.

Student: Did he not know the truth?

Shaykh: They did not know.

Student: Musa?

Shaykh: No, he knew the truth. He must have known, and his mother must have informed him too.

Student: The evidence?

Shaykh: The evidence is that she, when she cared for him and he grew up, he would certainly be in her custody constantly; meaning he would come to her, and of necessity she would be teaching him.

Student: No, perhaps not (...).

Shaykh: Never (...). For he feared for himself just as she feared for him. Never, there was no fear at all. As long as the man feared for himself, it is not possible (...).

Student: The naming, Shaykh, is it from her or from the people of Pharaoh?

Shaykh: The naming (...). It is possible that she named him that, or that it was from the people of Pharaoh. (...) the people of Pharaoh, how would they know whether she named him?

Student: A Hebrew name, I mean.

Shaykh: Yes, indeed, except that perhaps it was, for example, a mark of Allah's honour to him, that they named him with what his mother named him. I do not know, by Allah.

He says: (﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child, and did you not remain among us for years of your life?﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 18]) So the man remained with the king, honoured and esteemed.

---

[1] Abu Dawud narrated in al-Maraseel (332) from Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The example of those among my nation who fight and take a reward, that is, who strengthen themselves against their enemy, is the example of the mother of Musa: she nurses her child and takes her wage." Ibn Kathir cited it in his Tafsir without a chain of narration, in his commentary on Surah Ta-Ha verse 40 and Surah Al-Qasas verses 12-13, with the wording: "The example of the craftsman who works and seeks reward from Allah in his craft is like the mother of Musa: she nurses her child and takes her wage."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 11–13 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him," so she watched him from a distance while they did not perceive.﴾ [al-Qasas: 11].

﴿She said to his sister﴾. The author says: (Maryam). Maryam... we say to the author: from where do you have that her name is Maryam?

* Student: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾ [Maryam: 28] (...).

* The Shaykh: That is not her. This is not Maryam, because the one you mentioned is Maryam the mother of 'Isa, and between her and Musa there are long ages.

In any case, this is from the Israelite reports (al-Isra'iliyyat), and specifying her name, if any benefit depended on it, Allah, blessed and exalted, would have made it clear. But what concerns us is not specifying the name. What matters is that we know this woman's relation to Musa's mother and to Musa as well. She is Musa's sister, so what is she in relation to Musa's mother?
If she has become a sister of Musa, what is her relation to Musa's mother?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, did you not understand my words? Did you understand the question? ﴿And she said to his sister﴾. Sister of whom?

* The Student: Sister of Musa.

* The Shaykh: Sister of Musa. If this woman has become a sister of Musa, what is her relation to Musa's mother? Do you see that the question is not (...).

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: What is she to Musa's mother?

* The Student: You mean a relative?

* The Shaykh: Yes, a relative of Musa's mother.

* The Student: A relative of Musa's mother.

* The Shaykh: Yes, what is she?

* The Student: (...) his wet-nurse.

* The Shaykh: What is this?! Alright, what (...)?

* Student: (...) her mother (...).

* The Shaykh: If she has become Musa's sister, her relation to Musa's mother is what?

* The Student: That she is her daughter.

* The Shaykh: Her daughter?

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Certainly?

* The Student: Yes, certainly.

* The Shaykh: No doubt still?

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Or her daughter?

* The Student: Or her maternal aunt.

* The Shaykh: Or..

* The Student: The apparent meaning of the verse: her daughter.

* The Shaykh: Alright, what is the apparent meaning?

* The Student: ﴿And she said to his sister﴾.

* The Shaykh: Alright, his sister.

* The Student: Musa's mother, that is, she said to Musa's sister.

* The Shaykh: Alright, Musa's sister from his father, is that not possible?

* The Student: The apparent (...).

* The Shaykh: (...) from the apparent.

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: What is the basis of the apparent meaning?

* The Student: He did not say: (...) to his sister from his father.

* Student: The basis of (...).

* The Shaykh: No, the apparent... In any case, what you say may be correct, meaning that if she were from the father or from the mother, had she been from his father or from his mother, it would have been specified. When it is unrestricted, brotherhood is taken in its complete sense, which is from both mother and father, although there is a possibility that she is from his mother or from his father. But the apparent meaning, as you have said, is that since it is unrestricted, it is interpreted as the most complete kind of brotherhood, which is full (shaqiqah) sibling.

She said: ﴿Follow him﴾, that is: (follow his track until you know his news).

Al-qass means: tracing the trail, that is, follow his trail and search for him.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿so she watched him﴾, that is: (she saw him). The sister went, and the apparent meaning of the noble verse, ﴿so she watched﴾, with the fa' indicating sequence and immediacy, is that she did not go far before she saw him.

His saying: ﴿from a distance﴾ (from a far place). ﴿Junub﴾ means far, and on this basis the qualified noun is omitted, and the sense is: from a far place, far from her, but she recognized that this was her brother.

(Stealthily) he says: (﴿so she watched him from a distance﴾ from a far place, stealthily). What is the meaning of stealthily? Furtively; that is, she did not keep her gaze fixed on him, for if she had kept her gaze fixed on him and approached him quickly, and signs of her intention had appeared, they would have sensed it. But she did not look at him in a way that they would perceive. She was glancing furtively, stealing a look, and this is clear, although there is no proof for it in the verses, it is obvious that it must have been so, because if she had seen him and gone to him, and kept staring, and the like, they would have become suspicious of this matter and held her back. But she watched him from a distance, stealing glances.

﴿while they did not perceive﴾ that she was his sister and that she was watching him. Who are the ones who ﴿did not perceive﴾? Who? The people of Pharaoh. They did not know. But the woman was clever; she kept looking from afar until she reached him, ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ that she was his sister or was watching him, because she did not display movements that would indicate that.

As for his saying: ﴿while they did not perceive﴾, what is the grammatical position of this clause?

* Students: A circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

* The Shaykh: A circumstantial clause of whom? Of the subject of ﴿watched﴾, meaning: and the state being that they did not perceive (...). A circumstantial clause is not required to be a description of its referent. That is why you say: Zayd came while the sun was rising. This clause is circumstantial, though it is not one of Zayd's attributes.

So here: she watched him while they did not perceive. If someone said: how do you make it a circumstantial clause of the subject of (watched), when it is not one of her attributes? We say: a circumstantial clause requires only the slightest connection.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We had forbidden to him the wet-nurses before﴾ [al-Qasas: 12].

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...), the child in reality began to become restless and cry, wanting to nurse, and perhaps they took him out seeking a nurse, and it so happened that his sister saw him.

* The Student: Yes, this was before the request for nursing took place.

* The Shaykh: That is, how is it ﴿so she watched him﴾?

* The Student: Before the request for nursing, when he requested nursing.

* The Shaykh: What is your proof?

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: There is no proof.

* Student: We say: this verse indicates the author's statement: (﴿And the heart of Musa's mother became empty﴾ when she knew of his being taken up).

* The Shaykh: That is, was (...) that you should follow him?

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: (...).

* Student: She sent her to (...).

* The Shaykh: Had she not sent her, (...) in the town.

* Student: She was certain of the good news, his mother (...).

* The Shaykh: There is no doubt that she was certain; otherwise, had she not been certain, she would not have cast him into the river. She ordered her to go out seeking to nurse him, because she knew he would surely return to her.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, no, (...).

He said: (﴿And We had forbidden to him the wet-nurses before﴾, that is: before his return to his mother).

His saying: ﴿We had forbidden﴾ means: We prevented, and tahrim linguistically means prevention, and from it (...).

* * *

His saying: ﴿to his sister﴾. The author specified her as Maryam. What do you say about this specification?

* Student: (...) it is not valid.

* The Shaykh: Yes, and ignorance of it does no harm.

What is the meaning of ﴿Follow him﴾?

* Student: That is: follow his trail.

* The Shaykh: Follow him or track him?

* The Student: That is: track his trail.

* The Shaykh: Track his trail; that is: seek him and follow him.

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Alright, his saying: ﴿so she watched him﴾, what is the meaning of ﴿watched him﴾?

* The Student: That is, she saw him.

* The Shaykh: Alright, the meaning of ﴿from a distance﴾?

* Student: From a far place.

* The Shaykh: A far place. ﴿while they did not perceive﴾?

* The Student: ﴿while they did not perceive﴾, that is: they did not know that she was following him and watching him.

* The Shaykh: Yes, and it is in a position of accusative?

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes. His exalted saying: ﴿And We had forbidden to him the wet-nurses﴾, what is the meaning of ﴿We had forbidden﴾?

* Student: Before his return, (...) We prevented him from nursing at a breast, and this is a decreed prohibition, Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: A decreed prohibition.
Is prohibition divided into two kinds?

* Student: A legislated prohibition, and a cosmic decreed prohibition.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The Student: The legislated is what is from the Sharia.

* The Shaykh: The object of the legislated is what?

* The Student: (...) the Sharia.

* The Shaykh: Yes, what is it connected to? That is, what is the legislated prohibition connected to?

* The Student: To the legislated rulings.

* The Shaykh: To the legislated rulings, and the decreed one to the cosmic rulings.
Alright, is there (...)?

* Student: The decreed (...).

* The Shaykh: No, other than it. Did we mention other than these two examples?

* Student: ﴿And it is forbidden upon a city which We have destroyed that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiya: 95].

* The Shaykh: Alright, and the second example?

* Student: ﴿Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 26].

* The Shaykh: ﴿He said, "Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land"﴾, that is, a decreed prohibition.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: (...).

* * *

﴿to the people of a house﴾ [al-Qasas: 12], and she did not say: to his people. Of course, had she said: to his people, the matter would have become clear and they would have seized her, him and his people. Rather she said: ﴿to the people of a house﴾, indefinite, as if they did not know him, although she, or the people of the house, is his mother, Musa's mother.

﴿to the people of a house who will rear him for you﴾ (﴿the people of a house﴾ when she saw their compassion toward him). (When she saw their compassion) means: the compassion of the family of Pharaoh toward this child, and that they loved to find someone to undertake his upbringing and nursing, so she said: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household﴾.

(﴿who will rear him for you﴾ with nursing and otherwise). Kafl means undertaking the care of a child; undertaking a child's custody is called kafl, as in His saying: ﴿and Zakariyya took charge of her﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 37], and in another reading: ﴿and Zakariyya' took charge of her﴾. The meaning: I will direct you to a household who will undertake his custody in the most complete manner, as evidenced by her saying: ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾. The act came with a verb, and the intention came with a nominal clause: ﴿who will rear him﴾, because kafala is an act, and ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾, sincerity is based on intention in the heart.

The meaning of ﴿sincere﴾ is: pure, and the origin of nasih is purifying a thing from impurities, and from it His saying: ﴿O you who believe, repent to Allah with sincere repentance﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8], that is, pure from impurities, for Allah alone.

So ﴿sincere﴾: what is the meaning of nush? Purity from impurities, that is: they are wholly sincere to him. And is she truthful in her statement or not?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, truthful without doubt.

As for his saying: ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾, the pronoun in ﴿to him﴾ refers to this child. Without doubt it refers to this child. And if it refers to this child, then if someone says: what is the benefit of the family of Pharaoh being sincere to the people of this house toward him?

We say: the benefit of the family of Pharaoh in that is that they loved this child and wished for someone who would take care of his needs and his upbringing in the most complete way. Therefore...

Alright, the author says: (And she interpreted the pronoun in ﴿to him﴾ as the king, in answer to them, so she was answered). This is based on an Israelite story: when she said: ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾, it seems they raised a question and said: what made you know that they are sincere to him? So she said: I mean that they are sincere to the king. Who is the king? Pharaoh, meaning: and they are sincere to the king. This story is undoubtedly far from correct; rather it is not correct. What is meant is that ﴿to him﴾ refers to the child, and there is nothing that prevents the pronoun from referring to him. Nor is there any need to interpret it as the king, because they (the family of Pharaoh) love, that is, the family of Pharaoh loves whoever is sincere to him, so they are not asking about this matter. Yes, this interpretation by the author is unnecessary.

He says: (So she brought his mother, and he accepted her breast, and they were answered about his accepting it by her saying that her scent was pleasant and her milk was good, so he was permitted to be nursed by her in her house, and she returned with him, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We returned him﴾).

This account that the author mentioned also has no indication in the verse. And whoever says: she is the one who came, and he accepted her breast in front of the people, and she was accused of it, and she defended herself by saying that her breast had a pleasant scent and her milk was good, all of this has no basis.

The correct view is that when she said: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household who will undertake his custody for you and they are sincere to him﴾, they said, what did they say? They said: yes, direct us. So the story is very clear: direct us, so she directed them, and they brought him to his mother. This is more eloquent as a miracle and a sign: his mother, in her house, ordered his sister to go out seeking him, and his sister returned with him only to his mother. As for the claim that the mother went out, and that she put the breast to his mouth, and that she was accused of it and defended herself by saying she had a pleasant scent or pleasant milk, this is not correct, and such matters need not have known natural causes, because they are from the extraordinary, and extraordinary events are not something we need to fit to customary causes; rather they are above custom.

So we say: the matter proceeds according to what came in the noble Qur'an. The mother did not come; Allah did not mention that the mother came, rather He said: ﴿So We returned him to his mother﴾ [al-Qasas: 13].

﴿We returned him﴾, that is: Musa, (﴿to his mother that her eye might be comforted﴾ by meeting him).

﴿might be comforted﴾: it was mentioned before that it is derived either from qarr, which is coolness, or from qarar, which is stillness, and perhaps it includes both meanings: derived from qarar, the eye becomes still and cool.

﴿That her eye might be comforted﴾: here ﴿that﴾ is a particle of causation, and it is a verbal particle (masdariyyah) that puts the imperfect verb in the subjunctive, and for this reason ﴿might be comforted﴾ is in the subjunctive, and the sign of its subjunctive is a visible fatha on the qaf.

* Student: On the ra'.

* The Shaykh: On its end?

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: And the qaf (...).

* Student: The original.

* The Shaykh: This is the original, yes; because it is from qarra yaqarru, and not from qarra yaqirru.

(﴿That her eye might be comforted﴾ by meeting him ﴿and she would not grieve﴾ then). That is: she would not grieve over what had passed, rather the grief would leave her; the eye is comforted and grief leaves her.

(﴿And that she may know that the promise of Allah﴾ of returning him to her ﴿is true﴾). This also... there are three benefits: ﴿might be comforted﴾, ﴿and she would not grieve﴾, and the third: ﴿and that she may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾.

As for the first two, it is clear that her eye is comforted by his return and that she does not grieve, the grief leaves her. But as for his saying: ﴿and that she may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾, this cause had already preceded, for from the moment she cast him into the river she knew that the promise of Allah was true, and if it were not for her knowledge and certainty that the promise of Allah is true, she would not have cast him. So is the knowledge meant here the knowledge of certainty or the eye of certainty?

* The students: The eye of certainty.

* The Shaykh: The eye of certainty, or the truth of certainty if you wish. Her knowledge the first time was knowledge of the thing by report; her second knowledge was knowledge of the thing by its occurrence. There is a difference between a person's knowledge of a thing by report and his knowledge of it by its occurrence. That is why Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said, 'Have you not believed?' He said, 'Yes, but that my heart may be assured'﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. And it has come in a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The report is not like seeing with one's own eyes"[[Narrated by Ahmad (2446) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. So the conclusion is that His saying: ﴿and that she may know﴾ means knowledge of the thing after its occurrence, and as for her knowledge of it by report, that has already preceded, and had she not been confident in the first, she would not have acted.

His saying: ﴿and that she may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾, ﴿promise﴾: they mention that the wa'd (promise) is a promise of what gladdens, and the wa'id (threat) is a warning of what grieves; that is, a promise of good and a threat of evil. Is that so? They say that the evil is from (awada), and the good is from (wa'ada), so they say: awadahu, that is, with evil, and wa'adahu with good.

* Student: Regarding His saying: ﴿So that her eye may be comforted and she would not grieve﴾ [al-Qasas: 13], it is known that when a person's eye is comforted he forgets grief and is made glad.

* The Shaykh: Yes, but it is mentioned; the negation of grief here is to show that the comfort is complete, because the eye may be comforted with some grief still present.

Alright, the promise, what did we say its meaning is? The promise relates to what gladdens, and the threat to what distresses. So is the promise and the truth less than the threat, or are both (equal)?

* Student: Both.

* Another student: No, the threat may be left unfulfilled.

* Another student: The threat (...).

The Shaykh: It is true. The threat and the promise are both true. If we said that the threat is not true, it would follow that there is falsehood in the report of Allah, and that is impossible. But the threat may not be carried out, as a favour from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because it is His right. The threat is the right of Allah, and Allah, Blessed and Exalted, may overlook it, or not? As for the promise, whose right is it? It is the right of the one who is promised, and for this reason it cannot fail to be fulfilled. The poet said:

"Indeed I, whether I threaten him or promise him,
I break my threat and I fulfil my promise."

Because the promise is the right of the one promised, while the threat is the right of the one who threatens.

Let me give you an example. If I say to this man: "If you do such-and-such, I will give you a hundred dinars," what is this?

Student: A promise.

Shaykh: A promise or a threat?

Student: A promise.

Shaykh: Why?

Student: Because it is in (...).

Shaykh: Because it concerns good, yes. If he does what I said, I must fulfil it for him, because the right is his. But suppose I say to my son, for example: "If you do such-and-such, I will imprison you." Then he does it, but I pardon him. Is this permissible or not permissible?

Student: Permissible.

Shaykh: It is permissible, and it is a favour, especially when he pardons while he has the power to punish. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Whether you show good or conceal it, or pardon an evil, indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and All-Powerful﴾ [An-Nisa 149]. But pardoning in a state of incapacity is not praiseworthy.

In summary: the promise and the threat of Allah are both true. But since His promise is a right of the one promised, it must come to pass. And His threat, since it is His right, He may pardon, if He wills, out of generosity and favour, according to what His wisdom requires, glory be to Him.

Student: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾ [Al-A'raf 44]. This is a threat that was applied to a promise.

Shaykh: Yes, that is correct. It was called a promise, either because it is in contrast to (...), so it matches it, or because it is sometimes called that.

He says: ﴿And that you may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾. "True" here means "established." I think we have said that "true" in some contexts has one meaning and in other contexts another meaning. Which of the two meanings is this?

Students: It means "truthful."

Shaykh: Truthful, yes. When truth relates to reports, it means truthfulness, and in rulings it means justice. Accordingly, here it means truthfulness: ﴿And that you may know that the promise of Allah is true﴾, meaning it is truthful, and it cannot fail. For the failure of a promise is either due to the promiser lying or to his inability to carry it out. Both of these are impossible for Allah. There is no falsehood in His word and no incapacity in His action. For this reason, the servants of Allah, glory be to Him, end their supplications by saying: "Indeed You do not break Your promise."

He says: (﴿But most of them﴾, that is, the people, ﴿do not know﴾ this promise, nor that this is his sister.)

The author has restricted the verse, but in reality the verse is general, though most people do not know. That is, they do not possess knowledge that benefits them regarding Allah's promise. So the negation of knowledge here is either to establish ignorance or to negate beneficial knowledge. Most people do not know this, they do not know that the promise of Allah is true.

Student: ﴿Most of them﴾.

Shaykh: Yes, ﴿most of them﴾, meaning the people. I say: most people do not know that the promise of Allah is true, either because of their ignorance or because they do not benefit from this knowledge. The negation of a thing to negate benefit from it is established in the Qur'an: ﴿Do not be like those who say, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [Al-Anfal 21]. Allah, glory be to Him, constantly negates intellect or hearing from people, or things similar to that, because they do not benefit from them. So most people do not know. The author restricted this to the story of Musa, but the verse is general: most people do not know that the promise of Allah is true. I say: either they are ignorant of this, because they do not know what befits Allah's names and attributes, or they do not benefit from this knowledge. Those who do not strive to do good or to avoid evil are, in reality, like the ignorant of the truth that Allah's promise is true. For human nature and reason require that as long as you believe in something, whether it is a promise or a threat, you must strive for it according to the requirement of your faith. If you know that a person will die, and that a believer, when he dies, will find good, will be in Paradise and be saved from the Fire, is this true or not?

Students: True.

Shaykh: True. But the one who does not strive for this Paradise and is absorbed in striving for the perishing world, is this person in reality a knower that Allah's promise is true, or one who benefits from his knowledge?

Student: He did not benefit.

Shaykh: He did not benefit from it, he did not benefit from his knowledge. Had he benefited from it, he would not have missed this great opportunity.

Now, a person who knows that sin is a cause for entering the Fire, knows this, and knows that Allah's promise is true, yet he still dares to commit sins. We say: his knowledge here is deficient. For if he truly believed in that, he would avoid this thing. Thus the meaning of the saying of Allah, the Exalted, is fulfilled: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾.

May Allah have mercy on him, the author analysed the verse, saying: (﴿do not know﴾ this promise), meaning what Allah promised his mother of returning him to her, (nor that this is his sister). Accordingly, the pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ refers to the people of Pharaoh.

(And this is his mother, so he remained with her until she weaned him, and a wage was paid to her, a dinar per day.)

Breastfeeding was expensive at that time. As for his remaining with her until she weaned him, this is clear, for as long as he needed breastfeeding he would stay with her. As for (a wage was paid to her), this too is correct, for a wage was set for her, and they used to send her gifts and presents and honour her, because she was the one caring for this child whom they said would be ﴿a delight of the eye﴾ and ﴿perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾. For this reason it is narrated from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, concerning one who does his work well and takes a wage for it: "He is like the mother of Musa; she nurses her child and takes a wage for it." [1] This is one of the signs of Allah. Her son comes to her, she nurses him and is honoured because of him. What do you think if she had not done this, and had not thrown him into the river, and the people of Pharaoh had not picked him up? She would have remained fearful and anxious, and she would not have gained a wage, honour or esteem from these tyrants.

As for his saying (a dinar per day), this is not accepted, because our method in such matters is: what is established from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is accepted; what is not established from the reports of the Children of Israel, we withhold judgement on, and should not affirm it with such certainty. We may narrate it, but we do not affirm it.

He says (a dinar per day). Look, then he raised an objection: (she took it because it was the property of a combatant enemy). Glory be to Allah, the Most High, the Mighty! The notion of some scholars is strange. Did she take it because it was the property of a combatant enemy, or did she take it because it was a wage for nursing him?

A wage. There is no problem with that. But that she took a wage because it was the property of an enemy combatant, this has no basis, it has no basis. One cannot say, for example, that since Musa's mother was the only one he would accept breastfeeding from, her nursing him was an obligation upon her, and one may not take a compensation for an obligation, so the taking of compensation here becomes the taking of the property of an enemy combatant.

We say: even the property of an enemy combatant, if it comes by way of a contract, is it permissible to take it or not?

Student: It is not permissible.

Shaykh: No, it is not permissible. You take it only according to the terms of the contract. The dealing between you and the enemy combatants is like a safe-conduct; indeed, it is a safe-conduct in reality. So the correct view is that she took it because she was paid for her care and nursing of him.

Student: The service, (...).

Shaykh: That does not contradict it. Had she not taken it, there would have been a trial in that, and it would have been known that she was a relative of his or something similar. She took it because they believed she was not his mother, and they believed this child would belong to them.

Student: It is not permissible (...). If it were permissible outwardly, taking it inwardly would not be permissible.

Shaykh: It is permissible inwardly, because of her caring for him in their eyes.

The author says: (So she brought him to Pharaoh, and he was raised by him, as Allah the Exalted said, relating about him in Surah Ash-Shu'ara: ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child, and did you not remain among us for years of your life?﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 18]).

He was raised in the house of the king, and he rode the mounts of kings and wore the clothing of kings. Instead of being with his mother, where without doubt this would not have happened to him, he now became honoured and esteemed. This was by the subjugation of Allah, glory be to Him, for him.

Student: (...). It is not reported that Musa contacted his mother (...).

Shaykh: He contacted her?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: In any case he would visit her, because she was his mother.

Student: Because when he finished weaning, she returned to..

Shaykh: He was raised by Pharaoh, but he would come to his mother, because he would say: "This is my mother by nursing," and no one would object to his (...) his mother. No one would object that he went to her, because she was his mother through nursing.

Student: Did he not know the truth?

Shaykh: They did not know.

Student: Musa?

Shaykh: No, he knew the truth. He must have known, and his mother must have informed him too.

Student: The evidence?

Shaykh: The evidence is that she, when she cared for him and he grew up, he would certainly be in her custody constantly; meaning he would come to her, and of necessity she would be teaching him.

Student: No, perhaps not (...).

Shaykh: Never (...). For he feared for himself just as she feared for him. Never, there was no fear at all. As long as the man feared for himself, it is not possible (...).

Student: The naming, Shaykh, is it from her or from the people of Pharaoh?

Shaykh: The naming (...). It is possible that she named him that, or that it was from the people of Pharaoh. (...) the people of Pharaoh, how would they know whether she named him?

Student: A Hebrew name, I mean.

Shaykh: Yes, indeed, except that perhaps it was, for example, a mark of Allah's honour to him, that they named him with what his mother named him. I do not know, by Allah.

He says: (﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child, and did you not remain among us for years of your life?﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 18]) So the man remained with the king, honoured and esteemed.

---

[1] Abu Dawud narrated in al-Maraseel (332) from Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The example of those among my nation who fight and take a reward, that is, who strengthen themselves against their enemy, is the example of the mother of Musa: she nurses her child and takes her wage." Ibn Kathir cited it in his Tafsir without a chain of narration, in his commentary on Surah Ta-Ha verse 40 and Surah Al-Qasas verses 12-13, with the wording: "The example of the craftsman who works and seeks reward from Allah in his craft is like the mother of Musa: she nurses her child and takes her wage."

(﴿And when he reached his maturity and was fully grown﴾ [al-Qasas 14] — he was thirty years old, or thirty-three; is it like this in your copies?)

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: As for al-Ashudd (full maturity), it has been said: it is thirty-three years; it has been said: thirty years; and it has been said: near forty. That is because Allah says: ﴿Until, when he reached his full strength and reached forty years﴾ [al-Ahqaf 15]. This indicates that reaching al-ashudd is other than forty, since He said: ﴿reached his full strength and reached forty years﴾. Moreover, it is possible that reaching al-ashudd means the perfection of intellect, and there is no contradiction in the perfection of intellect occurring at the completion of forty.

He says: (﴿And he attained [istawa]﴾ meaning: he reached forty years). No, ﴿istawa﴾ means he became complete, and istiwa' in the Arabic language means perfection; from it is the saying: "the fruit has istawat", meaning it became ripe. It is in every context according to what fits it. However, when it is followed by (ila), it means intention, and when it is followed by (ala), it means height and settling; because that is perfection.

(﴿We gave him wisdom [hukman]﴾, i.e., ḥikmah, ﴿and knowledge [ʿilman]﴾, i.e., fiqh in religion, before he was sent as a prophet).

﴿Ataynāhu﴾ means "We gave him." Is this giving kawnī (by divine decree) or sharʿī (by divine law)?

* Student: Kawnī.

* Another student: Sharʿī.

* Another student: No, kawnī.

* Another student: Kawnī, because it is not revelation.

* Another student: Sharʿī, but (...).

* The Shaykh: The giving may be kawnī and may be sharʿī. If it is connected with qadar (divine decree), it is kawnī; if it is connected with the Sharīʿah, it is sharʿī. Allah's words ﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them and said, "Allah is sufficient for us"﴾ [al-Tawbah 59] — this giving is sharʿī, because it relates to the Sharīʿah and the legal ruling. Here, ﴿We gave him wisdom and knowledge﴾ [al-Qasas 14] is kawnī, because it relates to decree and destiny.

﴿And give them of the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾ [al-Nur 33]?

* Student: (...) sharʿī.

* The Shaykh: No, ﴿give them﴾ is sharʿī, but ﴿which He has given you﴾ is qadarī, that which He decreed for you. So the giving is sharʿī or kawnī according to its object.

As for the author's words: (﴿ḥukman﴾) he explained it as (ḥikmah), and said: (﴿wa-ʿilman﴾ meaning fiqh).

Why did he explain ḥukm as ḥikmah? Because ʿilm is the knowledge of the rulings; if we explain ḥukm as the ruling that is the content of the address of the Sharīʿah, there would be a kind of repetition, since it is knowledge. But it is permissible to say: ﴿We gave him ḥukm﴾, meaning knowledge of the legal rulings, ﴿and ʿilm﴾ of reports and secrets; in that case there is no repetition in the verse, and we do not resort to explaining ḥukm as ḥikmah, because it is known that ḥukm is other than ḥikmah, or not?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: So ḥukm is the content of the address of the Sharīʿah relating to the actions of the responsible persons, and ḥikmah is the reason (ʿillah) for that ruling.

As for His words: ﴿And when he reached... We gave him﴾, ﴿wa-lammā﴾ — what is its grammatical analysis (iʿrāb)?

* Student: Conditional.

* The Shaykh: Conditional?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: Conditional.

* The Shaykh: Conditional here, as is shown by the fact that it has a protasis and an apodosis: ﴿And when he reached his maturity and was fully grown, We gave him﴾. So it is conditional. It occurs in Arabic as conditional, as here, and it occurs with the meaning of (illa) ("except"), like the words of the Exalted: ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq 4], meaning: except that over it is a guardian. And it occurs as a temporal adverb: "I came to you lammā I knew that you were awake," for example, meaning: when I knew. And what determines these meanings is?

* Student: The context.

* The Shaykh: The context, yes.

﴿And when he reached his maturity and was fully grown, We gave him wisdom and knowledge.﴾

The author said: (﴿And thus﴾ as We recompensed him ﴿We recompense the good-doers﴾ for their own selves).

His words "as We recompensed him" indicate that the reference here is to this giving which Allah gave; i.e., "and likewise." The kāf here — and it is frequent (...) in the Qur'an — we parse as a absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq) with the meaning of "like"; i.e., like that recompense We recompense the good-doers. When it is an absolute object in the sense of "like," it is a noun; Ibn Mālik said:

Make it similar with the kāf, and with it the causal sense may be used, and extra for emphasis has come. It is used as a noun, and likewise ʿan and ʿalā, and from that reason min is added to them.

So the kāf comes with the meaning of "like," and is parsed as a noun, not a prepositional particle.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿najzī﴾ means nukāfi'u (We reward), and His words ﴿al-muḥsinīn﴾ — he says: (for their own selves). Is that so?

* Students: It is not correct.

* Another student: It is not permissible.

* Another student: It is not restricted.

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. ﴿The good-doers﴾ in reality includes good conduct in the worship of Allah and good conduct toward the servants of Allah. The evidence for this is that Jibril said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Tell me about iḥsān." He said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you." This is iḥsān; this is iḥsān in what? In the worship of Allah.

"That you worship Allah as if you see Him" is the worship of seeking (ṭalab), "and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4777), and Muslim (9/5), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah radiyallahu ʿanhu.]] is the worship of fleeing and fear. There is no doubt that the worshipper in the first sense is more perfect than the worshipper in the second sense, because the first worshipper's rank is higher: he worships Allah as if he sees Him, so he intends Allah, and he has a great longing for his Lord, glorified and exalted. As for the second, he worships Allah as if Allah sees him; he fears his Lord, so his worship is the worship of fleeing. The first is the worship of seeking.

Now, iḥsān toward creation — how do you explain it?

* Student: Desiring good for them.

* The Shaykh: No, that is not enough; desire is not sufficient.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Even if he desires, it is not enough. Some of them said: it is badhl al-nadā wa-kaff al-adhā — giving of generosity and restraining harm. This is iḥsān toward people: al-nadā means giving, and kaff al-adhā is clear. So iḥsān has two sides: badhl al-nadā, whether that relates to wealth, rank, or the body, and kaff al-adhā, both verbal and practical. One of them may be absent, and a person may be a doer of good in one respect and not in another, and he is a doer of evil if restraint from harm is absent.

* Student: (...) badhl al-nadā?

* The Shaykh: Yes, like giving.

* Student: (...) wealth.

* The Shaykh: How? We said it includes wealth, body, and rank; teaching knowledge is iḥsān of the body.

* Student: And advice?

* The Shaykh: It enters, because the one who advises you is giving you the best he can.

So in any case, iḥsān — I see this phrase as among the best that can be — is badhl al-nadā and kaff al-adhā: that you do not harm people, so that you would be an evildoer, and you do not withhold your goodness from them, so there is no iḥsān in you; there is no iḥsān if you do not give generously.

So the words ﴿al-muḥsinīn﴾ mean the good-doers in the worship of Allah and toward the servants of Allah; this includes both. As for iḥsān in the worship of Allah, the Prophet ﷺ explained it with his words: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4777), and Muslim (9/5), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah radiyallahu ʿanhu.]], and as for iḥsān toward the servants of Allah, it is badhl al-nadā and kaff al-adhā.

Alright, "And he entered the city" (Qur'an 28:15): was this after reaching maturity (ashudd) or not?

* Student: After it.

* The Shaykh: Yes, after it, after reaching maturity (ashudd). This is because the principle is that what is mentioned first is earlier in occurrence and in action. This is the principle: what is mentioned first is earlier in occurrence if it concerns reports, and earlier in action if it concerns rulings. For this reason, "the Prophet (ﷺ) approached al-Safa and said: 'Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah [2:158]. I begin with what Allah began with'" [[Recorded by Muslim (1218/147) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.]]. And the scholars said: the poor (fuqara') are in greater need than the needy (masakin), because Allah began with them in His saying: "The alms are only for the poor and the needy" [9:60]. So here we say: when Allah mentioned, "And when he reached his maturity and was firm, We gave him judgment and knowledge" [28:14], and then "And he entered," we know that his entering the city was after he had reached his maturity.

As for his saying, ("the city," the city of Pharaoh, and it is Memphis) or ("Munf"); I do not know whether the mim is pronounced with a damma, but the point is it is with a sukun on the nun (after he had been absent from it for a period). Specifying the city as the city of Pharaoh gives me some reservation, because the man was raised by whom?

* The students: By Pharaoh.

* The Shaykh: By Pharaoh, in the very city and the very place. Unless it is said that Pharaoh was in Egypt, and that Memphis is a town outside the general rule, the capital of the land, and that he went out one day and entered it. The better course in such a matter, when nothing is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), is to say: a city among the cities of Egypt, inhabited by Copts and Israelites, according to the evidence of the story.

"He entered the city" ("at a time of heedlessness of its people," at the time of midday rest).

Regarding his saying, "at a time of heedlessness of its people": some scholars say the meaning is "at a time of heedlessness" in terms of time, i.e., at a time when people are heedless. Others say "at a time of heedlessness of its people" means in speech, i.e., they had forgotten Musa and his story, the time had lengthened, so he entered at a moment when they were heedless of discussing this matter. But the first meaning is more apparent: that he entered at a time when its people were heedless.

Must it be the time of midday rest? It is not necessary. It may be the time of midday rest, or it may be at night, or at dusk, Allah knows best; what matters is a time when the people of the town are heedless.

("He found in it two men fighting: this one of his own party," i.e., an Israelite, "and this one of his enemy," i.e., a Copt.)

"He found in it two men fighting": fighting here means dispute, quarrel, and also striking; and it is not apparent that the intended meaning is that they wanted to kill one another.

However, "this one of his own party": the shi'a of a man means his followers. Allah the Exalted said: "And indeed, among his shi'a was Ibrahim" [37:83]. It is also said that the shi'a are those who support you; everyone who supports you is your shi'a, whether he follows you or not. In any case, the intended meaning of shi'a here is that he is of his tribe, and for this the author said, ("i.e., an Israelite").

"And this one of his enemy": from the enemies of Musa, from the family of Pharaoh, namely the Copts.

(i.e., a Copt who was forcing an Israelite to carry firewood to Pharaoh's kitchen). By Allah, what wonders! Who says this?!

In any case, "they were fighting" as is the custom of enemies: enemies constantly quarrel with one another and fight one another. Our shaykh 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in his tafsir that this indicates the strength of the Children of Israel: after they had been humiliated, their sons slaughtered and their women spared, they now made themselves equals of whom? Of the family of Pharaoh, the Copts; because they knew Musa was of them and that Musa held a great position with Pharaoh, so their backs were strengthened by this, and it is clear they would grow strong through this and regard themselves as equals of the family of Pharaoh.

As for his wanting to force him to carry firewood to the kitchen, this is not apparent, and it requires clear evidence; there is no evidence on the matter. Then he explained the situation with his saying: "And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people."

* Student: "They were fighting"?

* The Shaykh: "They were fighting" means they were disputing and contending, and perhaps there was striking between them.

The origin of the story is Musa's entry into the city, the presence of the two men, and the killing of the soul; all of this was the cause of Musa's departure and then his prophethood.

* From it is derived: that Allah the Exalted conducts affairs through their causes; the establishment of causes.

* And derived from this, from His saying: "So the one of his party sought his help against the one of his enemy" [28:15]: the permissibility of seeking help from a created being, but it is conditioned on what he can benefit in; as for what he cannot benefit in, it is not permissible. Accordingly, if one seeks help from a dead person, it is not permissible, because he cannot benefit him; and if one seeks help from a living person in what he cannot do, it is not permissible, because he cannot benefit him; and if one seeks help from a living person in what he is able to do, it is permissible. So seeking help from a created being is permissible on condition that it be in what benefits, and that is with a living person able to remove the hardship.

* Also in it: the establishment of enmity and allegiance; from His saying: "So the one of his party sought his help against the one of his enemy" [28:15]. This is a foundation of the religion, for loyalty to the believers is an obligation of the believer, and disavowal of the disbelievers is an obligation of the believer: "Indeed there has been for you an excellent pattern in Ibrahim and those with him, when they said to their people: Indeed we are free of you and of what you worship besides Allah" [60:4]. This is a matter that a person must do: to disavow every disbeliever.

* In the verse: evidence of Musa's strength; from His saying: "So Musa struck him and finished him" [28:15].

* Also in it: the establishment of his zeal and his swift response, for he did not delay in the matter but hastened to it.

Can it be derived from it the permissibility of repelling an aggressor (dafʿ al-sa'il) with what reaches the point of killing?

* Students: No, it is not derived.

* The Shaykh: (...).

* Student: He was not approved of it.

* The Shaykh: Yes, (...) on this, nor was it approved. But in Islamic law it is known that if a person is attacked by someone and he repels him in the best manner and it does not avert the attack, then he may kill him.

* Also in it: that sins are among the commands and works of Satan; from His saying: "This is of the work of Satan" [28:15].

* Also in it: the establishment of causation; from His saying: "of the work of Satan," because "min" (of) denotes causation.

* Also in it: the confirmation of Satan's enmity toward the children of Adam: "Indeed, he is a clear enemy" [28:15], and it is emphasized with "inna" because of the intensity of warning against him, for his enmity contains no ambiguity.

﴿ ﴾

* In this verse is the affirmation that the messengers, peace and blessings be upon them, may commit errors. [Note: look at this benefit. Is it accepted or not?]

* Student: No, this was before the prophethood.

* The Shaykh: This is not accepted, because it was before the prophethood. Before prophethood it is possible for them to commit this kind of thing, but they do not commit corruption of character, drinking wine, or the like. As for jealousy and zealous protectiveness (ghayrah wa hamiyyah), these may occur from them.

* Also in it: the permissibility of seeking a means (tawassul) to Allah, the Exalted, through the state of the one who supplicates. From where is this derived? From His words: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself﴾. The one who has wronged himself is in need of someone to rescue him, so this is a tawassul to Allah, the Exalted, through the state of the supplicant. Among its examples is the saying of Allah, the Exalted, about Musa: ﴿My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You would send down to me, in need﴾ [al-Qasas 24].

Tawassul to Allah, the Exalted, may be through the state of the supplicant, through praising Allah and His names and attributes, and likewise through His acts by which He bestows favor. All of these are combined in the Prophet's ﷺ teaching to Abu Bakr. He said: "Teach me a supplication to make in my prayer." He said: "Say: O Allah, I have wronged myself greatly, and none forgives sins except You. So forgive me with forgiveness from You and have mercy on me. Indeed, You are the Forgiving, the Merciful."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6326) and Muslim (2705/48), from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

* Student: We mentioned yesterday that (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, it is not this. (...) The first verse: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself﴾.

* Also in it: the affirmation of these two names of Allah: (al-Ghafur) the Forgiving and (al-Rahim) the Merciful. The affirmation of a name, as we have covered in the foundations of creed (usul al-aqidah), includes three matters if the name is transitive (muta'addiyan), and two if it is intransitive (lazimán): it includes affirming that this is one of the names of Allah, affirming the attribute indicated by it, and affirming its effect, which is its extension to the creation, for example. So ﴿the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ includes three things: affirming (al-Ghafur) and (al-Rahim) as names of Allah, affirming the two attributes of forgiveness and mercy for Allah, the Exalted, and affirming the effect that follows from them, namely that He forgives and has mercy.

* Also in it, in His words ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾: evidence for the affirmation of causes (al-asbab). From where is this derived? From the fact that the fa' here indicates causation. That is: because of the wronging of myself, I ask You to forgive me.

* Student: The saying ﴿So He forgave him﴾: is it not derived from it that Allah answered him?

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed.

* From the saying ﴿So He forgave him﴾ is derived Allah's answering, the Exalted, and the attributes included in this answering. For answering includes hearing, knowledge, power, and sufficiency. This (...). When Allah answers a person, it means that He heard him, knew his condition, and was able to grant him his request. All of this is derived from it.

* Also in it: the affirmation of Allah's generosity, from His saying ﴿So He forgave him﴾.

* Also in it: the affirmation that supplication is a cause, contrary to those who deny its causative role and say: "If a thing has been written for me, I do not need supplication, and if it has not been written for me, there is no benefit in supplication."

The answer to that is to say: it is written for you through supplication. It is written for you on this condition: through supplication.

Someone may say: "I will not supplicate, because what is written must occur, and what is not written cannot occur." Is this correct?

* Student: No, it is not correct.

* The Shaykh: We say: this is not correct, because it is written for you through this cause. It is like if someone says: "I will not marry. If Allah has decreed a child for me, a child will come to me, and if Allah has not decreed a child for me, there is no benefit in marriage."

We say: but He has decreed the child for you through what? Through marriage. Thus these unseen matters do not contradict the seen matters. Just as seen matters are not accomplished except by doing the causes that lead to them, so too the unseen matters are not accomplished. So we say: then do not work, do not do righteous deeds, for if you are among the people of Paradise you will be among the people of Paradise, and if you are among the people of the Fire you will be only among the people of the Fire!

It is said: you will be among the people of Paradise through your deed. For this reason, when the Messenger ﷺ said to his companions: "There is none of you but his seat has been written, either in Paradise or in the Fire." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, should we not leave off deeds and rely on what has been written?" He said: "No, work, for each is made easy for what he was created for." Or: "each is made easy." Then he recited the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿As for he who gives and fears Allah (5), and believes in the best reward (6), We will ease him toward ease (7). But as for he who is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient (8), and denies the best reward (9), We will ease him toward hardship﴾ [al-Layl 5-10].[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (4949), and the wording is his, and Muslim (2647/7), from the hadith of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet ﷺ was at a funeral. He took something and began to scratch the ground with it, and said: "There is none of you but his seat has been written, either in the Fire or in Paradise." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, should we not rely on our writing and leave off deeds?" He said: "Work, for each is made easy for what he was created for..."]]

The main point is that in this verse and in many other verses there is evidence for the effect of supplication in the attainment of what is sought. Is that not so?

* Student: Indeed.

* The Shaykh: Because whoever denies that is, in reality, either arrogant or ignorant.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 17:**

﴿قَالَ رَبِّ بِمَا أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيَّ فَلَنْ أَكُونَ ظَهِيرًا لِلْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾ [القصص: ١٧].

﴿He said: "My Lord, for that You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals."﴾ [Al-Qasas: 17]

This verse, as we went over yesterday, has been understood by scholars in two ways. Some say it is a supplication (du'a'), and others say it is a statement of commitment (iltizam), meaning a pledge.

* If we say it is a supplication, then the verse indicates the permissibility of seeking a means (tawassul) through the blessings of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because His words ﴿بِمَا أَنْعَمْتَ﴾ mean: "because of Your bestowing favour upon me."

If we say it is a commitment, then it indicates thankfulness for the blessing, and that a person, when Allah bestows a blessing upon him, must not become a helper, by means of this blessing, to the criminals.

We say that the second meaning is closer to correct and more preferred, because it is the apparent meaning of the verse, and one should not depart from its apparent meaning.

* If it admits of the second meaning, then what is derived from it is the perfection of Musa, peace be upon him, since he pledged to Allah, the Exalted, in gratitude for His blessing, that he would not be a supporter of the criminals.

* And in it there is evidence that supporting a criminal contradicts thankfulness, and so it is prohibited. Why is supporting a criminal prohibited?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Supporting (muzaahara), what is the meaning of supporting the criminal?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, the meaning of supporting him, I mean?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, this statement is not correct. What is its meaning?

* Student: It means his help (...).

* The Shaykh: His help. Supporting him means assisting him. Assisting criminals is prohibited, because it is in reality a form of criminality. The criminal is assisted by preventing his crime. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed.» They said: "O Messenger of Allah, this one is oppressed, so how do we help the oppressor?" (...) He said: «You prevent him from oppression.»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6952) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him.]] That is his help.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 18–20 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So he woke up in the city, fearful and watchful.﴾ [Al-Qasas: 18].
﴿Woke up﴾ means Musa. The meaning of (aṣbaḥa) is that he entered the morning; that is, he spent his night, but in its morning he woke up fearful and watchful.
And His saying ﴿in the city﴾: the (al) here is for mention (al-ʿahd al-dhikrī), because it was previously mentioned.
And His saying ﴿fearful﴾ is the predicate of (aṣbaḥa). (Aṣbaḥa) is one of the sisters of (kāna) (kāna wa akhawātuhā, the verbs of state), which raise the subject and put the predicate in the accusative; so ﴿fearful﴾ is the predicate of (aṣbaḥa).
And His saying ﴿watchful﴾ is a second predicate, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in ﴿fearful﴾: fearful while being watchful. Or: he woke up fearful, he woke up watchful. According to the second parsing, that it is a predicate, this falls under the category of multiple predicates with difference (taʿaddud al-khabar maʿa al-ikhtilāf), because it is permissible for the predicate to be multiple, whether it is multiple in the form of a single word, or multiple in the form of a clause, or multiple in the form of a single word and a clause.
And His saying ﴿watchful﴾: the author says: (awaiting what will befall him from the side of the slain man). Because this killing is a crime, every person who kills someone in a land, these Shiʿa, the Shiʿa of Musa (peace be upon him), are considered weak, so he must fear. This fear is part of human nature, not fear of worship. Fear is of two kinds: fear of worship, which requires drawing near to the one feared, committing to obey him, and the like; and natural fear of what one dreads. The second is not objectionable, because it is part of human nature, but it becomes blameworthy if it leads to abandoning an obligation or doing a prohibited act: ﴿It is only Satan who frightens you of his allies, so do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 175].
He said: ﴿Then behold, the one who had sought his help the day before was calling him for help﴾ [Al-Qasas: 18].
His saying ﴿then behold﴾: (idhā) is for sudden surprise (fujāʾiyya); meaning, it surprised him in the morning while he was fearful and watchful: his companion, the Israelite, who had sought his help the day before, today was calling him for help. Istiṣrākh means asking for rescue from hardship (...).
Here we have (istaghātha), (istanṣara) and (istaṣrakha). Which is more eloquent? (...) Istiṣrākh: ﴿calling him for help﴾.
As for (al-istinṣār), the apparent meaning of the noble verse is that it means istighātha (seeking aid), because He said ﴿so he sought his aid﴾, then He said ﴿the one who had sought his help﴾, so its apparent meaning is that istighātha and istinṣār have one meaning. But in reality, (istinṣār) is more general, because you may seek a person's help to support you even if you are not in hardship, while istighātha is more specific; however, the noble verse indicates that his seeking help was by way of istinṣār.
﴿Calling him for help﴾: he said: (seeking his aid against another Copt).
﴿Musa said to him: Indeed you are clearly misguided﴾ [Al-Qasas: 18]. ﴿To him﴾: to whom? To the Israelite who sought his help. Some exegetes claimed that the pronoun in ﴿to him﴾ refers to the Copt, and that Musa (peace be upon him) punished the Copt and said to him: ﴿Indeed you are clearly misguided﴾. But this is far from the context, and the correct view is that the pronoun in ﴿to him﴾ refers to the Israelite who sought his help.
(﴿Indeed you are clearly misguided﴾: manifestly in error, for what you did yesterday and today.) (Ghawī) is on the pattern (faʿīl) in the sense of (fāʿil), or it is an attributive adjective (ṣifa mushabbaha). Al-ghawī is the opposite of the one who is guided, and it is one who acts in a manner of harm; God Most High said: ﴿Right guidance has become clear from error﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 256]. Rushd (right guidance) is known to mean good conduct, and on this basis ghayy (error) is bad conduct. So the meaning of His saying ﴿you are misguided﴾ is: possessing misguidance, which is bad conduct; and His saying ﴿clearly﴾ means making it clear. The aspect of that, the aspect of your bad conduct, is that yesterday you were quarreling with a Copt, and the next day you were also quarreling with another Copt.
* Student: Troublemaker.
* Shaykh: Yes, a troublemaker. For this reason He said to him: ﴿Indeed you are clearly misguided﴾. Had he continued into the third and fourth day, each day he would bring about strife and create a problem; for this reason He said: ﴿Indeed you are clearly misguided﴾.
(﴿Then when﴾ [Al-Qasas: 19], (an) is superfluous.) That is, the word ﴿an﴾ is superfluous; it is a verbal, grammatical superfluity, not a semantic one, because it conveys emphasis; and all superfluous particles in the Qur'an are, verbally, superfluous but semantically original, because they convey the meaning of emphasis.
The superfluity of (an) is regular after (lammā), and likewise before (law), as in the poet's saying:

And like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they had remained upon the way, We would have given them abundant water﴾ [Al-Jinn: 16], where ﴿and if they had remained﴾ was previously noted to be a lightened form of the heavy (an); meaning: and that they, if they had remained upright.
Here he says: (﴿Then when﴾ superfluous ﴿he intended to strike the one who was an enemy to both of them﴾, to Musa and to the one who sought his help ﴿he said﴾, the one who sought help).
﴿When he intended to strike ... he said: Do you intend to kill me?﴾. How did he know that he intended it, when intention is an act of the heart?
He prepared himself and intended to act, and he must have relied on this knowledge; he relied on an apparent matter, for otherwise intention resides in the heart.
And His saying ﴿he intended﴾ means Musa. ﴿To strike﴾: what is the meaning of striking? It is seizing with force. He intended to strike him (﴿He said﴾: the one who sought help, supposing that he would strike him when he said to him ﴿O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed a person yesterday?﴾ [Al-Qasas: 19]).
His saying: (﴿He said﴾: the one who sought help), makes the subject of ﴿he said﴾ the one who sought help, and two things weaken this: one is semantic and one is verbal.
As for the verbal matter: the pronoun of ﴿he said﴾ refers to the nearest previously mentioned noun, and what is the nearest mentioned? The Copt, in ﴿the one who was an enemy to both of them﴾.
The second is that he said ﴿O Musa, do you intend to kill me?﴾ while Allah says ﴿then when he intended to strike the one who was an enemy to both of them﴾, so we interpret the second intention by the first intention, because it was the Copt who said: ﴿Do you intend to kill me as you killed a person yesterday?﴾.
If someone says: this is weakened by the fact that the Copt had no knowledge of that; from where did he know it?
We say: he deduced it from his saying to the Israelite ﴿Indeed you are clearly misguided﴾, and the story of the killing had become well known in the city and spread, and people began talking about it. So this Copt understood that the Israelite was his enemy, correct? And he rebuked him, Musa, saying ﴿Indeed you are clearly misguided﴾; from that he deduced that the one who killed the Copt yesterday was Musa, so he said: ﴿Do you intend to kill me as you killed a person yesterday?﴾. This view is the preferred one among the two opinions of the exegetes, and the exegetes have two views on this:
One: that the one who said that was the Israelite, even though Musa had prepared to strike the Copt; but he thought that he would strike him when he said ﴿Indeed you are clearly misguided﴾.
The second view we mentioned: that the speaker was the Copt, and what supports this is that when he said ﴿Indeed you are clearly misguided﴾, and it was known that the Israelites are enemies of the Copts, he knew that Musa (peace be upon him) was the one who... or he deduced from this story that he was the one who killed the Copt yesterday; so he said: Do you intend to kill me because I am a Copt, as you killed a person yesterday.
