(...) Brevity in supplication by mentioning only the state of the supplicant without making a request. From where is it taken? (...) the brevity of limiting supplication to mentioning only the state of the one supplicating; from his saying: ﴿رَبِّ إِنِّي لِمَا أَنْزَلْتَ إِلَيَّ مِنْ خَيْرٍ فَقِيرٌ﴾ [al-Qasas: 24].
* And also in it:
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It does not contradict this; this is a supplication (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, (...) great, alone, and fearful.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: He asked Allah to close his poverty and remove his need.
* And also among its benefits: that it is fitting to begin supplication by mentioning the Lord, in His lordship; from his saying: ﴿رَبِّ إِنِّي لِمَا أَنْزَلْتَ﴾. We mentioned yesterday that this is the most common way in which supplication is opened, namely the description of lordship, because by lordship comes the creation and the decree for the human being.
* And it is also derived from this verse: the human being's need for his Lord, blessed and exalted, and that he is in the utmost necessity for the good sent down to him from Allah.
* And it is derived from it: the highness of Allah. Or not? From his saying: ﴿لِمَا أَنْزَلْتَ إِلَيَّ﴾; for sending down from a thing occurs only if it is high. He, Glorified and Exalted, is high in His essence and His attributes, so His highness is of two kinds: highness of essence and highness of attribute. The affirmation of the highness of essence does not necessitate embodiment (tajsīm), as the negators (mu'aṭṭilah) claim, nor that place encompasses Him, as they also said, reaching by that to the denial of His highness; for these negators reach their negation by such phrases, because affirming this requires (...), among matters that are not necessary. But they see them with their intellects as necessary, so they impose them on others, and then reach by them to what? To the denial of the attributes with which Allah described Himself and with which His Messenger ﷺ described Him.

Then He said: ﴿فَجَاءَتْهُ إِحْدَاهُمَا تَمْشِي عَلَى اسْتِحْيَاءٍ﴾ [al-Qasas: 25].

* From this is derived first: the demonstration of the dignity (waqār) which Allah gave to Moses. She came to him in shyness, out of reverence for him, for whenever a person is more dignified, the shyness before him is greater. For this reason, you find that a man who is not dignified, people are not shy before him and do not care for him; they utter before him words that are not fitting and do things that are not fitting because he is not dignified. This is why it is said: "Be modest, and you will be respected."
* And from it also: the demonstration of the perfection of the character of these two women, in that she came walking, and did not hurry or run, but walked calmly; and this is evidence of the perfection of her good manners, and likewise that she was in shyness, which is also from perfection of manners.
* And in her saying: ﴿إِنَّ أَبِي يَدْعُوكَ﴾ [al-Qasas: 25] also is perfection of manners, in that she attributed the invitation to whom? To the father rather than to herself. And it is also from perfection of intelligence, because attributing the invitation to the father is closer to Moses's accepting the invitation, since the one inviting him is a man; and she had described him earlier as an elderly shaykh, so the issuing of the invitation from him to Moses is closer to acceptance.
* And in it also: evidence of her intelligence from a second aspect; by her saying: ﴿لِيَجْزِيَكَ أَجْرَ مَا سَقَيْتَ لَنَا﴾ [al-Qasas: 25]. Had she said: "My father invites you," and not said (...), for fear that an accusation would be directed at him, or for fear that (...), or the like, but she said: ﴿لِيَجْزِيَكَ أَجْرَ مَا سَقَيْتَ لَنَا﴾, so that he would be reassured, and so that it would be more conducive to accepting the invitation.
* And it is derived from the verse also: that a person should have perfection of manners in expressions and removing unease; by his saying: ﴿إِنَّ أَبِي يَدْعُوكَ لِيَجْزِيَكَ أَجْرَ مَا سَقَيْتَ لَنَا﴾, for in this is the removal of unease, and that a person should remove unease from the one addressed, especially in a place which calls for unease. Have you understood?

Just as this should be in speech, it should be in one's state, so that one meets others with cheerfulness, generosity, and an open face. For this reason, among the descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ was that he was constantly cheerful and frequently smiling[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in al-Shamā'il (351) from the hadith of 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him.]]; and the opposite of that is what? Frowning, scowling, and lack of openness; for this causes others to flee from you, and likewise causes no one to feel at ease with you, so that even if one sits with you, he does not feel at ease. But if a person sees you... ﴿ذَلِكَ فَضْلُ اللَّهِ يُؤْتِيهِ مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾. This matter may be by acquisition, and it may be by natural disposition; for among people there is one whom Allah, Glorified and Exalted, grants such a good trait, and among people there is one who is deprived of it, and among people there is one who tries to adopt it. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said to the Ashajj of 'Abd al-Qays: "Verily, in you are two traits Allah loves: forbearance (ḥilm) and deliberation (anā'ah)." (...). He said: "O Messenger of Allah, are they traits I acquired, or did Allah create me upon them?" He said: "Rather, Allah created you upon them"[[Narrated by Abū Dāwūd (54) with its chain from Zāri' (may Allah be pleased with him), with the wording: "Rather, Allah created you upon them."]]. From this it is taken that such characteristics may be by cultivation and may be by innate nature. Which of them is more firmly established?

* Student: Innate nature is more firmly established.
* Shaykh: Innate nature is more firmly established. For this reason the Messenger of Allah said: "Rather, Allah created you upon them," because cultivated character may sometimes be forgotten by a person; he forgets it, does not adopt it, and remains upon his natural disposition (...). But innate nature is without doubt more complete; it is only that a person, through habit and cultivating something, can make it a trait of his.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is not suitable; otherwise innate nature is more complete, that (...) I cultivate noble characteristics (...), this is innate nature; otherwise now (...), and how many people whose natures changed and whose characters became good by what Allah bestowed upon them.

* * *

He said: (﴿عَلَى اسْتِحْيَاءٍ﴾ means: placing the sleeve of her garment over her face out of shyness before him).

Ibn Kathir mentioned this from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: its chain is sound[[Ibn Kathir cited the mentioned report in his tafsir (6/228) from Abū Ḥātim with his chain from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "She came walking in shyness, speaking with her garment over her face." Then he said: this chain is sound.]]. Such a report from 'Umar may be by way of conjecture: he conjectured that her garment was over her face; but in the verse this is not what is meant.

The sleeve of the garment over the face: what is the dir' (garment)? The dir' is what people call (...), because it is like the garment worn in war; but how does she place her sleeve over her face? Does this mean it is so? Yes, it is so, (...) like this, out of shyness before him.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, she was one with wide sleeves; this is what is called a dir', and among women it must be very wide; what is called a dir' (...).

Then she said: ﴿إِنَّ أَبِي يَدْعُوكَ لِيَجْزِيَكَ﴾. I have a problem with ﴿أَبِي﴾. It is known that the Five Nouns are put in the accusative with the alif. Is it in the accusative with the alif here in her saying ﴿إِنَّ أَبِي﴾?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: How?
* Student: Allah knows best.
* Shaykh: Allah knows best.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. Well, the evidence from the words of Ibn Mālik is that it is required that it not be attached to the first person pronoun yā'.
* Student: As long as it is not attached, or (...).
* Shaykh: (...).
* Student: His saying:
"The condition for these to take the declension is that they be attached, but not to the yā' like jā akhū abīka dhā i'tilā."
* Shaykh: Yes.
"The condition for these to take the declension is that they be attached, but not to the yā' like jā akhū abīka dhā i'tilā."
Here it is attached to the yā', and therefore we say: ﴿أَبِي﴾ is the subject of (inna), in the accusative with a presumed fatḥah on what precedes the yā' of the speaker, its manifestation being prevented by the occupation of the position with the harmonizing vowel (ḥarakat al-munāsabah). Have you understood, everyone? As for the speech of the common people who say "qāl abwī," this is colloquial, not Arabic.

Now, ﴿إِنَّ أَبِي يَدْعُوكَ لِيَجْزِيَكَ﴾: the lām is for causation; that is, he invites you for this purpose. And the meaning of (yajziyaka) is that he rewards you, (...) the recompense, from jazā yajzī.

And His saying: ﴿أَجْرَ مَا سَقَيْتَ لَنَا﴾ [al-Qasas: 25], is the second object of (yajzī), he receives his wage or compensation. The ajr is the compensation taken in exchange for work.

And His saying: ﴿مَا سَقَيْتَ لَنَا﴾ means "for our sake." Is the mā in ﴿مَا سَقَيْتَ﴾ conditional?

* Student: It is not conditional.
* Shaykh: It is not conditional. Relative?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is not relative either (...).
* Student: Verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah).
* Shaykh: Yes, verbal-noun; that is: "that he reward you the wage of your watering." And it is not suitable to say "the wage of what you watered," because does she mean the wage of the one who watered or the wage of the watering? The wage of the watering. So the mā here is verbal-noun. Had she said "the wage of what you watered," it would have become the wage of the sheep, and she does not want him to be given the wage of the sheep; she only wants her father to reward him for his watering of the sheep. So it is necessary that the mā here be verbal-noun.

The lām in His saying ﴿لَنَا﴾ is like its counterpart in ﴿فَسَقَى لَهُمَا﴾, meaning it is for causation and not for transitivity.

"(So he answered her)": Moses answered her, that is, he answered the invitation of her father "(disapproving in himself of taking a wage)." That is, he answered her while concealing that he was not one who takes a wage. How do we know this? They said: we know that Moses did that for Allah, and whoever does something for Allah cannot take a wage for it in this world.

But this does not necessarily establish that Moses would take a wage. If we were asked: do you testify that Moses, in that situation when he answered the invitation, had concealed in himself that he was not one who takes a wage? Do you testify or not?

* Student: No.
* Shaykh: We do not testify; we do not know. Perhaps Moses, peace be upon him, would take the wage because he was in need and took it to meet his need, and perhaps he would not take it out of generosity. Either it is forbidden that a person take a wage in advance for what he does for Allah; then if he is rewarded for it, there is no objection to taking it. If he is rewarded for it as a reward, there is no objection to taking it. Indeed, "when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent 'Umar as a collector of charity and gave him, he said: give it to one poorer than me. He said: 'What comes to you of this wealth while you are not seeking it or asking for it, take it'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (7163) and Muslim (1045/110), from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. It is known that 'Umar was not looking forward to taking a wage; the evidence is that he said: give it to one poorer than me, and despite that the Messenger said: "take it." So the person who does a deed for Allah, if he is rewarded for it, his reward is not nullified so long as his intention at the root is sincere for Allah.

Therefore the claim that Moses was disapproving in himself of taking a wage has no evidence for it, and we have no right to speak of this (...).

"(As if she intended the reward, if he was one who desired it, so she walked before him.)"

"(As if)": the author (...). That is, "the wage of what you watered for us": it is known that a wage cannot exist except by a contract of hire.

Did a contract of hire occur between Moses and the two women, that he would water for them?

* Student: No, it did not occur.
* Shaykh: No. But he says: "(As if she intended the reward, if he was one who desired it)," so she named this reward a wage.

"(So she walked before him, and the wind kept striking her garment, uncovering her legs. So he said to her: walk behind me and guide me to the way.)" We say: the narration of this story has no transmitted basis (lā athar lahā). Its wording is "she walked before him," but they bring it as a preface to her saying: ﴿إِنَّ خَيْرَ مَنِ اسْتَأْجَرْتَ الْقَوِيُّ الْأَمِينُ﴾ [al-Qasas: 26], for it was previously mentioned that he lifted the great rock which only ten could carry.

* Student: He is strong.
* Shaykh: For strength, and here for trustworthiness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verses 24–28 (part 2 of 6):

(So she did, until he came to their father, who was Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and he had dinner prepared. He said to him: "Sit down and eat with us." He said: "I fear that it may be a recompense for what I gave them to drink, and we are a household that does not seek any recompense for a good deed." He said: "No, it is my custom and the custom of my forefathers to host the guest and feed the food." So he ate, and told him his situation.) All of this has no evidence to support it. There is no proof for it. What the evidence shows is that Musa ﷺ accepted the invitation and walked until he reached the father. This is sufficient for us to believe what the Qur'an indicates about this story. As for bringing in something that is not mentioned in the verse, no.

He says: ﴿So when he came to him and related to him the stories﴾ [Al-Qasas 25].

Who is the subject of ﴿came﴾? Musa. ﴿And related to him﴾, that is, Musa.

﴿the stories﴾ (...) means "the things related," because al-qasas is a verbal noun (masdar)(...); Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So they returned, retracing their footsteps, following the track﴾ [Al-Kahf 64], meaning they were tracing the trail by tracing it (qasasan). And al-qasas is "that which is related," because it relates what is related. On this basis it is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), and a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle occurs often, such as His saying: ﴿And if they are pregnant, then spend on them﴾ [At-Talaq 6]; ﴿ulat hamlin﴾ means "carrying (a child)." Likewise His ﷺ saying: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) in a similar wording, and Muslim (1718/18) with his wording, from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her], although the verse (...) because it is a description of the woman.

In any case, here ﴿al-qasas﴾ we say: it is a verbal noun in the sense of the thing related. Why do we not take it as a verbal noun in its literal meaning?

Because al-qasas is the action of the one who relates, and it is not the thing that is reported. What is reported and related is the thing related, meaning the matter, or the story, or the like. This is what is related.

What is the qasas that he related to him?

He said: (From his killing of the Copt, and their intention to kill him, and his fear of Pharaoh.) He related to him his whole matter: that he was in Egypt for example, and that such-and-such happened, the killing of the Copt, and that a man came to him and advised him to leave, and that he left. For this reason He said: ﴿the stories﴾.

﴿He said: "Do not fear."﴾ This ﴿He said﴾ is the answer to (lamma, when). ﴿So when he came to him and related to him ... he said﴾, that is, the lord of Madyan: ﴿"Do not fear. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people."﴾ [Al-Qasas 25].

﴿Do not fear﴾: the lam here is a prohibitive (lam al-nahy), and what is meant by it (...) is prohibition, or is the intent to reassure this man? It is reassurance. On this basis, His saying ﴿You have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾ is a confirmation of the sentence in meaning, a confirmation of the sentence in every (...); that is: there is no fear for you because you have escaped from the wrongdoing people. Glory be to Allah the Mighty! The speech of this man came matching Musa's request. Musa went out from it ﴿in fear, watching carefully. He said: "My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people"﴾, so the answer came here from this man: ﴿"Do not fear. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿"Do not fear"﴾ is a response to his saying ﴿in fear, watching carefully﴾, and ﴿"You have escaped from the wrongdoing people"﴾ is a response to his saying ﴿"save me from the wrongdoing people"﴾. So the answer of this man matched the request of Musa exactly, and this is how Allah the Exalted's answer to one in dire need is, perfectly matching his plea.

(Because Pharaoh has no authority over Madyan.) This is the apparent meaning: that he reassured him that he had escaped from the wrongdoing people, because where is Pharaoh's authority now? It is only in Egypt and its surroundings. As for Madyan, Pharaoh has no authority over it. For if he had authority over it, he would not have escaped from them, from the wrongdoing people.

* Shaykh: (...) close to Egypt. It was mentioned in the author's words that it is eight days from Egypt.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: It is possible, but within the borders. Borders, as you know, are not a small matter. It needs (...). Two kingdoms have nothing between them except an imaginary line.

﴿He said: "Do not fear. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people."﴾ (﴿One of the two women said﴾ [Al-Qasas 26], and she was the one who was sent, the elder or the younger.) That is, we do not know whether the one who spoke was the elder or the younger. Allah says: ﴿One of the two women said﴾, and as for her being the one who was sent, this is based on what preceded, that she walked in front of him and the wind revealed her shins, and he said: "Walk behind me." Thus she knew that the man was trustworthy. This is the reason for his words: (and she was the one who was sent). But I ask you now: must the one who spoke be the one who was sent, or the one who stayed behind?

* Student: It is not necessarily so.

* Shaykh: It is necessarily neither this nor that. She may be the one who was sent, and she may be the one who stayed behind. The important thing is that it is enough for us to leave unspecified what Allah left unspecified.

﴿One of the two women said: "O my father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy."﴾ [Al-Qasas 26]. ﴿O my father﴾: how is it ﴿O my father﴾? Do you say "ya abi" (O my father), or is the (ta) for feminine marking because she is feminine?

* Shaykh: It is permissible to replace the (ya) with a (ta), it is permissible to replace it with a (ta), so one says "abati" instead of "abi".

She said: ﴿O my father, hire him﴾. Here it means: make him a hired worker for you. This command is not in its literal meaning, it is not a request for the action in the manner of an action, because a daughter cannot command her father with a command. Rather it is (?)

* Shaykh: For supplication!
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Supplication. It is not appropriate to say "for supplication," nor "for entreaty," because entreaty, as they say, is from an equal to his equal.

* Shaykh: But... yes, for hoping, or for asking, for asking, because supplication should only be made directed to Allah, glory be to Him and exalted.

(﴿Hire him﴾: take him as a hired worker to pasture our sheep, that is, in our place.)

(...), and the second: the man is strong and trustworthy, and we are at ease with him. Likewise, we are at ease that he will water for us completely because of his strength.

﴿Hire him, for indeed the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy﴾ [Al-Qasas 26] (that is: hire him for his strength and trustworthiness).

She said: ﴿Hire him﴾ is the ruling, and ﴿indeed the best one you can hire﴾ is the causative explanation (ta'liliyyah). That is: hire him, because he is strong and trustworthy. But she gave the reason as a general principle. If she had said, "Hire him, for he is strong and trustworthy," this would have been a reason for a particular matter, namely hiring Musa. But she gave this cause embraced under a general rule: ﴿indeed the best one you can hire﴾, whether Musa or someone else, who? ﴿the strong and trustworthy﴾. These two qualities are the pillars of every work. Every work requires these two matters. It cannot be done except with them: strength and trustworthiness. By strength the action is done, and by trustworthiness the action is completed. As for one who is not strong, he does not act, and one who is not trustworthy does not complete the action, and perhaps does not do it at all. Therefore when a person is strong and trustworthy, the action is completed through him.

Alright, what about other than hiring? That is, this is specific to hiring, that we seek the strong and trustworthy, or is it in all works?

* Student: In all works.
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed, in all works. If we appoint someone to sell, the best one we appoint is the strong and trustworthy. If we appoint someone over a village, the best one we appoint is the strong and trustworthy. If we appoint someone as judge of a city, the best one we appoint to judgeship is the strong and trustworthy. For this reason the jinn, when he said to Sulayman: "I will bring you the throne of the Queen of Sheba before you rise from your place," said: ﴿And indeed I am for it strong and trustworthy﴾ [An-Naml 39]. ﴿Strong and trustworthy﴾, and this one is not a hired worker, this one is not a hired worker.

The important point is that strength and trustworthiness are two essential conditions in every work. One who is not strong cannot do it, and one who is not trustworthy cannot be entrusted and does not complete or perfect the work. ﴿Indeed the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy﴾, and Musa is strong and trustworthy.

(So he asked her about them both, and she told him what had preceded: the lifting of the stone from the well, and his saying to her, "Walk behind me," and in addition that when she came to him and he was aware of her, he lowered his head and did not raise it, so he desired to marry her to him.)

The words "so he asked her" means: her father. "About them both" means: about strength and trustworthiness. How did you know that the man is strong and trustworthy? So she mentioned it to him. (She told him what had preceded: the lifting of the stone from the well.) He lifted the stone of the well, and ordinarily no one lifts it except ten people, and this is evidence of his strength. She was walking in front of him while the wind revealed her shins, and he said: "Be behind me." This is evidence of his trustworthiness. Also, as an additional sign of trustworthiness, when Musa became aware of her, he lowered his head (that is, he lowered it), and did not raise it, and this is from trustworthiness.

But we do not need these three matters. Rather, they both knew that he was strong because of his drawing the bucket and watering for them, and that he was trustworthy in that he watered completely and did not take anything from the sheep, and this shows his trustworthiness. So trustworthiness and strength were derived from his watering. It is not necessary to fabricate something in order to establish that he is strong and trustworthy. What need is there for this fabrication? A person is known by his strength from his drawing of the bucket. A person (...). And his also watering completely, letting the sheep drink until they are satisfied, shows that he is trustworthy, because one who is not trustworthy does not water completely; he draws (...) one bucket or two. But the trustworthy is one who brings the thing as it should be. This is the way they knew his strength and trustworthiness.

* Shaykh: Yes, because what happened to Musa with the two women was only that he watered for them, then he turned to the shade.

* Shaykh: It is not mentioned to us. The original state is the absence of what was not done. The original state is its absence. We derive only from the story. * Shaykh: And this is what happened. The two of them did not agree with Musa except by watering (...).

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Clear. When a person knows one man who waters your sheep, this (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) his right. So when it is known that she gave him his right, it is known that he is strong and that he is trustworthy. A person who is hired (...), he does not know that the one who performs what he did in complete form is none other than trustworthy. This is not (...) hiring. Even if a person volunteers for you, someone may come and volunteer for you (...).

* Shaykh: Perhaps this is so, but only what is not present in the Qur'an (...) which we believe (...), but in this, it often occurs, perhaps (...).

* Shaykh: No, this idea is wrong (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, on the basis that trustworthiness (...).

(...) ﴿you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾ [Al-Qasas 25]. I think this is the beginning of the discussion and the benefits.

His saying: ﴿You have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿you have escaped﴾?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The meaning of escaping from something is what?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, it means deliverance from it.

Alright. Furthermore, this sentence matches Musa's request and also his condition. Do you know this?

* Student: Because he called upon Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, and he was in fear, watching carefully: ﴿My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes. So Allah replaced the fear with?
* Student: Allah replaced the fear with security.

* Shaykh: Alright.

* Shaykh: What he asked: ﴿My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people﴾.

Why did he say to him: "You have escaped from the wrongdoing people"?

* Student: Because (...).
* Shaykh: His saying: ﴿Indeed the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy﴾ [Al-Qasas 26]. What is its position in relation to what came before it in meaning?
* Student: Causative.
* Shaykh: Causative. As if she is saying: hire him, for he is strong and trustworthy.

Alright, these two qualities are the two essential qualities in works. Or not? Because the opposite of strength is weakness, and the weak cannot work, and the opposite of trustworthiness is treachery, and the traitor does not complete the work. Is that so?

These two qualities are essential in every authority: in the caliphate, the emirate, administration, agency, bequest, and other things. Every authority necessarily requires two things: strength and trustworthiness.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Strength in the work. The work that requires physical power must be physically strong. The work that requires mental power, such as arithmetical work and the like, requires being strong in that. So the meaning of strength in work is according to the nature of the work.

Now let us return to the benefits of the verses.

Among the benefits of the verses: we mentioned the good manners of these two women, which is with modesty (...). Or did we not mention them? The perfect manners of the two women?

* Student: Yes, we mentioned them.
* Shaykh: And we also mentioned the perfection of their intelligence from three aspects.

His saying: ﴿So when he came to him and related to him the stories, he said: "Do not fear. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people."﴾ [Al-Qasas 25].

* From the verse it is derived that relating reports is not considered complaining. If you relate to a person what misfortunes befell you, this is not considered complaining to him. For this reason it is said: "A report, not a complaint." The sick person says, for example, to one who asks about his condition: "A report, not a complaint." The difference between them is that complaint includes seeking the removal of the thing and feeling distress at it, feeling distress at the thing and seeking its removal. As for a report, it is free of that. It is simply a report of a matter that has occurred.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, I do not know (...).
* And in it also: evidence..
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) the person who reports his condition (...) such and such and such, this is not good.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: If it involves another, it is examined. If he was wronged, Allah says: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech except by one who has been wronged﴾ [An-Nisa 148], and the wrongdoer's injustice cannot be repelled except by mentioning his injustice, even if he dislikes that.
* Student: But in (...).
* Shaykh: It is to be examined. The important point is that the discussion concerns a person who reports what happens to him, we are speaking of this, that this is not considered complaining, even in disliked matters that befell him. This is not considered complaining. For this reason he related the report.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verses 24–28 (part 3 of 6):

* Also in it: evidence of the understanding (fiqh) of the man of Madyan. He reassured him and gave the reason, saying: ﴿Do not fear; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people.﴾ His saying ﴿Do not fear﴾ conveys reassurance to the man, and ﴿you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾ conveys the reason for it. Had he said ﴿Do not fear﴾ without saying ﴿you have escaped﴾, one might think he only wanted to make the matter easy for him, even though there was a possibility that he would not escape. But when he said ﴿you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾, this became a clarification of the ruling together with its reason.
* Also in it: evidence that the family of Pharaoh were known for wrongdoing among people at that time, from his saying ﴿from the wrongdoing people﴾.
* Also in it: evidence that the soldiers of a wrongdoer are wrongdoers. He did not say "you have escaped from the wrongdoer" but said ﴿from the wrongdoing people﴾, and that is so, for the soldiers of a wrongdoer are wrongdoers. For this reason, if he orders you...
The Shaykh: The basic principle is the obligation to obey the ruler, and nothing exists that prevents this basic principle, since you do not know whether he is a wrongdoer or not. Also, it is a hardship: if a soldier, for example, is ordered by his superior to strike or to imprison, he would say, "Why should I strike? Why should I imprison?" Also, this leads to chaos and the disintegration of the government and the state. Yes. Therefore it is said: obedience is obligatory unless you know that it is sinful.

Some scholars held a detailed position, namely that if the one giving the order is known for wrongdoing, then it is not permitted to proceed to comply, unless you know that wrongdoing is absent in this particular matter, giving precedence to the apparent over the original state. What is the apparent?

* A student: That he is a wrongdoer.
* The Shaykh: The apparent state of this ruler, for example, is that he is a wrongdoer, so that is given precedence over the original state, which is absence of wrongdoing and the obligation to obey. This distinction is not objectionable, yes, but it is also burdensome, because although he is a wrongdoer, he may not wrong in everything.

It is known that, (i.e., we ask Allah that He not test us or you), a soldier finds it extremely difficult to say to his commander: What is the reason for striking him? What is the reason for imprisoning him? For this reason, among the principles of study in military training and in the army, they teach that the junior obeys his superior with blind obedience, to the extent that some of them hold that it is obligatory to obey him even in disobedience to Allah. But this is not accepted. What I mean is that they obey with blind obedience, as if the person were deaf and blind.

In any case, on this matter, whoever adopts the view that obedience is obligatory absolutely, unless you know it is wrongdoing, has taken the basic principle and has room for it. Whoever is able to inquire when the ruler gives an order, about a ruler whose apparent state is wrongdoing, and a just ruler who ... is not a wrongdoer, obedience to him is obligatory, and he does not need the distinction. This is not objectionable.

The main point is that from this verse we derive that the soldiers of a wrongdoer are wrongdoers, yes. Of course, if they agree with him knowingly: ﴿you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Qasas 25].

* A student: Is it permissible for a person to be a soldier of someone known for wrongdoing?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is permissible, and sometimes it is even obligatory, if his presence in that role lessens some harms.
* The student: Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not incline toward those who wronged﴾ [Hud 113]?
* The Shaykh: Yes. ﴿Do not incline﴾ means do not lean toward them by helping them in wrongdoing. As for me becoming a soldier in order to lessen their wrongdoing, there is nothing wrong with that. But a person who joins them in order to assist them or strengthen their side, even morally, that is not permitted.
* The student: If there is not ...?
* The Shaykh: All of them ... few are those whose work is for Allah. Most people want this world and wealth.

Alright: ﴿He said, "Do not fear; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people."﴾ [al-Qasas 25].

﴿One of the two women said, "O father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy."﴾ [al-Qasas 26].

* It is derived from this: the permissibility of a woman speaking in the presence of a non-mahram man. Pay attention to this benefit. Do we agree with this or not?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, (...), no. It is the state of his condition, but Musa, until now, was he a prophet or not? So his law was not yet established.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...), this is a report, because after mentioning the polytheists and others, it is his speech.
* A student: We say: she spoke in the presence of Musa, meaning?
* The Shaykh: Yes, that is the apparent meaning. The apparent meaning is that it was during the lifetime of Musa, and for this reason he said: ﴿He said, "Indeed, I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine"﴾ [al-Qasas 27], immediately.

So we may not accept that this is evidence for permissibility, because the law of Musa at that time was not yet established. Yes, if Shu'ayb was upon a religion, and I say this because we do not agree with those who said that the intended one is the Prophet Shu'ayb. I say: if the man of Madyan (it is better to avoid the word Shu'ayb) was upon a religion, then yes, it may be derived from this the permissibility of a woman speaking in the presence of a non-mahram man (...), although this matter has no problem from the legal standpoint in our law: a woman may speak in the presence of men, women (...), the Messenger ﷺ in the presence of men, as long as there is no fear of what?
* A student: Temptation.
* The Shaykh: Temptation. If temptation is feared, then temptation is forbidden even in permissible matters.
* A student: Does this get an objection that (...)?
* The Shaykh: What is it?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Like what? (...), like what?
* The student: Like (...), that it is from the category of introducing supplication with the attribute of Lordship, like what Musa said, the permissibility of limiting oneself to it in supplication (...).
* The Shaykh: That is an action of Musa, and Allah the Exalted mentioned it in a manner of praise for him, not merely mentioning it that way. Furthermore, this has also come in the Sunnah from another evidence (...).

Likewise, from this verse it may also be derived: ﴿One of the two women said, "O father, hire him"﴾ [al-Qasas 26]. It may be derived that it is advice from the lower to the higher, from her saying ﴿hire him﴾, because the command here is not obligatory but is advice and suggestion. The lower may know better than the higher in some matters, right? Just as the less excellent may be better than the more excellent in some matters.

* From the noble verse it is also derived: referring matters of work to these two qualities, which are strength and trustworthiness.
* It is also derived from it: a person should, in all his circumstances, seek out one who is strong and trustworthy, from her saying: ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy﴾ [al-Qasas 26]. Strength here means strength suited to the work. Physical strength in physical work means bodily strength; strength in intellectual matters means strength of thought in that matter; strength in military matters means strength in war itself. Each thing has its strength according to its nature. When one of the two qualities is lacking, the work is disrupted. If strength is lacking and a person is weak, he cannot carry out the work, even if he is one of the most trustworthy of people. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said to Abu Dhar: "Indeed, you are a weak man, so do not take on leadership, nor authority over the property of an orphan." [Muslim (1826/17) narrated from Abu Dhar, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Abu Dhar, indeed I see you as weak, and I love for you what I love for myself. Do not be in charge of two persons, and do not take charge of the property of an orphan."] So his saying "Indeed, you are a weak man" here: is weakness the opposite of trustworthiness, or the opposite of strength?
* A student: The opposite of strength.
* The Shaykh: The opposite of strength. The man is trustworthy, but he is weak in taking on work.

Therefore we say: a person may lack strength or trustworthiness, and perfection is the presence of both strength and trustworthiness.

* * *

﴿He said, "Indeed, I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine, on [the condition] that you serve me for eight years."﴾ [al-Qasas 27]
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, (...).
﴿He said, "Indeed, I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine"﴾ [al-Qasas 27]. Now the man of Madyan is speaking: ﴿I want to marry you﴾. Is this a marriage contract or a promise of a marriage contract?
* A student: A promise.
* The Shaykh: ﴿I want to marry you﴾, and it is not a contract. On this basis there is no evidence here for the permissibility of contracting marriage with an unspecified person, because he says ﴿I want to marry you﴾. The meaning of ﴿I marry you off to﴾ is "I make you a spouse," because (nikah) originally means joining and gathering, so the meaning of ﴿unkihaka﴾ is "I make you a spouse," because a man joins his wife to himself and comes together with her.

And his saying: ﴿one of these two daughters of mine﴾.

His saying: ﴿one of my daughters﴾ is undetermined. We do not know whether she is the elder or the younger, and for this reason he says: (and she is the elder or the younger).

And his saying: ﴿ibnatayya﴾, originally "two daughters of mine," so the nun was dropped because of the annexation (idafa). For this reason we say: ﴿ibnatayya﴾ is in the genitive case with the ya' standing in for the kasra, since it is a dual, and the nun was dropped because of the annexation.

And his saying: ﴿hatayni﴾ is a demonstrative pronoun to identify the two daughters. From this we understand that he has other daughters, because the demonstrative excludes all others. Or the meaning is that Musa, peace be upon him, may not know that these two daughters are his. He may say: ﴿Indeed, I want to marry you to one of my daughters﴾ and not know which of his daughters is here. This is the better view, because identifying them by demonstration is so that the addressee does not assume that he has other daughters, yes. The meaning is not that he identifies these two to exclude the rest of the daughters. Strangely, some exegetes said that this is to exclude the other daughters, and that the daughters were seven, and these two were excluded by specification. It is said: this is not so, and there is nothing in the verse indicating it. But when he says... Now, if I say to someone: "I want to marry you to one of my daughters," and I have two wives, would it be understood that they are from among them?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: It would not be understood until I say "these two," and then it is understood that these are my daughters. So here we say ﴿hatayni﴾ with this meaning.

﴿on [the condition] that you serve me﴾ [al-Qasas 27]: ﴿you serve me﴾ means you give yourself to me as a hired worker ﴿for eight years﴾ [al-Qasas 27] (to be a hired worker for me in pasturing my sheep ﴿for eight years﴾, meaning years), and it is plural?
* A student: ḥijja.
* The Shaykh: ḥijja. (﴿And if you complete ten﴾, meaning pasturing ten years ﴿then it is from you﴾ [al-Qasas 27], meaning completion), that is, not obligatory.

He informed him that he wants to marry him to one of his two daughters, and the dowry is that he pastures the sheep for eight years. From where is it known that the intended work is pasturing sheep? He might say to him: "You serve me so that you become a builder or a farmer for me or something like that"?
* A student: From the context of the daughters' request (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, from the context of the story: ﴿O father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy﴾ [al-Qasas 26], and the whole matter concerns the work before him now, which is pasturing sheep. Thus it is known that he, the man of Madyan, wanted to hire Musa, peace be upon him, to pasture sheep for eight years. If he completes ten, it is from him, meaning the two years are a voluntary favor, and the contract is for eight years.

His saying: (﴿And I do not want to burden you﴾ [al-Qasas 27], by stipulating the ten), this is clearly open to question, because if Musa accepted the stipulation of ten, would there be hardship in it?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: There is no hardship in it. Otherwise we would say that stipulating eight instead of six involves hardship. But ﴿And I do not want to burden you﴾ refers to your dealings in carrying out the contract. Its meaning is: I will be lenient if a day or days pass when you do not pasture, or things like that, or if you suffer loss of property or other harm, then I will not burden you with this. So what is the absence of burden in? In carrying out the lease. As for increasing the duration, this is not a burden (...). Otherwise, if we say that eight compared to six is a burden, then the correct view without doubt is: I do not want to burden you during the carrying out of the work. For some people say: you have difficulty in dealing, in carrying out the contract, you find for example that he does not allow him to delay, and if he gets an illness that compels him, or he says: make up this day for me, or deduct from the wage for it, or things like that.

He says: ﴿And I do not want to burden you﴾, and for this reason he said: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the righteous﴾ [al-Qasas 27]. His promise in his saying ﴿you will find me﴾: is it now or in the future?
* A student: In the future.
* The Shaykh: In the future, because this sīn (sa-) transforms the present tense into the future, and it, as we have passed over, conveys certainty and proximity. So there are three benefits when it enters upon the present tense: converting it to future, affirming it, and bringing it near. Do you understand?

His saying ﴿you will find me, if Allah wills﴾ is from (wajada, yajidu), when one attains something.

But he said ﴿if Allah wills, among the righteous﴾, and this indicates that the man of Madyan is a believer, because this speech of his indicates his faith and that he is upon the religion.

His saying ﴿if Allah wills﴾ is a conditional. Is it a conditional intended in its literal sense?

The author says that it is (for blessing). What led the author to that is that his saying ﴿you will find me﴾ is a promise from him, and a promise, if it is made conditional, is not affirmed, so for this reason he said: (﴿if Allah wills﴾ for blessing), so that it does not contradict the promise.

But in reality, we should not interpret it as for blessing, rather we should interpret it as a true conditional by the will of Allah, because a person's resolve on something is affirmed, but the carrying out of a thing a person can never affirm, however great the work: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow, unless Allah wills"﴾ [al-Kahf 23–24]. So what we see is that this conditional is in its true sense, not for blessing. Why? Because carrying out this thing is not in the hand of the man of Madyan, or is it? It is not in his hand, for matters may be unrestricted.

His saying ﴿if Allah wills, among the righteous﴾: this is a clause whose place in grammar they call a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'tariḍa) between the verb and its object, because ﴿you will find me﴾ takes two objects: the first object is the ya' (me), and the second object is ﴿among the righteous﴾, the prepositional phrase. Here the parenthetical clause has come between the verb and its two objects.

His saying: (﴿among the righteous﴾, those who fulfill the covenant), yes, because the righteousness of everything is according to its nature. Here the matter is a contract of hire, and righteousness in it is by fulfilling. In every place it is according to its nature: righteousness in religion is performing the obedience of Allah, and the righteousness of food is that it not be altered by a foul smell or (...). So righteousness is according to its place in each case.

﴿He said, "That is between me and you"﴾ [al-Qasas 28].

("He said" Musa, "that" which you have said, "is between me and you"), look: ﴿That is between me and you﴾ actually is this acceptance, because every contract needs an offer and an acceptance, an offer from the one giving and an acceptance from the one receiving, right? An offer from the one giving, whether a seller, a lessor, a marrying guardian, or the like, and acceptance from the one receiving. The offer from the man of Madyan is his saying: "I want to marry you on [the condition] that you serve me," and the acceptance from Musa is: ﴿That is between me and you﴾, meaning: I agree and accept.

Although at first the man of Madyan says: "I want to marry you on," or did he say: "I have married you on [the condition] that you serve me," which indicates also that contracts are concluded by whatever indicates them, because wanting something is not the thing itself. The wanting of a thing is not the thing itself. For this reason, if a man says to his wife, "I want to divorce you," or "I intend to release you," does it become a divorce?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: No, because wanting is not the act.

But this indicates... The preponderant view on this question, which we will address, God willing, in mentioning the benefits, is that contracts are concluded by whatever indicates them, with no specific formula, yes, even that they may be concluded by an act, as in the conclusion of a sale by what? By exchange (mu'ata).

He said: (﴿That is between me and you, whichever of the two terms I fulfill﴾ [al-Qasas 28], the eight or the ten, and "ma" is superfluous, meaning: his grazing).

﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfill﴾ [al-Qasas 28]. The author says that "ma" is superfluous for emphasis, and accordingly "ayy" is the object placed before ﴿I fulfill﴾, or not?
* A student: Yes.

Sheikh: "Is it not valid under the construction of *al-ishtighal* (the verb-with-pronoun construction)? It is not valid, because the *ishtighal* construction requires that the verb contain a pronoun referring back to the fronted noun. If there is no such pronoun, the fronted word is the object. For example, you say *Zaydun akramtuhu* ("Zayd, I honored him"), which is *ishtighal* because the verb has a pronoun. But *Zaydan akramtu* (without a pronoun) is the fronted object (*al-maf'ul al-muqaddam*), not *ishtighal*. Which fits what we have here, *Zaydan akramtu* or *Zaydun akramtuhu*?"

Student: "*Zaydan akramtu*."

Sheikh: "*Zaydan akramtu*, because He said ﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾, and did not say ﴿Whichever of the two terms﴾ followed by a pronoun. So this is not a case of *ishtighal* but of the fronted object.

The author says regarding ﴿al-ajalayn﴾ ("the two terms"): "(i.e., his herding)." In fact, there is no need to supply this, because it is known from the context. Does Musa fulfil the two terms, or does he fulfil the herding?"

Student: "The herding."

Sheikh: "What is his work?"

Student: "Herding."

Sheikh: "Herding. So he fulfils the herding over the two terms. This is why the author said: (i.e., his herding)."

"But this is common in the Arabic language, and it is frequently the case that *ajal* (term) is used for the work itself. So the meaning is ﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾ [Al-Qasas 28], meaning: whichever of the two periods I complete by herding. The correct view is that the text stays on its apparent meaning, and it is said that ﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾ refers to herding, so that "herding" is omitted because it is understood. As for supposing that the object is *ri'yahu* (his herding), and that this is a figurative extension (*tawassu' wa majaz*), there is room for scrutiny.

And His words ﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾: the two terms we have now are eight years, which are obligatory, and ten, which are a voluntary extra for Musa. This is why He said ﴿And if you complete ten, it is from you﴾ [Al-Qasas 27].

The author says: (﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾ by it, i.e., I finish it.)

*Al-qada'* (fulfilment) in the linguistic sense means finishing something. From it is His saying ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [Fussilat 12], meaning He perfected them and finished with them. This is its meaning in the Arabic language.

As for its technical meaning, among the jurists *qada'* is what is performed after its time has passed. This is why they say that if a person prays the prayer after its time, it is called *qada'*. And if a person misses part of the prayer with the imam and stands up to complete it, they also call this *qada'*. This is why they say he recites a surah along with al-Fatiha, begins with the opening supplication, and seeks refuge, as though he has now entered the prayer. But the correct view is that *qada'* means completing and finishing something. The matter of prayer is explained by the words of the Messenger ﷺ in another narration: "Whatever you miss, complete."[[Al-Bukhari (636) and Muslim (602/153) from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "When you hear the iqamah, walk to the prayer with calm and dignity, and do not hurry. Pray what you catch, and complete what you have missed."]]

﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfil, there shall be no transgression against me﴾. Is *la* negating?"

Student: "No, prohibiting."

Sheikh: "Prohibiting?! Think again."

Student: "(...)"

Sheikh: "What do you say?"

Student: "*La* is negating."

Sheikh: "Prohibiting?"

Student: "Negating."

Sheikh: "What shows that it is negating?"

Student: "Because *la* (...) the verb."

Sheikh: "Yes. The prohibitive *la* is specific to verbs. And here, *ma* is also merely negating, negating the genus, which is why its subject is stated with it, saying ﴿there shall be no transgression against me﴾.

The meaning of *'udwan* is wrongdoing and aggression. That is, once I have fulfilled these things, there is no transgression against me in that, because I have completed the contract, and whoever completes the contract is not subject to aggression.

But what do you imagine as transgression in a contract like this?"

Student: "(...)"

Sheikh: "The author says: (by demanding more from him). This is correct. If the employer says to him, 'Add more,' this is transgression. Likewise, ﴿there shall be no transgression against me﴾ includes imposing on him what the mind cannot bear, such as if he asked him to herd the sheep at night and by day. Likewise there is no transgression against him by delaying payment of the wage. Yes, when the term is fulfilled, the contract is completed.

The point is that transgression is not limited to demanding more, but includes everything that contradicts the contract in general.

(﴿And Allah is Witness over what we say﴾, I and you, ﴿a Guardian﴾ [Al-Qasas 28], i.e., a Protector or Witness. Thus the contract was concluded by that.)

His words ﴿And Allah is Witness over what we say, a Guardian﴾: ﴿Allah﴾ is the subject, and ﴿a Guardian﴾ is its predicate. What is meant by *wikalah* (guardianship) here is both protection and witness together. His words "(or a Witness)" are for variety, not for doubt. But the more accurate view is that it is general, because Allah's *wikalah* over a thing means protection and witness.

Student: "Is *hafiz* (protector) not the same as (...)?"

Sheikh: "And witness (...). Fine, here I have it with *aw* (or)."

His words here ﴿over what we say﴾: placing it before its governing word, *wakil* (guardian), is known to indicate restriction. It is known that Allah is Guardian over every thing, not only over what we say. But it is restricted to this for increased emphasis. Otherwise there is no doubt that Allah is Guardian over everything. It is as if he is saying: if Allah were not a witness over anything, He would still be a witness over what we say of the contract that has taken place between us.

In this there is evidence that Musa ﷺ knew Allah and had the natural disposition (*fitrah*), even though he had not yet been made a prophet. For his words ﴿And Allah is Witness over what we say, a Guardian﴾ [Al-Qasas 28] are an acknowledgement by him of Allah, and of His attributes, that He is the Guardian over every thing.

Sheikh: "Is it apparent that there were no witnesses?"

Student: "Yes."

Sheikh: "Or not? Because he said ﴿And Allah is Witness over what we say, a Guardian﴾, meaning they had no witnesses to establish this contract. So would something like this suffice in our law, if we agreed with someone and wrote: 'And Allah is Guardian or Witness over what we say'? Would that suffice or not?"

Student: "It does not suffice."

Sheikh: "It does not suffice. This is why some people now argue against you, saying: 'Allah is witness to this.' We say: Yes, Allah is a witness, and an excellent witness. But let him give his testimony in a verse that shows the truth of what you said, or not? We say: Indeed, Allah the Exalted is without doubt an excellent witness, because His testimony is above everything: ﴿Say: What thing is greatest as testimony? Say: Allah﴾ [Al-An'am 19]. But we say: where is the verse from Allah the Exalted that testifies that such and such happened? Often, when zakat is given to us, a poor man comes and says: 'By Allah, I have nothing. Allah is witness that I have nothing.' He says: 'By Allah, He is witness of that.' He says: 'Will you not accept it from Allah?' What is the answer?"

Student: "Yes, I accept."

Sheikh: "I accept it. I accept it for Allah's sake. But bring a verse that shows that Allah is a witness to that. As for your mere statement, that does not exist. Everyone says, 'Allah is the witness.' Yes. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'If people were given claims by their assertions alone, some men would claim the blood and property of other people. But the burden of proof is on the claimant.'[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (4552) and Muslim (1711/1), and al-Bayhaqi (21201), the wording is his, all from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] So you, for example, bring it: if Allah sent down a revelation about this, or if a verse came to you showing your truth, then we accept Allah's testimony, which is above every testimony. But your saying that this is in your opinion is not acceptable."

He says: (The contract was concluded with that. Shu'ayb ordered his daughter to give Musa a staff with which to drive away predators from his sheep. The staffs of the prophets were with him, and Adam's staff of myrtle from Paradise happened to be in her hand, so Musa took it with Shu'ayb's knowledge.)

This is among the *isra'iliyyat* (narrations from Israelite sources) that should not be believed. Do we take from the verse that Musa ﷺ took a staff? There is no evidence in the verse that he took a staff or anything else. The contract was concluded with this, and he began to work for him.

Student: "(...)?"

Sheikh: "Yes, it is conditional."

Student: "(...)."

Sheikh: "The verb ﴿fulfil﴾ is transitive, and its object is *ayy*, like His saying ﴿Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ [Al-Isra' 110]. In ﴿Whichever you call upon﴾, but here we do not know if *ma* is negating? We do not know."

Student: "(...)?"

Sheikh: "No, he did not say the object is now. Its object is *ayy*."

Student: "Is there also ﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾ [Al-Qasas 28]?"

Sheikh: "The verse after it came: ﴿Then when Musa had fulfilled the term﴾ [Al-Qasas 29]. We have not reached it yet. It will come, God willing."

Student: "(...)?"

Sheikh: "It will come to us in the benefits, God willing. Is it permissible for the dowry to be stipulated from the father, or do we say that its reality returns to the daughter, since she gained a benefit: that she is spared the herding of sheep and the hardship in it?"

(...)

Sheikh: "...the hamzah (on the alif) prevented its appearance because of difficulty. Fine. He says: ﴿Do you await for us but one of the two best things?﴾ [At-Tawbah 52]. He did not say *ila ihda al-husnayayn*. Yes, this matter is clear and has no difficulty.

Fine. His saying ﴿Indeed the best one you hire﴾ [Al-Qasas 26] (...) specifies which action?"

Student: "The action of His saying ﴿Hire him﴾ [Al-Qasas 26]."

Sheikh: "﴿Hire him﴾."

His saying ﴿I want to marry one of these two daughters of mine to you﴾ [Al-Qasas 27]: is this a contract or a promise to contract? ﴿I want to marry one of these two daughters of mine to you﴾. Is it a contract or a promise of a contract?"

Student: "A promise of a contract."

Sheikh: "A promise?"

Student: "Yes."

Sheikh: "What is the evidence that it is a promise and not a contract?"

Student: "He did not say, 'I have married one of my daughters.'"

Sheikh: "'I have married you'?"

Student: "Yes."

Sheikh: "Rather he said ﴿I want to marry you﴾, and one who wants something may or may not do it."

Student: "Yes, and he may not do it."

Sheikh: "And he may not do it. So? Then the verse does not show that he concluded the contract with him."

Fine. But His saying ﴿That is between me and you﴾ [Al-Qasas 28] does it not show the contract?

Student: "It shows acceptance."

Sheikh: "That he accepted to marry him?"

Student: "Yes."

Sheikh: "Fine. What is the benefit of His saying ﴿these two﴾ [Al-Qasas 27]?"

Student: "(...) so if he says, for example, ﴿these two﴾."

Sheikh: "It specifies the intended ones who are present."

Student: "Yes."

Sheikh: "So that it is not thought that these two are not his daughters."

Student: "Yes."

Sheikh: "Fine. And His saying ﴿eight years﴾ [Al-Qasas 27]: what are the *hijaj*?"

Student: "That is (...)."

Sheikh: "*Hijaj* is from the pilgrimage to the Sacred House of Allah?"

Student: "No, *hijjah* means a year."

Sheikh: "A year? So ﴿eight years﴾ means eight?"

Student: "Years."

Sheikh: "Eight years."

Fine. His saying ﴿And I do not want to burden you﴾ [Al-Qasas 27]: in what?"

Student: "(...)."

Sheikh: "If we say this, we can then say: eight compared to six is a hardship."

Student: "His saying ﴿to burden you﴾ (...)."

Sheikh: "Yes, ﴿to burden you﴾ in the execution, and the meaning is not about the increase in years, because this is refuted by the fact that eight compared to six is an increase, and also he accepted the ten."

Student: "It is not objected that he (...)."

Sheikh: "Yes, it did not burden him, since (...) Musa had no hardship from the start."

His saying ﴿You will find me, God willing﴾ [Al-Qasas 27]: what is meant by this conditional?"

Student: "We might say the intended meaning is information, that (...), but the correct view is that it is on its apparent meaning, because a person does not know whether his matter will be completed or not."

Sheikh: "Yes, yes."

His saying ﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾ [Al-Qasas 28]: what is the grammatical analysis of ﴿Whichever of the two terms﴾? (...) What is meant by ﴿the two terms﴾?"

Student: "The ten or the eight."

Sheikh: "The ten or the eight. And is *ma* in His saying ﴿ayyama﴾ negating or superfluous?"

Student: "Superfluous, for emphasis."

Sheikh: "Superfluous for emphasis, and the estimated sense would be: 'Which of the two terms?'"

Student: "I fulfil."

Sheikh: "And is *ayy* here conditional or interrogative?"

Student: "Conditional."

Sheikh: "Conditional."

His saying ﴿Over what we say, a Guardian﴾ [Al-Qasas 28]: what is meant by *wikalah* here?"

Student: "*Wikalah* is protection."

Sheikh: "Protection. And witness?"

Student: "And witness."

Sheikh: "Fine. Placing the complement before its verb indicates restriction: ﴿over what we say﴾."

Student: "Yes."

Sheikh: "Although Allah the Exalted is a guardian over everything."

Student: "Yes, it is more eloquent in guardianship here. It is known that Allah is a guardian over everything, but it is more eloquent."

Sheikh: "More eloquent in preserving the contract."

Student: "Yes."

Sheikh: "Yes, more eloquent in preserving the contract. It is as if he is saying: if Allah were not a guardian, He would be a guardian over what we say."

Yes, now let us return to the benefits.

His saying: ﴿One of the two said: O my father, hire him﴾ [Al-Qasas 26]. Yes?"

Student: "Did the marriage take place at the start of the contract or at the end?"

Sheikh: "At the start."

Student: "At the start of the contract?"

Sheikh: "Yes."

- From the noble verse we benefit, first: the explanation that a person's counsel to his father is not considered belittling him, from her saying ﴿One of the two said: O my father, hire him﴾.

- And from it: the gentleness of this woman in addressing her father, from her saying ﴿O my father, hire him﴾. This is why they said: a person should not call his father by his name, saying for example: "O Abd al-Rahman, O Abd al-Aziz," and the like. Some even say that if he calls his father by name he is to be disciplined (*yu'azzar*, i.e., subjected to discretionary punishment), because it is a kind of contempt toward him. But speaking about him by name is fine. Speaking about him by name, such as saying, "So-and-so said," is not a problem. This is why we often hear in the hadith Ibn 'Umar say, "'Umar said, 'Umar said," and the like, and this is not objectionable. Unlike address, which has its own rules and speech about him has different rules.

- And from the noble verse we benefit: that for one who is in charge of something, whether he volunteers or is paid, the important thing is that everyone in charge of a work should have these two qualities observed in him: strength and trustworthiness.

Student: "(...)."

Sheikh: "Yes, there is no doubt. It may come. This is if you have not written it at the beginning."

Student: "We mentioned (...)."

Sheikh: "Yes."

- From this it is benefited: that one in charge of something should be observed in these two matters: strength and trustworthiness, because strength gives the ability to execute, and trustworthiness gives completion and perfection.

- And from the noble verse: that Musa ﷺ possessed these two qualities, strength and trustworthiness. For we said that this sentence is the reason given for her saying ﴿Hire him﴾ [Al-Qasas 26].

Then He said: ﴿I want to marry one of these two daughters of mine to you, on condition that you hire yourself to me for eight years﴾ [Al-Qasas 27].

Student: "(...)?"

Sheikh: "I do not know, but he should only address him with the title of fatherhood."

Student: "(...)."

Sheikh: "(...) What is appropriate is that he addresses him by name, although this is less than being called by name. Likewise, addressing someone by a title is fine, such as saying, 'O Commander of the Faithful,' for example. This is fine."

Student: "Some say: 'The old man (*ash-shayib*) came, the old man left'?"

Sheikh: "Yes, this is actually a mistake, because it is a kind of contempt. It is a statement, which is fine, but there is a kind of contempt in describing him as 'the old man.'"

Student: "(...)."

Sheikh: "(...) this, but apparently among the Bedouins it is not considered disobedience."

Student: "No, it is not considered; it is considered honour, meaning a mark of respect."

Sheikh: "Amazing!"

Student: "Yes."

Sheikh: "Yes."

Student: "Yes, the *shayib* is considered..."

Sheikh: "The leader of the people."

Student: "Yes."

Sheikh: "Fine."

Student: "Or (...) 'the father of so-and-so,' like one of my maternal uncles; I want to say to him, 'O father of so-and-so.'"

Sheikh: "The *kunyah* (teknonym) you brought up is what he asked about. I say that the *kunyah* is less than the name."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verses 24–28 (part 5 of 6):

Good. I say: ﴿He said, "I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine, on condition that you serve me for eight years"﴾ [Al-Qasas 27].

* From this noble verse we derive: the father's advice to his daughters. For when they described him as trustworthy and strong, he chose him. Likewise, a person should choose for his daughters someone who is characterised by strength and trustworthiness.

* From this also: the permissibility of a man proposing to a woman through her father, that is, you (the father) propose a husband for your daughter, although the usual custom is the reverse. But this is permissible. Also evidence for it is that the Commander of the Faithful (...) was aware of his (own) eagerness, in that he had heard the Prophet ﷺ mention her, so he did not wish to go ahead of him, as you know. Then the Prophet ﷺ proposed to her.[[Al-Tabarani recorded in al-Kabir (10305) from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "Allah commanded me to marry Fatimah to Ali."]] The point is that a person proposing a man to his daughter is a matter that is legislated and well known in earlier times and in this nation.

* From this also: the generosity of this man. Its aspect is that he gave Musa a choice, offering him the two daughters, saying: "Choose one of them." This is generosity, because in reality, giving someone a choice is broader for a person and more pleasing to his heart, so that he may choose what he sees as most suitable. But if he had said, "I wish to marry you to this daughter," the man might have had no desire for her. Whereas "one of my two daughters" involves a choice, which indicates generosity, and that he placed him in ease.

* From this: the permissibility of contracting marriage with an unspecified person, with the offer (ijab) alone and not the acceptance (qabul) being specific. That is, he says, "I marry you to one of my daughters," and the husband says, "I accept the marriage to so-and-so." This issue has three forms. Either the specification occurs in both the offer and the acceptance, so he says, "I marry you to my daughter Aisha," and he says, "I accept," and this is valid.

* A student: There is disagreement about this.

* The Shaykh: No, there is no disagreement. This is specification in both the offer and the acceptance. In the offer, the guardian says, "I marry you to my daughter Aisha," specifying her, and the husband says, "I accept the marriage of this woman."

Or the ambiguity is in both the offer and the acceptance, and then it is not valid. For example, he says, "I marry you to one of my daughters," and he says, "I accept the marriage to one of them." Here it is not permissible, and the marriage is not concluded, because we do not know which of them the marriage has been concluded to.

Or the specification is in the offer but not in the acceptance. For example, he says, "I marry you to my daughter Aisha," and the husband says, "I accept the marriage to one of your daughters." What is the ruling?

* A student: It is not permissible.

* The Shaykh: It is not permissible; it is not concluded.

We have remained with the fourth form. We said there are three forms, but in fact there are four.

The fourth form is that he says, "I marry you to one of my daughters," and he says, "I accept the marriage to so-and-so, naming her." Here the ambiguity is in the offer and the specification is in the acceptance. Is it valid or not?

* A student: It is valid.

* The Shaykh: The (official) school position is that it is not valid, because specification must occur in both the offer and the acceptance. But what appears to be correct is that it is valid, because when he said, "I marry you to one of my daughters," and he (the husband) said, "I accept Aisha," the specification has occurred, has it not? It has occurred. But the one making the offer, who is the guardian, wished to give him room to choose. So the apparent ruling is that the contract is valid, especially if he said, "I marry you to one of these daughters of mine," and indicated them, and he said, "I accept Aisha," and she is one of those indicated. This is also closer to validity, because here the specification occurred by what means? By gesture. Then he specified one of them by the acceptance. Can we say that this story is evidence for this issue? "One of my two daughters" [Al-Qasas 27], and Musa, in any case, accepted one of them. He accepted (...). Is there evidence in the story?

* A student: No, there is no evidence in it.

* The Shaykh: Why?

* The student: It happened before he was a prophet.

* The Shaykh: And also because he did not conclude the contract. He said, "I wish to marry you" [Al-Qasas 27], meaning, "so choose." Perhaps a contract was concluded afterwards, a new contract. We mentioned a little earlier that the intention to do something is other than doing it.

Can it be derived from this noble verse that the husband may conclude a marriage for his daughter without her consent?

* A student: The father.

* The Shaykh: I mean the father, yes. Can the father conclude a marriage for his daughter without her consent?

* A student: Yes, it is permissible.

* The Shaykh: Wait. The verse contains no evidence. The verse itself contains no evidence, since it is possible that the father had asked their permission beforehand, or that he understood their consent from the fact that they presented him (as a suitor) and described him as strong and trustworthy. In any case, even if we assume the possibility that he did not seek their permission, our law has come with the opposite: it is not permissible for a person to marry off his daughter without her consent, and if he marries off his daughter without her consent, the contract is considered null and invalid, not valid.

* From the noble verse also: the permissibility of the father stipulating for himself some of the bride-price. Is it permissible? Is it allowed or not?

* A student: In whose law, Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: No, we want to know: can it be derived from the verse that it is permissible for the father to stipulate for himself some of the dowry?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: To whom do the sheep belong?

* The student: To the father.

* The Shaykh: To the father. And their grazing?

* The student: To him.

* The Shaykh: To him. Here he is marrying (Musa) to him on condition that he serve him for eight years by herding sheep. So there is evidence that it is permissible for the father to stipulate the bride-price of his daughter for himself. This is problematic with respect to our law, because Allah says: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift; but if they, of their own accord, remit to you anything of it, then consume it with satisfaction﴾ [Al-Nisa' 4], and He says: ﴿Then half of what you have appointed, unless they forgo it or he in whose hand is the marriage tie forgoes it﴾ [Al-Baqarah 237]. These two verses indicate that the dowry belongs to whom? To the wife, who has the authority to dispose of it by forgoing or giving. The father has no right in that. The Sunnah also indicates this: whatever is stipulated or given before the contract belongs to the wife, and whatever is after it, the most deserving of honour that a man shows is his daughter and his sister.[[Abu Dawud (2129) recorded from Abdullah ibn Amr, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whatever woman marries for a dowry, a gift, or a promise, before the bond of marriage, it is hers; and what is after the bond of marriage belongs to the one to whom it is given. And the most honoured thing a man can give is to his daughter or his sister."]]

So the entire bride-price that is given before the contract must be for the wife. This is the correct view: the dowry belongs to whom? To the wife. No one shares it with her, because it is in exchange for her person, so it is hers. The father has no right to stipulate anything for himself from it. Yes, for the father, once the wife has given it and it has become her property, he may take from it.

* A student: She gives it to him.

* The Shaykh: No, she did not give it. She gives it to (...) that he may take possession of it from her, because the father has the right to take from his child's property what he does not need and what does not harm the child, by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "You and your property belong to your father."[[Ibn Majah (2291) from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] As for stipulating something for himself from it, no, for the law does not permit it. It is also a cause of corruption and of the father looking at the dowry: he may marry (his daughter) to whoever stipulates more for him, even if that person is not a suitable match, and prevent whoever does not stipulate for him, even if he is a suitable match. The interest and the law both require that it is not permissible for the father to stipulate anything of the dowry for himself.

Well, what about the mother and the brother?

* A student: It is a fortiori.

* The Shaykh: It is a fortiori. Now, the Bedouins, may Allah protect us, are contrary to this: the father stipulates something for himself, and the mother something, and the brother something, and the wet-nurse something, and the dog something, and the donkey they have something... and so on, and the woman is left with nothing of the dowry, like the donkey and the dog. This is not permitted; it is forbidden. The entire dowry must belong to whom? To the wife. No one has authority over it, except the father, who has authority over it. When?

* A student: After she has taken possession of it.

* The Shaykh: After she has taken possession of it, and it has entered her ownership. Then the father may take from his child's property what does not harm the child and what the child does not need.

Now, some scholars have used this verse to argue that it is permissible for a person to stipulate something from his daughter's dowry, the whole of it or part of it. We say to them: this is not valid, because our law came with what?

* A student: Its opposite.

* The Shaykh: Its opposite. Some scholars also used it to argue that it is permissible for the dowry to be a benefit that the wife enjoys from her husband, that is, that he work for her, build her a house, or bring her something absent. Is the inference clear or not?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Because herding sheep is a benefit to her. For if Musa had not herded them, who would have herded them? These two daughters. So in reality it is a benefit to her. Furthermore, our law came in agreement with it. The Prophet ﷺ said to the man who did not have anything with him: "I have married her to you," with what? "With what you have of the Quran."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5871) and Muslim (1425/76) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, may Allah be pleased with him.]] And this is a benefit. But if she stipulated that he serve her, that her dowry be his service to her, for example, this is an elderly woman who was proposed to by a man who has no wealth, or has wealth, and she says: the dowry is that you serve me, carry me for example so that I may perform ablution, and likewise (...) my shoes, and wash my garment, and similar things. Is this permissible or not?

* A student: It is not permissible.

* The Shaykh: There is disagreement among the scholars. Some say it is not permissible, because the husband's station should be higher than the wife's. The husband is a master, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they found her husband at the door﴾ [Yusuf 25]. The husband is a man, so he is a guardian over women: ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ [Al-Nisa' 34]. The woman is a captive with the husband, a captive: "Fear Allah concerning women, for they are prisoners with you."[[Al-Tirmidhi (1163) from the hadith of Amr ibn al-Ahwas, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording "Be good to women, for they are prisoners with you."]] And if we say that it is permissible for the dowry to be her service, the situation is reversed: the superior becomes the inferior, so it is not permissible. But the (official) school position is that it is permissible. Our school's position is the permissibility of this, because it is a benefit. Just as it is permissible for her to marry him on condition that he build her house and herd her sheep, likewise that he serve her. This reasoning does not prevent it. Yes: he serves her in what she has stipulated of him, and she serves him in what is obligatory upon her. So she is a servant and one served, like a preposition that governs a noun: the verb acts upon it, and it governs the noun, being both agent and object of governance.

* A student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: Perhaps she has wealth and expects that she will die before him and he will inherit from her!

* The student: Yes (...).

* The Shaykh: In any case.

* The student: Perhaps he will die before her?

* The Shaykh: Yes, he may die before her. But it depends on the situation. This is a young, poor man, and this is an elderly woman with great wealth, and he says: perhaps she will die before me and I will inherit from her. There is nothing contrary to my serving her.

* A student: Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: The permissibility of the father's stipulation.

* The Shaykh: It may also be for other than this reason. It may be to raise his status: this woman, for example, is from a well-known tribe, and he wishes to raise his lineage, because among people, for example, he may be considered not to be of a tribe, so if he marries this woman who is known to belong to a particular tribe, that becomes known. In any case, it is a consideration.

* The student: The permissibility of the father stipulating something from his daughter's dowry.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: Is it not refuted by the fact that (...)?

* The Shaykh: (...) this is not correct, because if the woman marries now, her sheep (...) for her husband to herd, the sheep would be lost. In any case, praise be to Allah, in our law it is contrary to this and does not permit it.

* From this verse also: it is permissible for a person to make one work into two works: one obligatory work and one voluntary work. Is it permissible? That is, he says: I want to rent this car from you for ten years, and twelve years from you? Is it permissible or not? It is permissible; there is no objection.
