Yes, and this is not a comparison, but what I mean is that He did not care for them and they did not overpower Allah, glorified and exalted.
* And from it: the wisdom of Allah, glorified and exalted; in that the destruction of Pharaoh and his people was by the water in which he took pride, when he said: ﴿O my people, is not the dominion of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Do you not then see?﴾ [az-Zukhruf 51]. Indeed, that which he took pride in became the place of his destruction.
* And from it: that Pharaoh perished along with those who perished; because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today We will save you in your body﴾ [Yunus 92] does not mean that he is alive and remaining; rather, what was saved and appeared to the people was only his body, so that it would be a sign for those who came after him. For the Children of Israel, as the scholars said, had been terrorized by Pharaoh, so if they had not gone out and witnessed him in his body, they would have had some anxiety: did he perish or not? But when they saw him, they became certain and the anxiety left them.
So he is perishing along with those who perished; due to His saying: ﴿so We cast them away﴾.
* And from it, i.e., from the benefits of the verse: that a person is required, either obligatorily or recommendedly, to reflect upon the end of the wrongdoers: ﴿So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾. From this verse it follows that we should take warning from the end of these people and not wrong as they did; for as long as the end of the wrongdoer is destruction, a person fears that he will be destroyed if he wrongs.
* And from it: that wrongdoing is prohibited; because it is a cause of punishment, and whatever is a cause of punishment is prohibited. Whether the wrong is against oneself or against others, it is prohibited in all its forms. Allah, exalted is He, said in the sacred hadith: "O My servants, I have forbidden injustice to Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another."[[Narrated by Muslim (2577) from the hadith of Abu Dhar, may Allah be pleased with him.]]
﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾ [al-Qasas 41].
* From this verse is derived: the wisdom of Allah, glorified and exalted, regarding the likes of Pharaoh and his people; that there is wisdom in their creation. For Allah is able to make a person upon guidance, but He, glorified and exalted, has the wisdom in bringing into existence such people who call to the Fire.
* And also derived from it: the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, regarding those He created by the command of Allah, and that they are a trial and a test.
* And from it: the affirmation of leadership in evil just as it is established in good. Observe this in the family of Pharaoh, and observe this among the Children of Israel: ﴿And We made among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient, and they were certain of Our signs﴾ [as-Sajdah 24]. So there is a distinction between one who leads people by the command of Allah, who leads them by His law, and those who call to the Fire.
* And also among its benefits: that calling to the Fire and calling to good both occur by speech and by action. Calling by speech and calling by action; which of them is stronger? Sometimes calling by speech is stronger, and sometimes calling by action is stronger. Yes, but in every case, calling by both is established, for a person calls people by his words and by his condition.
* And from it: the affirmation of the Day of Resurrection in His saying: ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾. It is called "the Day of Resurrection" for three reasons:
That people rise from their graves to the Lord of the worlds; that justice is established therein, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Anbiya 47]; and that the witnesses stand therein: ﴿Indeed, We will help Our messengers and those who believed in the life of this world and on the Day the witnesses stand﴾ [Ghafir 51]. So for this reason it was named the Day of Resurrection. Why was it named the Day of Resurrection?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: We have now mentioned three reasons.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...), do not rely on (...), as it may bring up issues that confuse him.
* And also, it is derived from the noble verse: that the family of Pharaoh have no helper in the Hereafter, and likewise those who are of their kind among the arrogant toward the truth; for they will not find anyone to help them against the punishment of Allah when it descends upon them on that day.
﴿And We followed them in this world with a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised﴾ [al-Qasas 42].
* It is derived from this verse: that the punishment of the family of Pharaoh continues until the Day of Resurrection through the evil remembrance of them; ﴿And We followed them in this world with a curse﴾; for everyone who mentions the family of Pharaoh mentions them with evil, hatred, and detestation.
* And also, from the benefits of the verse: the belittling of this world; for His saying: ﴿in this world﴾ is an indication of nearness, due to its low rank and because it is a "dunya." The word "dunya" is the feminine of "adna" (nearer, lower), and it derives from nearness both physical and figurative. As for physical nearness: it is because it precedes the Hereafter, so it is nearer to created beings than the Hereafter. As for figurative nearness: it is because of the deficiency it contains in all its perfections; there is no perfection in this world except that it is deficient. Indeed, if you reflect upon all worldly benefits and harms, you will find them mixed with harm and danger, even time itself, as the poet said:
"A day for us and a day against us, and a day we are grieved and a day we are gladdened."
If you reflect on this, you will find it constant. Yes, and on this basis we say: the world was named so for two reasons: physical and figurative nearness. Physical nearness: its closeness, because it precedes the Hereafter; and figurative nearness: that there is nothing in it (...) except that it is mixed with deficiency.
* And from the benefits of the verse: that the curse - and we seek refuge in Allah - which was distributed (...) will be upon them in the Hereafter; due to His saying: ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised﴾ [al-Qasas 42]; for "al-maqbuhun" means those who are removed and reviled, and "al-la'n" (curse) is expulsion and distancing.
* * *
Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses the Scripture﴾ [al-Qasas 43].
"Ataynā" means "We gave."
Know that Allah's giving, exalted is He, is of two kinds: a legislative giving and a decreed giving. What relates to the cosmos and creation is decreed giving, and what relates to the Law is legislative giving.
﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them﴾ [at-Tawbah 59] – this is legislative giving, and what is meant is the portion of the charities or the spoils.
Is His saying ﴿We gave Moses the Scripture﴾ legislative or decreed?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Or decreed, yes; because the sending down – the sending down of the Qur'an – is among the matters related to Allah's will, not to His law.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Acting upon the Book is legislative.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it would not be; because the origin of the sending down is decreed, relating to Allah's will and decree, but acting upon it is legislative.
And His saying: ﴿We gave Moses the Scripture﴾ – "Moses" is the first object of "ataynā," and "the Scripture" is the second object, and it is of the category of "ẓanna."
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: It is of the category of "kasā"; because if the first is not the subject and the second the predicate, then it is of the category of (...). If you say "Mūsā al-kitābu" – does it work? It does not work. So any two objects where one cannot be the subject and the other the predicate are of the category of "kasā," and whatever can be subject and predicate is of the category of "ẓanna."
And His saying: ﴿the Scripture﴾ – he says: (the Torah), and it is "fa'āl" in the sense of "maf'ūl," because the Torah was written; for Allah, exalted is He, wrote it on tablets and gave it to Moses.
And He said: ﴿after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ [al-Qasas 43] – it is related to "ataynā." Meaning: We gave him it after We had destroyed the former generations.
"Qurūn" is the plural of "qarn," and what is meant by them is nations; it may also refer to a period of time, the measure of which is a hundred years. So "qurūn" is sometimes used to mean nations, and sometimes to mean eras of time. Here, is what is meant eras of time or nations? Nations; because eras of time are not destroyed; it is nations that are destroyed.
(﴿We destroyed the former generations﴾: the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, and others.)
(The people of Noah.)
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: I have here "ʿĀd," do you have "ʿĀdan" or not?
* Student: (...).

Alright, they are: "the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, and others."

It was also said that the former generations include even the family of Pharaoh; because the Torah was not revealed to Moses until after Allah had destroyed the generation of Pharaoh and his people. It is said that it includes these as well, and some scholars inferred from it that no nation was destroyed after the Torah was revealed, meaning (...), and that this is among the benefits of His saying: ﴿after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ [al-Qasas 43]; because the destruction of earlier nations is past and gone, and there is no destruction after the revelation of the Torah.
In reality, whoever reflects on history finds that no nation was destroyed after the revelation of the Torah, no nation was destroyed; but does His saying, exalted is He: ﴿after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ point to this? This is the point of examination and discussion.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, no general destruction occurred (...); as for whether a general destruction did not occur, the important thing is this (...).
He said: (﴿clear evidence for mankind﴾ [al-Qasas 43] is a state of "the Scripture.")
Where is "the Scripture"?
﴿And We had certainly given Moses the Scripture﴾ – ﴿clear evidence﴾. "Baṣāʾir" (plural of "baṣīrah," which is the light of the heart), just as "baṣar" and "abṣār" are the light of the eye. The light of the heart is called "baṣīrah" and "baṣāʾir," and the light of the eye is called "baṣar" and "abṣār": ﴿So their hearing did not avail them, nor their sight﴾ [al-Ahqaf 26].
And His saying: ﴿clear evidence for mankind﴾ – the "al" here is for mental reference (al-ʿahd al-dhihnī), not for generality; because the Torah was revealed only to whom? To the people of Moses only, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Every prophet was sent to his own people specifically, but I have been sent to mankind generally."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (438) and Muslim (521/3) from the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] Take note of this.
Now, His saying: ﴿for mankind﴾ – does it exclude the jinn?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, in terms of obligation and binding, the jinn are excluded, for none of the jinn has been obligated by the message of any messenger; but in terms of action, the jinn may gain insight from it, as they said: ﴿O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path﴾ [al-Ahqaf 30]; for it is apparent that they had benefited from what was revealed to Moses just as they benefited from the Qur'an.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not obligatory upon them; because the Messenger says: "He is sent to his people," and the jinn are not from them.
And His saying: ﴿for mankind﴾ – I have mentioned that the "al" here is for mental reference, alright.
He said: (the plural of "baṣīrah," which is the light of the heart, meaning: lights for hearts), and likewise all the books that Allah, mighty and majestic, sends down are lights for hearts, because guidance is by them; and for this reason he said: (﴿and guidance﴾ from misguidance for whoever acts upon them).
The author's restriction "for whoever acts upon them" is not appropriate, and it is better to leave the verse on its apparent meaning: that the Torah is guidance. But this guidance is not benefited from except by one who is granted success; so it is guidance from misguidance without doubt, but does everyone benefit from it and be guided by it? No, as Allah said in the Qur'an: ﴿a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and criterion﴾ [al-Baqarah 185], and He said: ﴿a guidance for the pious﴾ [al-Baqarah 2]; in the first, guidance is in the sense of indication, and in the second, guidance is in the sense of granting success.
As for the Torah: if we say "guidance for whoever acts upon it," we have restricted the verse to the guidance of success even though it is unrestricted; and for this reason it is better to say: guidance from misguidance in every matter, as He said: ﴿clear evidence for mankind﴾; we say: and guidance also for mankind, but the guidance in the sense of indication is general, and the guidance in the sense of being guided – meaning a person is guided by it – is specific to whoever is granted success in it.
(﴿and guidance and mercy﴾ for whoever believed in it.)
Yes, (...) that the context requires specification, that it is mercy, but not for everyone; unless it is said: mercy, meaning a means to mercy; if we say that "mercy" means a means to mercy, it becomes general. We say: guidance in terms of knowledge, and mercy in terms of action; for whoever acts upon it is shown mercy. As for guidance, it is in terms of knowledge, as Allah said: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth﴾ [at-Tawbah 33]; so guidance is beneficial knowledge, and the religion of truth is righteous action.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, meaning it is not mercy to others; it is guidance; guidance is for everyone.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, that is not the apparent meaning; the apparent meaning is that if it were restricted as the author stated, because one is only shown mercy by it if he acts upon it; one is only shown mercy by it if he acts, only that.
﴿and guidance and mercy, that they may remember﴾ [al-Qasas 43].
Here "la'alla" means causation; as for its operation, it puts the subject in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative, and its predicate is the clause ﴿they may remember﴾. He said: (they admonish themselves with what is in it of admonitions), meaning with what is in the Book – which is the Torah – of admonitions.
﴿la'allahum yatadhakkarūn﴾ – the pronoun in "yatadhakkarūn" refers to those to whom the Torah was revealed, namely the Children of Israel.
Allah said to His Prophet ﷺ: (﴿And you were not﴾ O Muhammad ﴿on the side of﴾ the mountain, or the valley, or the place ﴿the western﴾ [al-Qasas 44] of Moses at the time of the communion).
﴿And you were not on the western side﴾ – "janib" means direction; the side of a thing is its direction or its edge.

And His saying: ﴿al-gharbiyy﴾ (the western) is an adjective modifying a noun that has been omitted. What is this omitted noun? The author said: "the mountain, or the valley, or the place." The "or" here is not for giving a choice but for distinguishing, since some say the intended meaning is the mountain, some say the valley, and some say the place. The word "place" is more general, because it includes being a valley or a mountain. As you know, Musa (Moses) descended from the side of Mount Tur, and he was in the sacred valley. So the verse (...) and what determines whether it is the valley, the place, or the mountain is the word (...). The western side of it, meaning as if He said: "from the western side of the mountain," so this is of the type of attributing the noun to its adjective, as when one says "masjid al-jami'," meaning "the congregational mosque."

On this last interpretation, the intended meaning is the western side of the same side: ﴿bi-janibi al-gharbiyy﴾, that is, "from the western side of the mountain." As for the opinion of the author, he says: ﴿bi-janibi al-gharbiyy﴾, "by the side of the place," with "western" being an adjective of "side," relative to Musa while he was speaking with Allah. Then we say: when Musa's face was toward the sky, what was his western side?

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: On the assumption of the west. If his face was toward the east, then his western side would be behind him, because for one facing east, his western side is behind him. Now I cannot picture whether Musa was beside the mountain from the east or from the north. In any case, "western" is a relative term. For example, Qasim may be to the west relative to one place and to the east relative to another place. Relative to Madinah it is to the west or south, and relative to Kuwait it is to the west.

The point is that you were not on that side (at the time of the intimate conversation, ﴿idh qadayna﴾, "when We decreed," meaning We revealed to Musa the command of the message to Pharaoh and his people).

﴿idh qadayna﴾: the author says "We revealed." Based on this, is the qada' (decree) legislative (shar'i) or universal (kawni)?

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: Good, it relates to the will, but the author made it legislative, because "qadayna al-amr bi-al-risalah" means "We commanded him with it." So he made "al-amr" a singular of "awamir" (commands), not of "umur" (affairs). If we make it the singular of "awamir," then the decree here is legislative.

It is possible that the intended meaning of "al-amr" here is the singular of "umur" (affairs), meaning: "We decreed to him that great matter, which is the message," as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura 52]. In this case, "al-amr" is the singular of "umur," not "awamir," and on this basis the qada' is universal (kawni).

The decree, as you know, is divided into two types: universal decree (qada' kawni) and legislative decree (qada' shar'i). The universal decree must have its object actually existing, while the legislative decree may or may not come to exist. The universal decree may be loved by Allah or disliked by Him, while the legislative decree is always loved by Him, because it means a command.

For example, the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book that you will surely cause corruption in the land twice and you will surely become arrogant with great arrogance﴾ [al-Isra 4]. This is a universal decree. Does Allah love it or dislike it? He dislikes it.

﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ [al-Isra 23]. This is a legislative decree, because if it were a universal decree, it would necessarily follow that all people worship Allah, and that is not the case. And "qadayna"...

Student: (...)?

The Shaykh: No, this verse (...). As for combining both, it is only possible in an event that has occurred. For example, if we say: "Allah decreed for Abu Bakr to become Muslim," this is a decree of destiny and legislative, because He commanded him to believe and he believed. And we say: "Allah decreed for Abu Lahab to believe," (this is legislative).

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: No, he may believe. This is a legislative decree and not a universal one. But "Allah decreed for Abu Lahab to disbelieve" is a universal decree. Yes indeed.

He said: ﴿idh qadayna ila Musa al-amr﴾ [al-Qasas 44]. According to the author's view, it is the singular of "awamir," and for this reason he said: "(﴿al-amr﴾) with the message to Pharaoh and his people." Or we say that "al-amr" is the singular of "umur," and it is (...) which is the message to Pharaoh and his people.

The author's statement is in reality open to interpretation, so the command of the message remains (...), and his intended meaning is the singular of "umur," so this (...) is for the message.

(﴿And you were not among the witnesses﴾ [al-Qasas 44], so that you would know it and then inform about it).

﴿And you were not beside Mount Tur﴾ [al-Qasas 46], ﴿and you were not among the witnesses﴾. Is there not repetition here?

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: No, they do not come from Allah the Exalted, because the original principle is that there is no repetition.

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: Yes indeed. We say: there is no repetition in the verse, because one who is beside a place may see or may not see. For this reason He said: ﴿and you were not among the witnesses﴾.

Now if someone says: why did He not limit Himself to His saying: ﴿and you were not among the witnesses﴾?

We say: it is the same thing, because a person may witness from afar without being close. So here it includes that he was near and that he was a witness. There is a difference between saying "you were not a witness," meaning you were not present or observing with your own eyes even if you were far away. For this reason there is no repetition in the noble verse, but there is some emphasis in it. That is: neither presence nor observation, as it says here. So the Prophet (ﷺ) was neither present so as to hear, nor near so as to observe.

So then, what he reported about that is from the category of revelation, not from the category of observation or hearing, but it is a revelation that was revealed to him.

Student: (...)?

The Shaykh: No, the revelation concerns the message.

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: Yes, this is contrary to (...).

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: As will also come (...).

He says: (﴿But We produced generations﴾ [al-Qasas 45], nations after Musa).

﴿We produced﴾, meaning We brought into existence and created nations. ﴿So the lifetime grew long for them﴾ [al-Qasas 45].

("Grew long" means it increased in length. The tā' and alif are for intensification.) The word ﴿al-umr﴾ (lifetime) means the time period, because lifetimes are periods of time. He said: (meaning: their lives were prolonged, so they forgot the covenants, the sciences were effaced, and revelation ceased. So We sent you as a messenger and revealed to you the account of Musa and others).

His saying ﴿But We produced﴾: the particle of contrast here does not imply cancelling what came before. The meaning is not: ﴿And you were not among the witnesses (44) But We produced generations﴾ [al-Qasas 44-45], so you witnessed. Rather, this contrast is for our understanding, and the meaning is that the covenants were long and you were neither a witness nor present. And since the covenants lengthened, people became in need of the message, so We revealed to you what happened and sent you to the people. And Allah knows best.

Student: (...)?

The Shaykh: This is it. It is said, and Allah knows best, that since it was in one land (...).

Student: (...)?

The Shaykh: Likewise (...), and these people, as long as they were in one land (...).

Student: (...)?

The Shaykh: This obligation, some scholars say that it is for the Prophet, that it does not necessitate (...), based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And on the Day He gathers them all together, then He will say to the angels﴾ [Saba 40].

(...) from Allah, because of the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We had certainly given Musa the Book﴾ [al-Qasas 43], and it is one of the three books whose effects remain: the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an.

* It is derived from this that the giving of the Torah occurred after the destruction of the earlier nations, including Pharaoh. Some scholars deduced from His saying ﴿after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ [al-Qasas 43] that no nation was destroyed in general after the Torah was revealed, because He said ﴿after We had destroyed the generations﴾, and it is as if after the Torah was revealed, no one from the generations was destroyed. This deduction is not far-fetched, because reality confirms it.

Student: (...) ﴿And We had certainly given Musa the Book﴾?

The Shaykh: No, we did not mention it.

Student: We mentioned these benefits in the explanation.

The Shaykh: Yes indeed, (...).

* It is derived from this verse that the books sent down from heaven are lights for people by which they are guided, because of His saying: ﴿as insights for the people﴾.

* Also among the benefits of the verse: that adherence to the laws of Allah brings mercy, because of His saying: ﴿and guidance and mercy﴾.

* Also among its benefits: that the books sent down from heaven are what bring guidance out of misguidance, because of His saying: ﴿and guidance﴾.

* Also among its benefits: that the wisdom in sending down these books is to remind people of the admonitions they contain, because of His saying: ﴿so that they may remember﴾.

* Also among its benefits: affirming wisdom in the actions of Allah the Glorified and Exalted, and likewise in His laws, because "la'alla" (so that) means causation, so it is derived from it that wisdom is affirmed in the actions of Allah and His laws.

Who denied wisdom? The Jahmiyyah (a sect that denied Allah's attributes and wisdom), who say that Allah the Exalted has no wisdom in what He does or legislates, and that He acts merely by will.

He said: ﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed to Musa the command, and you were not among the witnesses﴾ [al-Qasas 44].

* It is derived from this noble verse: the establishment of the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), by his reporting these events in which he was neither present nor a witness.

* Also among the benefits of the verse: that revelation is called a decree, because of His saying: ﴿when We decreed to Musa the command﴾.

* Also among its benefits: that revelation is of great importance, because Allah called it "the command" with the definite article (al-), which indicates greatness and perfection. There is no doubt that the greatest of matters is what the messengers brought from the revelation of Allah the Exalted, because of the benefit it contains for the lands and the servants.

* Also among its benefits: that a person's report is not accepted unless he was present and heard, or was a witness and saw, because of His saying: ﴿and you were not﴾ and His saying: ﴿and you were not among the witnesses﴾, since the one who can report is one who was present and heard, or who was near and witnessed. As for a person who reports without witnessing, presence, or observation, his report is not accepted. This is known from the Shari'ah from another direction, from other verses and other evidences: a person only testifies to what he knows by seeing, hearing, or other means of knowledge.

* * *

﴿But We produced generations, so the lifetime grew long for them﴾ [al-Qasas 45].

He said: ﴿And you were not dwelling among the people of Madyan﴾. We will leave the benefit for the end of the verse.

(﴿And you were not dwelling among the people of Madyan﴾, residing). The people of Madyan are the people to whom Musa (peace be upon him) came, and what he mentioned happened with him, such as his being hired, his marriage, and his journey with his family. So was the Messenger (peace be upon him) residing among the people of Madyan so that he could report what happened? The answer is no. Therefore, what came to him of the accounts of the people of Madyan came through revelation.

His saying: ﴿reciting to them Our verses﴾. (﴿among the people of Madyan, reciting to them Our verses﴾ is a second predicate.) Where is the second predicate? The phrase ﴿reciting to them﴾ is the predicate. That is: and you were not reciting to them Our verses (so that you would know their story and report it).

His saying ﴿to them﴾: the pronoun in the author's words apparently refers to the people of Madyan, and this also appears to be the apparent context of the verse: that it refers to the people of Madyan: ﴿reciting to them Our verses﴾ (so you would know their story and report it). Some scholars, meaning some exegetes, said: the pronoun refers to the Quraysh, meaning: ﴿And you were not dwelling among the people of Madyan﴾, so ﴿reciting to them﴾ is the story that you narrated with ﴿Our verses﴾. This is closer to the meaning, although the first is closer to the wording, because a pronoun refers to the nearest previously mentioned noun. But it would refer to the people of Madyan only with extreme strain. So the correct view is that it refers to the Quraysh, meaning: ﴿And you were not dwelling among the people of Madyan﴾, so ﴿reciting to them﴾ is the story that came with ﴿Our verses﴾.

So you are a messenger, because you brought what you did not witness, ﴿reciting to them Our verses﴾.

For this reason He said: (﴿But We were sending messengers﴾ [al-Qasas 45] to you and toward you with the reports of the earlier ones).

(﴿Sending messengers﴾ to you) to the people, (and toward you) by revelation. So the Messenger (peace be upon him) is sent to the people and sent to by revelation.

His saying: ﴿But We were sending messengers﴾.

(Kana, "was," is a past-tense verb, and it is stripped of time, and what is meant by it is the attribution of its subject to its predicate.)

His saying: ﴿But We﴾: this "na" is for the plural, and "kunna" is for the plural, and ﴿mursilin﴾ is plural, even though Allah is One, the Unique. But that is for magnification, because "na" is used for a speaker who magnifies himself, or for a speaker together with others, and here, without doubt, it is for the speaker who magnifies himself.

His saying: ﴿But We were sending messengers﴾, and He did not say "But We sent you," as He said in the verse before it: ﴿But We produced generations﴾ [al-Qasas 45], because the message continued among creation from the time they differed until the last of the messengers, Muhammad (ﷺ). And when did they differ? They differed after Adam, after generations had passed, perhaps ten or fewer or more, then people differed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Mankind was one nation, and Allah sent the prophets as bringers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth to judge between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqarah 213]. So the verse says: mankind was one nation, then they differed, and Allah sent down (guidance).

Student: Shaykh, the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And they did not differ except after knowledge had come to them﴾ [al-Jathiyah 17], what is (...)?

The Shaykh: That is by revelation. But this refers to the difference of the Children of Israel. ﴿Except after knowledge had come to them﴾ is about the Children of Israel. As for the first verse, ﴿Mankind was one nation, and Allah sent the prophets﴾, there is a reading in it that is not among the seven canonical readings: ﴿so they differed, then Allah sent﴾. This reading is indicated by His saying: ﴿to judge between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾.

(﴿But We were sending messengers﴾ to you and toward you with the reports of the earlier ones.) The benefit of mentioning the reports of the earlier ones to the Messenger (ﷺ) so that he would recite them to the people: the benefit is affirming that he is a prophet, because he did not used to recite any book before, nor write it with his right hand. So what he reported about those who came before is from pure revelation.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿And you were not beside the mount Tur﴾, the mountain, ﴿when﴾ at the time when ﴿We called﴾ [al-Qasas 46] Musa, that take the Book with strength.)

﴿And you were not beside Mount Tur﴾: this is another report, different from the first report, which concerns the beginning of revelation. After Allah destroyed the earlier generations, He promised Musa thirty nights and completed them with ten, and Musa chose some of his people and then went to Allah the Exalted for intimate conversation and the sending down of the Torah upon him.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And you were not beside Mount Tur﴾. ("Janib" means the direction of Tur, or the vicinity of Tur, and Tur is the well-known mountain in Sinai.)

(﴿When﴾ at the time when ﴿We called﴾.) The author informed us that ("idh," "when," here is not causal but temporal, and it is an adverb of past time. "Idha" is an adverb of future time, and "idhan" is an adverb of the present. With this, the three adverbs are complete: "idha" for the future, "idh" for the past, and "idhm" for the present.)

He said: (﴿When We called﴾ Musa, that take the Book with strength). Did Allah say to Musa, "Take the Book with strength"? Or to the Children of Israel when He lifted the mountain above them, saying: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ [al-A'raf 171]? It appears that the author was mistaken in this, yes.

Let us reflect further on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And enjoin your people to take the best of it﴾ [al-A'raf 145]. And what is before it? Look in Surat al-A'raf, what is the verse?

Student: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything﴾.

Shaykh: "And We wrote for him on the Tablets of everything an admonition and a detailing of all things. So take them with strength and enjoin your people to take the best of them" [al-A'raf 145]. So the author's statement, "take the Book with strength," is correct in meaning, though he expressed it in meaning rather than in wording. Otherwise, Allah says: "So take them" — that is, the Tablets which contain the Torah — "with strength" (فَخُذْهَا بِقُوَّةٍ). It follows that the command to Musa was to take the Tablets with strength.

In any case, the author's words are correct, but he expressed them by meaning, not by wording: "And We wrote for him on the Tablets of everything an admonition and a detailing of all things, so take them with strength" — that is, take these Tablets "with strength, and enjoin your people to take the best of them" [al-A'raf 145].

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "But [I sent you] as a mercy from your Lord" [al-Qasas 46]. We understand that His words "a mercy" (رَحْمَةً) is an object of purpose (مفعول لأجله), its governing verb being omitted, and the implied sense is: "We sent you as a mercy." His words "a mercy" do not mean that he himself is the mercy, but that he was sent for mercy, so that through him people might be shown mercy. Mercy comes from Allah, Glorified and Exalted, and He sent him as a mercy, as He said in another verse: "And We did not send you except as a mercy to the worlds" [al-Anbiya 107]. The meaning is not "And We did not send you except" in the state of being "a mercy," but rather: except for the sake of mercy. There is a difference between the two meanings.

"But a mercy from your Lord": He attributed lordship (الربوبية) to the Messenger ﷺ as a form of specification and honour, and this is the special mercy, while there is also a general mercy.

In it there is evidence — that is, in His words "from your Lord" — that the sending of the Prophet ﷺ to creation so that they may be shown mercy through him belongs to special lordship, because among Allah's blessings upon a servant is that He inspires him with guidance so that he may guide people by it; this is in reality one of the greatest blessings.

So the Prophet ﷺ was revealed to, so that he might show mercy to creation through what was revealed to him, and this is a requirement of special lordship. For this reason He said "from your Lord" and did not say "from their Lord," for "from your Lord" is the One who nurtured you with a special nurturing.

"So that you may warn" (لِتُنْذِرَ): is the lam here a preposition?

Student: It is the lam of causation (لام التعليل).

Shaykh: Yes, it is not a preposition, because it governs an implied (أن), meaning "in order that you warn," then it is converted into a verbal noun, becoming "for your warning a people." Therefore, according to the school of the Basrans, you say: the lam is a preposition, and "tundhira" is a present-tense verb in the subjunctive, governed by an optionally implied (أن) after the lam. According to the Kufans, they say the lam itself is the governing particle, and they say it is the lam of (kay) and it is governing. But the Basrans are more precise than them in this respect; indeed the reality is that the lam is a preposition, and (أن) is the governing particle, implied.

Now, where is the complement of "litundhira"? Its complement is this omitted element which the author estimated: "We sent you."

"To warn a people": warning (الإنذار) is informing about what is feared. This warning is informing about what is feared; and informing about what is desired is called what?

Student: Good tidings (بشارة).

Shaykh: Good tidings or giving glad tidings (تبشير).

As for His words "a people" (قَوْمًا), what is meant by them is the Quraysh. This does not mean that the Messenger ﷺ was sent to them specifically, but because the first whom he warned were the Quraysh; otherwise he was sent to them and to others. Allah the Exalted said: "Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant, that he may be a warner to the worlds" [al-Furqan 1] — to the Quraysh and others.

"So that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you."

"Ma" is negating, "atahum" means "came to them," "min" is a preposition that is superfluous in terms of grammar but not in meaning, and "nadhir" is the subject of (ataa): meaning, no warner came to them.

The benefit of adding "min" is to emphasize generality: in all past times, no one came to warn them before the Messenger ﷺ.

As for His words "so that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come": the clause "ma atahum" is in the accusative position as a description of what?

Student: Of "qawman" (a people).

Shaykh: A description of "qawman."

As for His words "to whom no warner had come before you," the author said: "They are the people of Makkah." This is an explanation of "qawman."

If someone says: Was not Isma'il a messenger?

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: Then he had come to them before the Prophet ﷺ, or not?

Student: The intended meaning is his descendants, and his descendants did not (...).

Shaykh: It may also be said: when the time lengthened until the traces faded, they became in need of a warner, and no warner came to them. So "no warner came to them" refers to after the traces of Isma'il's message had vanished. Otherwise there is no doubt that Isma'il was sent to them, because he was a prophet, but it had been effaced. For this reason, among the supplications of Isma'il and Ibrahim was that they said: "Our Lord, and raise up among them a messenger from themselves" [al-Baqarah 129], and the exegetes agreed that what is meant by this is Muhammad ﷺ. So from Isma'il until the Messenger ﷺ was sent, no prophet came to them, and the traces of prophethood were effaced. The first to alter it was Amr ibn Luhayy al-Khuza'i, for he was the one who introduced the worship of idols and introduced the sawa'ib (free-roaming beasts) among the Arabs, until the reality was obliterated through him.[[Ibn Hibban (7490) narrated from Abu Hurayrah from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who said: "The Fire was displayed to me and I saw in it Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qam'ah ibn Khindif dragging his intestines in the Fire, and he was the first to alter the covenant of Ibrahim and to institute the sawa'ib..."]]

Student: And they had no connection (...)?

Shaykh: No, they had no connection, because the message of Musa and Isa was to their own people, the Children of Israel.

"So that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, that they may remember" [al-Qasas 46].

"La'allahum" here is causal, and it is connected to "tundhira": you warn them so that they may remember, i.e., "be admonished" by what you have brought. We will mention in the benefits, if Allah wills, what its benefit is.

Student: The predicate of the negating "ma"?

Shaykh: It is not a predicate, because it did not enter upon a noun.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: No. "Min" is added to the predicate of "ma," but here "ma" entered upon a nominal clause.

Student: The rule on addition?

Shaykh: The rule for the addition of "min" is that if it is deleted the sentence is complete without it.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: The rule is that if you delete it here and say "ma atahum nadhir," it is correct, and this is the evidence that it is superfluous.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 39–46 (part 1 of 4):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And he and his soldiers were arrogant in the land without right﴾ [al-Qasas 39]. ﴿Arrogant﴾ (istakbara) is derived from al-kibriya', which means greatness. The meaning is that he and his soldiers rose up and magnified themselves. The addition of the hamzah, the sin and the ta' (in istakbara) is for emphasis (mubalaghah) and not for seeking (istid'a'); for the usual function of the hamzah, the sin and the ta' is seeking, such as (istaghfara lahu), meaning he asked for his forgiveness, and (istarhamahu), meaning he asked for his mercy. But sometimes it comes for emphasis, as in (istakbara), meaning he exaggerated in greatness and magnificence.

﴿He and his soldiers﴾: who are his soldiers? Al-jund (soldiers) originally means a man's retinue and helpers, and it is applied to everyone who follows him, so they are of his soldiers.

As for His saying ﴿in the land﴾, it is connected to ﴿and was arrogant﴾, and the (al) in (al-ardh) is for the mental (dhihni) reference. The author said: (the land of Egypt), not the whole earth, because he had no authority over the rest of the lands; rather, what is meant is the land of Egypt. Accordingly, the (al) here is for what? For the mental reference, not for generality.

As for His saying ﴿without right﴾, it is a clarification of the reality, because all arrogance opposes the truth; but it is a clarification of the reality to add to its ugliness. Arrogance is ugly, and when it is described (...) it becomes uglier and uglier.

A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿and they killed the prophets without right﴾ [al-Baqarah 61]. Could the killing of the prophets be with right? No; every killing of the prophets is without right, but He mentioned it for emphasis in condemning it, and in reality it is not right.

Allah says: ﴿without right﴾, and the haqq (right/truth) originally means that which is established. When it is attached to (...), what is meant is truthfulness, and when it is attached to rulings, what is meant is justice, as in His saying: ﴿And the word of your Lord is fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am 115]. So by their arrogance these people lacked the truth in two respects, since they took falsehood and deceit, and by what they were arrogant about.

﴿Without right, and they thought that they would not be returned to Us﴾.

﴿And they thought﴾: is the meaning of (thann, thought) here probability (rujhan) or certainty (yaqin)?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Those who were certain (...)?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: They did not deny (...), so shall we say the meaning is probability, meaning it was more likely to them that they would return, or certainty? Both in reality contradict His saying: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them﴾ [al-Naml 14]; for can one who is certain of a thing think the opposite? That he is certain that what Musa brought is true, does he become certain of the opposite, or think the opposite? No; for whoever is certain of a thing has believed in it. But it seems to me that the thann here is either in the sense of claiming, meaning they claimed that they would not be returned to Us, or that what is meant by it...

And its verb here is the verb of one who thinks.

As for His saying ﴿that they would not be returned to Us﴾ [al-Qasas 39], there are two readings: ﴿la yarji'un﴾ with the active form and ﴿la yurja'un﴾ with the passive form. How do I pronounce the active? ﴿la yarji'un﴾. And the passive: ﴿la yurja'un﴾. The pillars of the reading (...):

Every reading that agrees with the face of Arabic grammar, and that the script allows as a possibility, and that is transmitted soundly, is the Qur'an; these are the three pillars.

So here ﴿yarji'un﴾ (...) or not? That is, they differ only in the vowelling.

The meaning of ﴿yarji'un﴾ is: they return and are brought back to Allah the Exalted, for everything will return to Allah, and a person returns to Allah in his life and in his death. After death he returns to Allah, and likewise in this world his affair returns to Allah, for it is He who manages it.

﴿So We seized him and his soldiers﴾: the fa' is conjunctive, and what is meant by it is also causation; that is, because of his arrogance and that of his soldiers, We seized him ﴿and his soldiers, so We cast them﴾ [al-Qasas 40]. Look: in contrast to the arrogance, Allah mentioned their punishment in a manner of contempt and belittlement: ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers, and cast them﴾; for nabdh is to throw, and throwing means with force, and what is thrown with force, is it great or contemptible? Rather it is contemptible, for the great cannot be simply thrown; you cannot cast away the great (...). Only the lowly and contemptible is cast away, and for this He said: ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers, and cast them﴾.

(Them) refers to the soldiers, or to whom? To Pharaoh and the soldiers: ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers﴾, and these soldiers did not avail him anything, for nothing can confront Allah the Exalted with the strength of humans.

﴿And We cast them﴾ (We threw them).

﴿Into the sea﴾ [al-Qasas 40]. ﴿Al-yamm﴾: he said (the salt sea), to exclude what? The rivers; for rivers are seas but they are not salty. Allah says: ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, palatable, pleasant to drink, and that one is salty and bitter﴾ [Fatir 12], and He says: ﴿He released the two seas, meeting together﴾ [al-Rahman 19], so Allah called the rivers and the salty seas by the name of seas.

As for his saying (the salt sea), it is a clarification of the reality in which Pharaoh and his soldiers were found, for they were found in the Sea of Qulzum, or Qulzum, which is the Red Sea between Jeddah and Egypt, and this is where Pharaoh and his people drowned.

﴿So We cast them into the sea﴾. Consider the wisdom in Allah the Exalted drowning them in the sea: for Pharaoh used to boast of his rivers and say to his people: ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me; do you not see? Am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 51–52]. So he boasted of the water, and was drowned by it.

* Student: ﴿He said, O my people, does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flow beneath me?﴾
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿He said, O my people, does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flow beneath me? Do you not see?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 51], so Allah removed him from the kingdom of Egypt and destroyed him by what he had boasted of, the rivers.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes; for the salt sea is far from the kingdom of Egypt (...).

He said: ﴿So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Qasas 40]. ﴿So see﴾: the address is to whom? ﴿So see﴾ meaning: O Muhammad, or: ﴿so see﴾ O reader or listener? The address is to everyone to whom address may be directed. What do you say?

* Student: The last.
* Shaykh: The last, that is: ﴿so see﴾, O you who hear this address and to whom it is directed.

The seeing meant here is seeing of reflection (i'tibar), which is seeing with the heart, for the end is not seen with the eye, except when a person travels in their traces, when he may see with his eye and his heart.

﴿So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾: ﴿how﴾ here is interrogative, and what is meant by it is glorification, meaning because of the greatness of the end, but not the glorification of exaltation; rather the glorification of punishment, and we seek refuge with Allah.

﴿How was the end of the wrongdoers﴾: it is an emphasis of it and a magnification of an end that is dreadful and extremely evil. What is the grammatical position of ﴿how﴾?

* Student: An interrogative noun.
* Shaykh: An interrogative noun, built on the fatha, in what position?
* Student: Accusative.
* Shaykh: Accusative, yes.
* Student: Object of (see).
* Shaykh: Object of (see)! In ﴿So see how﴾, it is not valid to be the object of (see), for the interrogative must head its sentence; if we make it the object of (see), it would no longer have the front position of the sentence; it would be displaced.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, (...) with the object of (see), but I want only the parsing of ﴿how﴾.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Predicate.
* Shaykh: Predicate?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: That is not correct.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, its predicate is understood: ﴿So see how was the end of﴾, so ﴿how﴾ here is an interrogative noun (...) a predicate preceding ﴿was﴾.

Is fronting its predicate here obligatory or permissible?

* Student: Obligatory.
* Shaykh: Obligatory.

﴿How was the end of the wrongdoers﴾: ﴿end﴾ means ʻuqbā, and it has the form of the active participle, and what is meant is the final outcome.

And ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ are those who diminished the rights of themselves and the rights of their Lord, for injustice (zulm) originally means diminishing. Allah says: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therein at all﴾ [al-Kahf 33], meaning did not diminish.

As for His saying ﴿how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾, is the wrongdoers here meant as the disbelievers or not?

* Student: The disbelievers.
* Shaykh: Yes, the disbelievers; because it points to what happened to Pharaoh and his people, and they were wrongdoers with the wrongdoing of disbelief, for injustice is of two kinds: the injustice of disbelief, and the injustice of disobedience short of disbelief. In His saying: ﴿So for you is your principal; you do not wrong and you are not wronged﴾ [al-Baqarah 279] (...) it is the injustice of disobedience that is meant; and in His saying: ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 254] the injustice of disbelief is meant; and in His saying: ﴿And they did not wrong Us, but they wronged themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 57] it includes both, disbelief and what is below it.

(﴿So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾ when they came to destruction).

To destruction by the most trivial of things, which is water. This is part of the wisdom of Allah the Exalted, that He seizes each person for his sin, as Allah says in Surah al-'Ankabut: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ [al-'Ankabut 40], meaning according to what his sin required of punishment. The 'Ad were arrogant in the land and defied, saying: ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾. Allah says: ﴿Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15]. His saying ﴿who created them﴾ rather than saying that Allah (...) by being mightier than them, because the Creator is undoubtedly stronger than the created. By what were they seized? They were seized by the subtlest of things, which is the wind. Allah sent against them the wind, ﴿which He subjected against them for seven nights and eight days in succession﴾ [al-Haqqah 7]; all the days of the age; it was sent to them throughout all the days of the age. Had Allah willed, He would have sent it against them in a single night and destroyed them utterly; but for a wisdom He wished that they be punished more. He did not seize them all at once; He seized some (...) ﴿as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Qamar 20]. This is a more severe punishment, for if it had come to them once and destroyed them, they would not have suffered; they would have died and perished and the matter would have ended. But this is more severe.

So then, here they were drowned in the sea, for they, we seek refuge with Allah, (...).

He says: (﴿And We made them﴾ in this world ﴿leaders﴾ [al-Qasas 41] with the two hamzahs made clear), ﴿a'immah﴾, (and the second changed to a ya'), how is it said? ﴿ayimmah﴾, and the second reading here is one of the seven canonical readings.

He says: (leaders in disbelief), for the imam is the leader who is followed, so he, we seek refuge with Allah, has an effect in disbelief; and they were not merely leaders; they were leaders who were followed in disbelief.

* Student: (in shirk).
* Shaykh: (in shirk), yes, leaders in shirk, meaning followed. The imam is the one followed; the meaning is that they were leaders, we seek refuge with Allah, toward disbelief and polytheism.

But this, the author says: (﴿And We made them﴾ in this world ﴿leaders﴾).

Had he placed (in this world) later it would have been better, and said: (﴿And We made them leaders﴾ in this world ﴿calling to the Fire﴾ [al-Qasas 41]), for the reality is that their leadership in disbelief was when? In this world; their leadership was in this world; they were made in this world leaders, meaning followed and emulated in disbelief; so everyone who came after them, whose disbelief was out of arrogance, is an imitator of them.

As for His saying ﴿calling to the Fire﴾, it is not calling to faith. ﴿Calling to the Fire﴾: by speech or by action?

By both together: before they were destroyed they called by speech and by action, and after they were destroyed they call by action, for whoever people emulate by his deeds has in reality called them to it.

As for His saying ﴿calling to the Fire﴾, certainly they did not call people by saying: "O people, enter the Fire"; had they said that, they would not have been obeyed. But ﴿calling to the Fire﴾ means calling to the deed that leads to it, which is shirk and disbelief, and how evil was what they were leaders in: calling to disbelief in Allah, blessed and exalted, and associating others with Him.

Now, His saying: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾ [al-Qasas 41].

﴿And on the Day﴾ is an adverbial phrase connected to ﴿they will be helped﴾, meaning: they will not be helped on the Day of Resurrection. In this world they were followed leaders, but in the Hereafter ﴿they will not be helped﴾; they cannot help themselves, so they cannot be leaders who are followed.

As for His saying ﴿they will not be helped﴾, it means they will not find anyone to help them (by repelling the punishment from them); no one will repel the punishment from them, neither they nor others; even others cannot repel the punishment from them.

(﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾ [al-Qasas 41–42] ﴿And We followed them in this world with a curse﴾, disgrace, ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised﴾ [al-Qasas 41–42], the banished).

﴿And We followed them﴾: the pronoun refers to whom? To Pharaoh and his soldiers; ﴿and We followed them﴾ meaning: We made it follow them after their destruction. Curse (la'nah), originally, is expulsion and distancing; the author explained it by its consequence, which is disgrace, meaning that everyone who mentions them curses them, drives them away, and keeps away from them. But there is no contradiction between what is here and His saying: ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾ [al-Qasas 41], for the one who follows them is the one who agrees with their disbelief; as for the one who does not follow them, he curses them.

As for His saying ﴿a curse﴾, is it from Allah or from others? From Him and from others; Allah says: ﴿Those are whom Allah curses, and the cursers curse﴾ [al-Baqarah 159]; so whoever Allah curses, the believers in Allah curse. Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said concerning cursing the woman who plucks her eyebrows and the one who asks for it, he said: "And why should I not curse one whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed?"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (5943).]]

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised﴾.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is also an adverbial phrase connected to what?

* Student: With the Fire.
* Shaykh: With the Fire?! It is connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial state of (they), meaning: and they, in the state of being on the Day of Resurrection, are among the despised; or it is connected to "the despised" (...) what has preceded us: that (al) is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun does not govern what follows it with what precedes it; so either (al) is stripped of the verbal-noun sense, or this occurs by way of extension, because they extend with prepositional phrases and adverbs more than they extend with other things.

As for His saying ﴿they are among the despised﴾ [al-Qasas 42], He brought a nominal sentence indicating that at that time it is absolutely impossible for them to be praised for what they did or to be brought near; rather, at that time they are among the despised, banished ones whom everyone who mentions them disgraces, so no one can bring them near.

So, these people, we seek refuge with Allah, who used to call to the Fire, were punished with two things; rather, with three things:

The first: when the punishment befalls them on the Day of Resurrection, they will find no one to help them; for He said: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾ [al-Qasas 41].

The second: the shame that clung to them from the curse that clung to them until the Day of Resurrection; for His saying: ﴿And We followed them in this world with a curse﴾ [al-Qasas 42].

The third: that on the Day of Resurrection they can never be among the beloved and the brought near; rather, they are among the despised, the banished, the distanced (...).

* * *

(﴿And We had certainly given Musa the Book﴾ [al-Qasas 43]: the Torah), and it is a book in the sense of something written, and the sentence is emphasized by three emphases: the oath, the lam that falls in its answer, and (qad).

Here, someone might ask: why is it emphasized with these three emphatic particles, when it is not addressed to one who denies it?

The answer: we have already said that emphasis is not caused only by the addressee's denial. Its cause may also be the importance of what is being reported, so it is emphasized with an oath, with the lam, with qad, and with other emphatic particles.
(...)
* From this verse is derived: a clarification of the condition of Pharaoh and his soldiers, and that they are a people who are arrogant toward the truth and exalt themselves above it.
* Second, it is also derived from it: that whoever is arrogant toward the truth has some resemblance to Pharaoh and his soldiers.
* And from it, i.e., from the benefits of the verse: the obligation to submit to the truth. A person must submit to the truth, whether it agrees with his desire or opposes it.
* And from it: that the arrogant one has no right to arrogance; due to His saying: ﴿without right﴾.
* And also from it: that these arrogant people act as one who does not think he will return to Allah; for whoever thinks he will return to Allah will not be arrogant toward Him, since he fears Him. But the one who is arrogant is the one who thinks he will not return to Allah, glorified and exalted is He.
* And from it: the affirmation of resurrection; because His saying: ﴿and they thought that they would not be returned to Us﴾ [al-Qasas 39] affirms the supposition, which entails that the return to Allah is a established matter.
* And it is derived from His saying: ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers, and We cast them into the sea. So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾: that sins are a cause of punishment, because the fa' (...) indicates causation.
* And from it: the demonstration of the greatness of Allah, glorified and exalted; in that He seized these tyrants with their power and cast them away as one casts away a date pit from (...). Yes, and this is not a comparison, but what I mean is that He did not care for them and they did not overpower Allah, glorified and exalted.
* And from it: the wisdom of Allah, glorified and exalted; in that the destruction of Pharaoh and his people was by the water in which he took pride, when he said: ﴿O my people, is not the dominion of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Do you not then see?﴾ [az-Zukhruf 51]. Indeed, that which he took pride in became the place of his destruction.
* And from it: that Pharaoh perished along with those who perished; because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today We will save you in your body﴾ [Yunus 92] does not mean that he is alive and remaining; rather, what was saved and appeared to the people was only his body, so that it would be a sign for those who came after him. For the Children of Israel, as the scholars said, had been terrorized by Pharaoh, so if they had not gone out and witnessed him in his body, they would have had some anxiety: did he perish or not? But when they saw him, they became certain and the anxiety left them.
So he is perishing along with those who perished; due to His saying: ﴿so We cast them away﴾.
* And from it, i.e., from the benefits of the verse: that a person is required, either obligatorily or recommendedly, to reflect upon the end of the wrongdoers: ﴿So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾. From this verse it follows that we should take warning from the end of these people and not wrong as they did; for as long as the end of the wrongdoer is destruction, a person fears that he will be destroyed if he wrongs.
* And from it: that wrongdoing is prohibited; because it is a cause of punishment, and whatever is a cause of punishment is prohibited. Whether the wrong is against oneself or against others, it is prohibited in all its forms. Allah, exalted is He, said in the sacred hadith: "O My servants, I have forbidden injustice to Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another."[[Narrated by Muslim (2577) from the hadith of Abu Dhar, may Allah be pleased with him.]]
﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾ [al-Qasas 41].
* From this verse is derived: the wisdom of Allah, glorified and exalted, regarding the likes of Pharaoh and his people; that there is wisdom in their creation. For Allah is able to make a person upon guidance, but He, glorified and exalted, has the wisdom in bringing into existence such people who call to the Fire.
* And also derived from it: the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, regarding those He created by the command of Allah, and that they are a trial and a test.
* And from it: the affirmation of leadership in evil just as it is established in good. Observe this in the family of Pharaoh, and observe this among the Children of Israel: ﴿And We made among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient, and they were certain of Our signs﴾ [as-Sajdah 24]. So there is a distinction between one who leads people by the command of Allah, who leads them by His law, and those who call to the Fire.
* And also among its benefits: that calling to the Fire and calling to good both occur by speech and by action. Calling by speech and calling by action; which of them is stronger? Sometimes calling by speech is stronger, and sometimes calling by action is stronger. Yes, but in every case, calling by both is established, for a person calls people by his words and by his condition.
* And from it: the affirmation of the Day of Resurrection in His saying: ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾. It is called "the Day of Resurrection" for three reasons:
That people rise from their graves to the Lord of the worlds; that justice is established therein, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Anbiya 47]; and that the witnesses stand therein: ﴿Indeed, We will help Our messengers and those who believed in the life of this world and on the Day the witnesses stand﴾ [Ghafir 51]. So for this reason it was named the Day of Resurrection. Why was it named the Day of Resurrection?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: We have now mentioned three reasons.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...), do not rely on (...), as it may bring up issues that confuse him.
* And also, it is derived from the noble verse: that the family of Pharaoh have no helper in the Hereafter, and likewise those who are of their kind among the arrogant toward the truth; for they will not find anyone to help them against the punishment of Allah when it descends upon them on that day.
﴿And We followed them in this world with a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised﴾ [al-Qasas 42].
* It is derived from this verse: that the punishment of the family of Pharaoh continues until the Day of Resurrection through the evil remembrance of them; ﴿And We followed them in this world with a curse﴾; for everyone who mentions the family of Pharaoh mentions them with evil, hatred, and detestation.
* And also, from the benefits of the verse: the belittling of this world; for His saying: ﴿in this world﴾ is an indication of nearness, due to its low rank and because it is a "dunya." The word "dunya" is the feminine of "adna" (nearer, lower), and it derives from nearness both physical and figurative. As for physical nearness: it is because it precedes the Hereafter, so it is nearer to created beings than the Hereafter. As for figurative nearness: it is because of the deficiency it contains in all its perfections; there is no perfection in this world except that it is deficient. Indeed, if you reflect upon all worldly benefits and harms, you will find them mixed with harm and danger, even time itself, as the poet said:
"A day for us and a day against us, and a day we are grieved and a day we are gladdened."
If you reflect on this, you will find it constant. Yes, and on this basis we say: the world was named so for two reasons: physical and figurative nearness. Physical nearness: its closeness, because it precedes the Hereafter; and figurative nearness: that there is nothing in it (...) except that it is mixed with deficiency.
* And from the benefits of the verse: that the curse - and we seek refuge in Allah - which was distributed (...) will be upon them in the Hereafter; due to His saying: ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised﴾ [al-Qasas 42]; for "al-maqbuhun" means those who are removed and reviled, and "al-la'n" (curse) is expulsion and distancing.
* * *
Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses the Scripture﴾ [al-Qasas 43].
"Ataynā" means "We gave."
Know that Allah's giving, exalted is He, is of two kinds: a legislative giving and a decreed giving. What relates to the cosmos and creation is decreed giving, and what relates to the Law is legislative giving.
﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them﴾ [at-Tawbah 59] – this is legislative giving, and what is meant is the portion of the charities or the spoils.
Is His saying ﴿We gave Moses the Scripture﴾ legislative or decreed?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Or decreed, yes; because the sending down – the sending down of the Qur'an – is among the matters related to Allah's will, not to His law.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Acting upon the Book is legislative.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it would not be; because the origin of the sending down is decreed, relating to Allah's will and decree, but acting upon it is legislative.
And His saying: ﴿We gave Moses the Scripture﴾ – "Moses" is the first object of "ataynā," and "the Scripture" is the second object, and it is of the category of "ẓanna."
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: It is of the category of "kasā"; because if the first is not the subject and the second the predicate, then it is of the category of (...). If you say "Mūsā al-kitābu" – does it work? It does not work. So any two objects where one cannot be the subject and the other the predicate are of the category of "kasā," and whatever can be subject and predicate is of the category of "ẓanna."
And His saying: ﴿the Scripture﴾ – he says: (the Torah), and it is "fa'āl" in the sense of "maf'ūl," because the Torah was written; for Allah, exalted is He, wrote it on tablets and gave it to Moses.
And He said: ﴿after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ [al-Qasas 43] – it is related to "ataynā." Meaning: We gave him it after We had destroyed the former generations.
"Qurūn" is the plural of "qarn," and what is meant by them is nations; it may also refer to a period of time, the measure of which is a hundred years. So "qurūn" is sometimes used to mean nations, and sometimes to mean eras of time. Here, is what is meant eras of time or nations? Nations; because eras of time are not destroyed; it is nations that are destroyed.
(﴿We destroyed the former generations﴾: the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, and others.)
(The people of Noah.)
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: I have here "ʿĀd," do you have "ʿĀdan" or not?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: There is no doubt about it (...); the correct form is to say: "the people of Noah, ʿĀdan, and Thamūd," but as for "Thamūd," it is not declined; but the discussion is about "ʿĀd" (...) an explanation of "qurūn."
Alright, they are: "the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, and others."
These are the former generations, and Allah, exalted is He, only said: ﴿after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ to indicate that people were in need of a scripture such as the one revealed to Moses; because the generations had been destroyed and much time had passed, so people needed a message, and Allah sent Moses with this Book, which is the Torah.
It was also said that the former generations include even the family of Pharaoh; because the Torah was not revealed to Moses until after Allah had destroyed the generation of Pharaoh and his people. It is said that it includes these as well, and some scholars inferred from it that no nation was destroyed after the Torah was revealed, meaning (...), and that this is among the benefits of His saying: ﴿after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ [al-Qasas 43]; because the destruction of earlier nations is past and gone, and there is no destruction after the revelation of the Torah.
In reality, whoever reflects on history finds that no nation was destroyed after the revelation of the Torah, no nation was destroyed; but does His saying, exalted is He: ﴿after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ point to this? This is the point of examination and discussion.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, no general destruction occurred (...); as for whether a general destruction did not occur, the important thing is this (...).
He said: (﴿clear evidence for mankind﴾ [al-Qasas 43] is a state of "the Scripture.")
Where is "the Scripture"?
﴿And We had certainly given Moses the Scripture﴾ – ﴿clear evidence﴾. "Baṣāʾir" (plural of "baṣīrah," which is the light of the heart), just as "baṣar" and "abṣār" are the light of the eye. The light of the heart is called "baṣīrah" and "baṣāʾir," and the light of the eye is called "baṣar" and "abṣār": ﴿So their hearing did not avail them, nor their sight﴾ [al-Ahqaf 26].
And His saying: ﴿clear evidence for mankind﴾ – the "al" here is for mental reference (al-ʿahd al-dhihnī), not for generality; because the Torah was revealed only to whom? To the people of Moses only, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Every prophet was sent to his own people specifically, but I have been sent to mankind generally."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (438) and Muslim (521/3) from the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] Take note of this.
Now, His saying: ﴿for mankind﴾ – does it exclude the jinn?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, in terms of obligation and binding, the jinn are excluded, for none of the jinn has been obligated by the message of any messenger; but in terms of action, the jinn may gain insight from it, as they said: ﴿O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path﴾ [al-Ahqaf 30]; for it is apparent that they had benefited from what was revealed to Moses just as they benefited from the Qur'an.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not obligatory upon them; because the Messenger says: "He is sent to his people," and the jinn are not from them.
And His saying: ﴿for mankind﴾ – I have mentioned that the "al" here is for mental reference, alright.
He said: (the plural of "baṣīrah," which is the light of the heart, meaning: lights for hearts), and likewise all the books that Allah, mighty and majestic, sends down are lights for hearts, because guidance is by them; and for this reason he said: (﴿and guidance﴾ from misguidance for whoever acts upon them).
The author's restriction "for whoever acts upon them" is not appropriate, and it is better to leave the verse on its apparent meaning: that the Torah is guidance. But this guidance is not benefited from except by one who is granted success; so it is guidance from misguidance without doubt, but does everyone benefit from it and be guided by it? No, as Allah said in the Qur'an: ﴿a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and criterion﴾ [al-Baqarah 185], and He said: ﴿a guidance for the pious﴾ [al-Baqarah 2]; in the first, guidance is in the sense of indication, and in the second, guidance is in the sense of granting success.
As for the Torah: if we say "guidance for whoever acts upon it," we have restricted the verse to the guidance of success even though it is unrestricted; and for this reason it is better to say: guidance from misguidance in every matter, as He said: ﴿clear evidence for mankind﴾; we say: and guidance also for mankind, but the guidance in the sense of indication is general, and the guidance in the sense of being guided – meaning a person is guided by it – is specific to whoever is granted success in it.
(﴿and guidance and mercy﴾ for whoever believed in it.)
Yes, (...) that the context requires specification, that it is mercy, but not for everyone; unless it is said: mercy, meaning a means to mercy; if we say that "mercy" means a means to mercy, it becomes general. We say: guidance in terms of knowledge, and mercy in terms of action; for whoever acts upon it is shown mercy. As for guidance, it is in terms of knowledge, as Allah said: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth﴾ [at-Tawbah 33]; so guidance is beneficial knowledge, and the religion of truth is righteous action.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, meaning it is not mercy to others; it is guidance; guidance is for everyone.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, that is not the apparent meaning; the apparent meaning is that if it were restricted as the author stated, because one is only shown mercy by it if he acts upon it; one is only shown mercy by it if he acts, only that.
﴿and guidance and mercy, that they may remember﴾ [al-Qasas 43].
Here "la'alla" means causation; as for its operation, it puts the subject in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative, and its predicate is the clause ﴿they may remember﴾. He said: (they admonish themselves with what is in it of admonitions), meaning with what is in the Book – which is the Torah – of admonitions.
﴿la'allahum yatadhakkarūn﴾ – the pronoun in "yatadhakkarūn" refers to those to whom the Torah was revealed, namely the Children of Israel.
Allah said to His Prophet ﷺ: (﴿And you were not﴾ O Muhammad ﴿on the side of﴾ the mountain, or the valley, or the place ﴿the western﴾ [al-Qasas 44] of Moses at the time of the communion).
﴿And you were not on the western side﴾ – "janib" means direction; the side of a thing is its direction or its edge.

And His saying: ﴿al-gharbiyy﴾ (the western) is an adjective modifying a noun that has been omitted. What is this omitted noun? The author said: "the mountain, or the valley, or the place." The "or" here is not for giving a choice but for distinguishing, since some say the intended meaning is the mountain, some say the valley, and some say the place. The word "place" is more general, because it includes being a valley or a mountain. As you know, Musa (Moses) descended from the side of Mount Tur, and he was in the sacred valley. So the verse (...) and what determines whether it is the valley, the place, or the mountain is the word (...). The western side of it, meaning as if He said: "from the western side of the mountain," so this is of the type of attributing the noun to its adjective, as when one says "masjid al-jami'," meaning "the congregational mosque."

On this last interpretation, the intended meaning is the western side of the same side: ﴿bi-janibi al-gharbiyy﴾, that is, "from the western side of the mountain." As for the opinion of the author, he says: ﴿bi-janibi al-gharbiyy﴾, "by the side of the place," with "western" being an adjective of "side," relative to Musa while he was speaking with Allah. Then we say: when Musa's face was toward the sky, what was his western side?

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: On the assumption of the west. If his face was toward the east, then his western side would be behind him, because for one facing east, his western side is behind him. Now I cannot picture whether Musa was beside the mountain from the east or from the north. In any case, "western" is a relative term. For example, Qasim may be to the west relative to one place and to the east relative to another place. Relative to Madinah it is to the west or south, and relative to Kuwait it is to the west.

The point is that you were not on that side (at the time of the intimate conversation, ﴿idh qadayna﴾, "when We decreed," meaning We revealed to Musa the command of the message to Pharaoh and his people).

﴿idh qadayna﴾: the author says "We revealed." Based on this, is the qada' (decree) legislative (shar'i) or universal (kawni)?

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: Good, it relates to the will, but the author made it legislative, because "qadayna al-amr bi-al-risalah" means "We commanded him with it." So he made "al-amr" a singular of "awamir" (commands), not of "umur" (affairs). If we make it the singular of "awamir," then the decree here is legislative.

It is possible that the intended meaning of "al-amr" here is the singular of "umur" (affairs), meaning: "We decreed to him that great matter, which is the message," as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura 52]. In this case, "al-amr" is the singular of "umur," not "awamir," and on this basis the qada' is universal (kawni).

The decree, as you know, is divided into two types: universal decree (qada' kawni) and legislative decree (qada' shar'i). The universal decree must have its object actually existing, while the legislative decree may or may not come to exist. The universal decree may be loved by Allah or disliked by Him, while the legislative decree is always loved by Him, because it means a command.

For example, the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book that you will surely cause corruption in the land twice and you will surely become arrogant with great arrogance﴾ [al-Isra 4]. This is a universal decree. Does Allah love it or dislike it? He dislikes it.

﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ [al-Isra 23]. This is a legislative decree, because if it were a universal decree, it would necessarily follow that all people worship Allah, and that is not the case. And "qadayna"...

Student: (...)?

The Shaykh: No, this verse (...). As for combining both, it is only possible in an event that has occurred. For example, if we say: "Allah decreed for Abu Bakr to become Muslim," this is a decree of destiny and legislative, because He commanded him to believe and he believed. And we say: "Allah decreed for Abu Lahab to believe," (this is legislative).

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: No, he may believe. This is a legislative decree and not a universal one. But "Allah decreed for Abu Lahab to disbelieve" is a universal decree. Yes indeed.
